source: PubMed (NCBI E-utilities). Summaries written from abstracts only.
disclaimer: General information from published research, not medical advice. Talk to your doctor or midwife about your situation.

topics.label: Folic acid before and in pregnancy
Sleep and sleep position in pregnancy
Food safety and fish in pregnancy
Lifestyle, stress and supplements during IVF
Mood and brain fog in menopause
Weight, heart and metabolism after menopause

items.title: Preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidies (abnormal number of chromosomes) in in vitro fertilisation
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 13 trials with 2794 women to see whether testing embryos for an abnormal number of chromosomes (PGT-A) during IVF improves the chance of a baby. For the newer testing methods, it is uncertain whether PGT-A helps, because few trials exist and the evidence is low quality. The older FISH-based method probably lowered live births after the first transfer. The authors conclude there is not enough good evidence to support routine use of PGT-A.
keyPoints: For newer genome-wide testing methods, it is uncertain whether PGT-A increases the chance of a live birth (low-quality evidence).
PGT-A done with the older FISH method probably reduces live births after the first embryo transfer and probably reduces clinical pregnancies (moderate-quality evidence).
There is probably little or no difference in miscarriage rate with the FISH method; results for newer methods are uncertain.
Women should know it is uncertain whether PGT-A is an effective add-on to IVF, given its invasiveness and costs.

items.title: Advanced Maternal Age: Adverse Outcomes of Pregnancy, A Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review combined ten studies of single-baby, naturally conceived pregnancies to compare women aged 35 and over with women aged 20 to 34. Older mothers were more likely to have gestational diabetes, high blood pressure in pregnancy, induced labour, planned caesarean births, preterm birth, low birthweight babies and baby intensive care admission. Rates of stillbirth and perinatal death were also higher, and the risks were greater again in women over 40 than in women aged 35 to 40. The authors note that these risks may partly reflect age-related health conditions, but age appears to be a risk factor on its own too.
keyPoints: Women aged 35 and over were more likely to be overweight and to have gestational diabetes and gestational hypertension.
They had more induced labours and planned caesarean births, and more preterm births and low birthweight babies.
Babies of older mothers were more often admitted to neonatal intensive care and had lower Apgar scores.
Stillbirth and perinatal death rates were higher, and worse outcomes were more common in the oldest group (over 40).

items.title: No-271-Delayed Child-Bearing
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline looks at what is known about having children later in life. It says that a woman's age is the most important factor in fertility, and that medical risks in pregnancy and birth rise with age. Many women are not aware of the real success rates and limits of fertility treatments (assisted reproductive technology). The guideline aims to help doctors counsel women about their reproductive choices.
keyPoints: Maternal age is the most important factor in fertility.
Risks in pregnancy and birth increase with maternal age, including multiple births, preterm delivery, stillbirth and Caesarean section.
Delayed child-bearing is linked to a higher chance of infertility and pregnancy complications.
Many women do not know the success rates or limits of assisted reproductive technology.

items.title: Prevention of alcohol exposed pregnancies in Europe: the FAR SEAS guidelines
items.summary: These European guidelines look at how to prevent babies being exposed to alcohol in the womb, which can cause lifelong problems called fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASD). The authors built 23 recommendations from a review of existing programmes, advice from international experts and a pilot project in Poland. They stress that support should respect women's choices and avoid blame or stigma, and that help should fit each woman's level of need.
keyPoints: Drinking during pregnancy is described as the leading cause of birth defects and child developmental disorders in Europe.
Recommendations call for screening all women of childbearing age for alcohol use, along with other risks such as domestic violence.
Women who need more help, such as those with alcohol use disorders, should get individual, multidisciplinary support, and their partners should be included.
Public health messages should combine information about risks with encouraging messages that help people feel able to change.

items.title: Psychosocial and medication interventions to stop or reduce alcohol consumption during pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at eight trials (1369 pregnant women) testing ways to help women stop or cut down on alcohol during pregnancy. All of the trials tested talking-based support, mostly brief sessions, and none tested medications. Brief support may help more women stay completely alcohol-free than usual care, but the evidence is low certainty. The effect on how many drinks women had per day is very uncertain, and none of the studies looked at side effects.
keyPoints: Brief talking-based (psychosocial) support may increase the number of women who stay completely alcohol-free during pregnancy compared with usual care (low certainty evidence).
The effect on the number of drinks per day is very uncertain (very low certainty evidence).
Brief support probably makes little to no difference to how many women complete the treatment (moderate certainty evidence).
No trials tested medications for alcohol problems in pregnancy, and none reported adverse events, so more research is needed.

items.title: Guideline No. 405: Screening and Counselling for Alcohol Consumption During Pregnancy
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline sets out how health care providers should ask women of child-bearing age and pregnant women about alcohol, and how to support them. It recommends using validated screening tools and short counselling conversations (brief interventions). The aim is for providers to notice alcohol use and problem drinking earlier and help women reach the healthiest pregnancy possible. The abstract does not list the individual recommendations or their evidence ratings.
keyPoints: Pregnant women and women who could become pregnant should be asked about alcohol use and possible alcohol use disorder.
Validated screening tools and brief intervention approaches are recommended for providers.
The goal is for providers to feel confident and skilled in supporting women with alcohol use so they can reach the best health and pregnancy outcomes.
The guideline drew on trials, observational studies, reviews and consensus statements published between 2010 and September 2018.

items.title: High feedback versus low feedback of prenatal ultrasound for reducing maternal anxiety and improving maternal health behaviour in pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review compared two ways of running a pregnancy ultrasound: 'high feedback' (the woman sees the screen and gets detailed explanations) and 'low feedback' (she cannot see the screen and only gets a short summary). Four small trials with 365 women were included. High feedback did not clearly change anxiety. One small study found women given high feedback were more likely to stop smoking and avoid alcohol, but the evidence was low quality, so overall the review could not say which approach is better.
keyPoints: Three trials (346 women) found no clear difference in anxiety scores between high and low feedback during ultrasound.
One small study (129 women) found women given high feedback were more likely to stop smoking and to avoid alcohol in pregnancy.
The evidence was rated low quality, because of unclear risk of bias and wide uncertainty in the results.
The authors concluded there is not enough evidence to support either high or low feedback to reduce anxiety or promote healthy behaviour.

items.title: Individualised gonadotropin dose selection using markers of ovarian reserve for women undergoing in vitro fertilisation plus intracytoplasmic sperm injection (IVF/ICSI)
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 26 trials (8,520 women) of IVF/ICSI to see whether choosing the daily FSH hormone dose using ovarian reserve tests, such as AMH, antral follicle count or basal FSH, leads to better results. It is unclear whether dose-tailoring raises the chance of a live birth or ongoing pregnancy. Tailoring may lower the chance of moderate or severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), but the evidence is low certainty and the size of the effect is uncertain.
keyPoints: Using an ovarian-reserve-based dosing plan compared with a standard dose may or may not increase live birth or ongoing pregnancy (low-certainty evidence).
Ovarian-reserve-based dosing may reduce moderate or severe OHSS; for example, a 5% chance with standard dosing might fall to between 2% and 5%.
The evidence does not clearly support changing the standard 150 IU dose in predicted poor or normal responders, and higher doses mean more medication and cost.
Studies used different dosing plans, and some plans may work better than others.

items.title: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) treatment of the ovaries significantly improves fertility parameters and reproductive outcomes in diminished ovarian reserve patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 38 studies (2,256 women with diminished ovarian reserve) that looked at platelet-rich plasma (PRP) treatment of the ovaries. After treatment, AMH levels went up, FSH levels went down, and women had more antral follicles, retrieved eggs and embryos. Some women also became pregnant, including a small share who conceived naturally. Most studies were observational (not randomised trials), and the authors say larger, better trials are needed to confirm the results.
keyPoints: AMH rose and FSH fell after PRP ovarian treatment, with changes seen at 1, 2 and 3 months.
Antral follicle count, retrieved eggs and embryos created all increased on average.
Spontaneous pregnancy rate was about 7%, biochemical pregnancy about 18% and live birth about 11%.
The studies were mostly observational with no comparison group other than the women's own earlier results, so larger randomised trials are still needed.

items.title: Evidence-based guideline: premature ovarian insufficiency†‡
items.summary: This international guideline, from several fertility and menopause societies, sets out how premature ovarian insufficiency (POI, when the ovaries stop working normally before age 40) should be diagnosed and managed. It gives 145 recommendations covering symptoms, causes, long-term health effects and treatment. New data suggest POI is more common than once thought, affecting about 3.5% of women. The authors note that for most management options, the supporting evidence specific to POI is limited.
keyPoints: POI is estimated to affect about 3.5% of women, higher than previously thought.
A diagnosis now needs only one raised FSH result above 25 IU; AMH testing or a repeat FSH test may be used when the diagnosis is unclear.
The guideline covers effects on bone, heart, brain, sexual function, fertility and wellbeing, and treatment options including hormone therapy.
Recommendations on estrogen doses, the combined oral contraceptive, testosterone, genetic testing and non-hormonal and lifestyle options were updated.

items.title: Recommendations from the 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
items.summary: This is the 2023 international guideline on how polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) should be diagnosed and managed. It was built from systematic reviews, expert input and the views of women with PCOS. Key updates include using an AMH blood test as an alternative to ultrasound for diagnosis in adults, and continued emphasis on healthy lifestyle and emotional wellbeing. The evidence behind the recommendations is generally low to moderate quality, so more research is still needed.
keyPoints: AMH blood levels can now be used instead of an ultrasound to help diagnose PCOS in adults only.
PCOS is recognised as affecting more than periods and fertility, including metabolic health, heart disease risk, sleep apnea, mental health and a higher risk of problems in pregnancy.
Healthy lifestyle, emotional wellbeing and quality of life remain a focus, with awareness of weight stigma.
The guideline favours evidence-based medical treatment and cheaper, safer fertility management, with shared decision making between patients and clinicians.

items.title: Hysterectomy with opportunistic salpingectomy versus hysterectomy alone
items.summary: This review looked at whether removing the fallopian tubes during a hysterectomy for a non-cancer reason (to help prevent ovarian cancer) affects safety or ovarian reserve. It found seven small trials with 350 women, and the evidence was low to very low quality. No trials reported ovarian cancer rates, there were too few surgical complications to compare, and AMH (a marker of egg reserve) showed no clear difference, though the results were uncertain.
keyPoints: No trials reported whether removing the tubes during hysterectomy changed ovarian cancer rates.
There were too few surgery-related complications to tell whether the two approaches differ in safety.
AMH results were compatible with no difference or a small drop that the authors judged not clinically relevant (low-quality evidence).
Follow-up lasted only up to six months, and AMH can recover over several months, so longer-term effects, especially in younger women, are still unknown.

items.title: FIGO good practice recommendations on anemia in pregnancy, to reduce the incidence and impact of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH)
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: This is a 2025 guideline from the international obstetrics federation FIGO on anaemia (low iron or low haemoglobin) in pregnancy. It reviewed the best available evidence and made recommendations on screening, diagnosis, prevention and treatment. It also highlights the link between anaemia and heavy bleeding after birth. Anaemia is still very common in pregnancy worldwide, especially in lower-income countries.
keyPoints: All pregnant women should be screened for anaemia at their booking visit and again at 28 weeks, using a full blood count.
Anaemia is diagnosed when haemoglobin is below 11 g/dL, in every trimester and after birth.
Routine iron and folic acid supplements, alone or as part of multiple micronutrient supplements, are recommended during pregnancy.
Anaemia is linked with postpartum haemorrhage (heavy bleeding after birth), so preventing it matters.

items.title: Screening and Supplementation for Iron Deficiency and Iron Deficiency Anemia During Pregnancy: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force looked at whether routine screening for low iron, and routine iron supplements, help pregnant people without symptoms and their babies. It found the current evidence is not strong enough to say whether the benefits outweigh the harms for either one. This does not mean these steps are harmful or useless, only that the research cannot yet settle the question.
keyPoints: Iron deficiency is the leading cause of anemia in pregnancy; about 18% of pregnant people have iron deficiency and about 5% have iron deficiency anemia.
Iron deficiency becomes more common as pregnancy goes on, from about 7% in the first trimester to about 28% in the third.
The Task Force found the evidence insufficient to judge the balance of benefits and harms of screening for iron deficiency or iron deficiency anemia in pregnant people without symptoms.
The Task Force also found the evidence insufficient to judge the balance of benefits and harms of routine iron supplementation in pregnant people without symptoms.

items.title: The effects of oral ferrous bisglycinate supplementation on hemoglobin and ferritin concentrations in adults and children: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled 17 randomised trials comparing a type of iron supplement called ferrous bisglycinate with other iron supplements. In pregnant women, taking it for 4 to 20 weeks led to higher haemoglobin levels and fewer reported stomach and gut side effects. There was no clear difference in children, and the authors say more trials are needed in other groups.
keyPoints: In pregnant women, ferrous bisglycinate raised haemoglobin more than other iron supplements.
Pregnant women taking it reported fewer gastrointestinal side effects than those taking other iron supplements.
Ferritin levels showed a trend towards being higher in pregnancy, but the difference was not statistically significant.
No significant differences in haemoglobin or ferritin were found in children.

items.title: Serum or plasma ferritin concentration as an index of iron deficiency and overload
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at how well a blood ferritin test can show whether someone has low iron stores (iron deficiency) or too much iron (iron overload). For people seeking medical care, a ferritin level below 30 micrograms per litre was fairly good at picking up iron deficiency and very good at ruling it in, though the evidence was low certainty. For iron overload, and for screening people with no symptoms, the evidence was too weak to draw firm conclusions.
keyPoints: At a cutoff of 30 micrograms/L, ferritin was reasonably sensitive (about 79%) and very specific (about 98%) for iron deficiency in people presenting for medical care, based on low-certainty evidence.
For iron overload, the evidence was very low certainty, and no studies included pregnant women, infants or children.
There is not enough evidence to know if ferritin works equally well for screening people who have no symptoms.
Ferritin can be raised by inflammation and infection, which can affect how the result is read.

items.title: Canadian Network for Mood and Anxiety Treatments 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Perinatal Mood, Anxiety, and Related Disorders: Guide de pratique 2024 du Canadian Network for Mood and Anxiety Treatments pour le traitement des troubles de l'humeur, des troubles anxieux et des troubles connexes périnatals
items.source: Canadian Journal of Psychiatry. Revue Canadienne de Psychiatrie
items.journal: Canadian Journal of Psychiatry. Revue Canadienne de Psychiatrie
items.summary: This is a 2024 Canadian guideline on how to care for mood, anxiety and related problems during pregnancy and after birth. It was written with people who have lived experience of these conditions, along with specialist clinicians, and is based on reviews of the best available research. It covers medicines and non-medicine options, and how safe each is in the perinatal period. The abstract describes the guideline's scope rather than listing specific treatment findings.
keyPoints: The guideline covers depression, bipolar, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive and post-traumatic stress disorders in pregnancy and postpartum.
It sets out both medication and non-medication options, including lifestyle, psychosocial and psychological approaches, brain stimulation (neuromodulation) and complementary treatments.
Recommendations are ranked by lines of treatment, balancing how well they work with safety, tolerability and practicality.
It also covers finding cases early, how care is organised, high-risk situations and the mental health of fathers or co-parents.

items.title: Psychotherapies for Generalized Anxiety Disorder in Adults: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials
items.summary: This review pooled 65 trials of talking therapies for adults with generalized anxiety disorder, with about 70% of participants being women. Cognitive behavior therapy (CBT), newer 'third-wave' versions of CBT, and relaxation therapy all reduced anxiety symptoms more than usual care in the short term. Only CBT was still clearly better when people were checked 3 to 12 months after treatment ended. People were no more likely to drop out of these therapies than out of usual care.
keyPoints: CBT and third-wave CBTs reduced anxiety symptoms compared with usual care, with moderate certainty of evidence.
Relaxation therapy also helped in the short term, but the evidence was low certainty and the benefit disappeared when high-risk-of-bias studies were left out.
Only CBT stayed significantly more effective than usual care 3 to 12 months after treatment finished.
The authors suggest CBT may be the first-line therapy for generalized anxiety disorder, with third-wave CBTs and relaxation therapy as other options.

items.title: Advocacy interventions to reduce or eliminate violence and promote the physical and psychosocial well-being of women who experience intimate partner abuse
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 13 trials (2141 women) testing advocacy, meaning informal counselling, safety planning and help reaching services, for women who have experienced abuse by a partner. Advocacy seemed to bring some benefits, but most studies were small, so it is unclear how large the benefits are. Brief advocacy may help with depression and abuse, especially in pregnancy, while intensive advocacy may help women leaving shelters over the following one to two years.
keyPoints: Brief advocacy (under 12 hours) may give small short-term mental health benefits: fewer women developed depression in two healthcare studies.
In pregnancy, brief advocacy was linked to less minor physical abuse and less emotional abuse at about one year in one study.
Intensive advocacy for women leaving shelters may slightly improve quality of life and reduce severe physical abuse at 24 months, but did not clearly reduce depression.
Advocacy showed no clear effect on sexual abuse, and the authors say the size of benefit is uncertain because most studies were small.

items.title: Prenatal and postnatal factors associated with sudden infant death syndrome: an umbrella review of meta-analyses
items.summary: Researchers pulled together eight earlier reviews (152 studies in total) to see which factors are linked to sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). Smoking or drug exposure during pregnancy, smoking around the baby, bed sharing, and a baby's head being covered by bedclothes were linked to higher SIDS risk. Sleeping on the back and pacifier use were linked to lower risk. The strength of the evidence varied a lot, and the authors say more research is needed where it was weak.
keyPoints: Prenatal drug exposure, prenatal opioid exposure and prenatal maternal smoking were linked to higher SIDS risk, with evidence rated from suggestive to highly suggestive.
Bed sharing and postnatal maternal smoking were linked to higher risk, but the evidence for these was rated weak.
Babies found with their heads covered by bedclothes after sleep had a much higher risk, with evidence rated suggestive.
Sleeping on the back (supine) and pacifier use were linked to lower risk; the evidence was rated suggestive for back sleeping and weak for pacifiers.

items.title: Brief Resolved Unexplained Events (Formerly Apparent Life-Threatening Events) and Evaluation of Lower-Risk Infants
items.summary: This American Academy of Pediatrics guideline is about babies under 1 year who have a sudden, brief scary episode that then fully passes, such as turning blue or pale, breathing oddly, going floppy or stiff, or not responding normally. The old name for this was ALTE; the guideline replaces it with 'brief resolved unexplained event' (BRUE). A BRUE is only diagnosed when a careful history and physical exam find no explanation. Babies are sorted into lower-risk and higher-risk groups, and the guideline gives evidence-based advice on evaluating and managing the lower-risk group, aiming to avoid unnecessary and costly tests and treatments.
keyPoints: The term ALTE is replaced by 'brief resolved unexplained event' (BRUE) for infants younger than 1 year.
A BRUE involves a sudden, brief episode that has resolved, with one or more of: blue or pale colour, absent or irregular breathing, a marked change in muscle tone, or altered responsiveness.
It is diagnosed only when no explanation is found after an appropriate history and physical exam.
Infants are grouped as lower-risk (with evidence-based recommendations) or higher-risk (needing further investigation, but no recommendations given).

items.title: Effects of mind-body exercise on perimenopausal and postmenopausal women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 11 randomized trials with 1,005 women who were perimenopausal or postmenopausal. It looked at mind-body exercises such as tai chi, yoga, Pilates, qigong, baduanjin and mindfulness-based stress reduction. Compared with control groups, women doing these exercises had better bone density, sleep quality, anxiety, depressed mood and fatigue. Results for sleep, anxiety and depression varied quite a bit between studies.
keyPoints: Mind-body exercise was linked to higher bone mineral density compared with control groups.
Sleep quality improved in women doing mind-body exercise.
Anxiety, depressed mood and fatigue were all reduced.
Results for sleep, anxiety and depression differed a lot between the included trials.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D for increasing bone mineral density in premenopausal women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled seven trials (941 healthy women, average ages roughly 18 to 42) comparing calcium, vitamin D, or both against placebo for at least three months. None of the combinations made a meaningful difference to bone density at the hip or lower spine. The authors say the evidence is of moderate to low certainty, and most studies had some risk of bias. No trial reported fractures.
keyPoints: Calcium alone, vitamin D alone, or both together did not improve bone mineral density at the hip or lumbar spine compared with placebo in healthy premenopausal women.
The authors conclude these supplements are unlikely to help prevent fractures in this group and do not support them as a public health measure to improve bone density.
Studies of women with low bone mass, osteoporosis, or a higher risk of bone disease may still be useful, according to the authors.
The certainty of the evidence was moderate to low, and no trials reported fractures.

items.title: Management of Postmenopausal Osteoporosis: ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 2
items.summary: The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) updated its guidance on treating osteoporosis in women after menopause. The guideline looks at who should be offered osteoporosis medicines, the benefits and risks of the different medicine options, and how treatment should be monitored. It also covers what role calcium and vitamin D play. Each recommendation is rated by strength and quality of evidence, and where evidence was lacking, the authors gave general good practice points instead.
keyPoints: Gives updated recommendations on who should receive osteoporosis medicines after menopause.
Weighs the benefits and risks of the available medicine options.
Covers how treatment should be monitored and followed up.
Addresses the role of calcium and vitamin D in managing postmenopausal osteoporosis.

items.title: AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF CLINICAL ENDOCRINOLOGISTS/AMERICAN COLLEGE OF ENDOCRINOLOGY CLINICAL PRACTICE GUIDELINES FOR THE DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT OF POSTMENOPAUSAL OSTEOPOROSIS-2020 UPDATE
items.summary: This is a 2020 update of clinical practice guidelines from two American endocrinology organisations on diagnosing and treating osteoporosis after menopause. It contains 52 recommendations, most graded A or B, built on reviews of the evidence. New or updated topics include how osteoporosis is diagnosed, sorting patients into high-risk and very-high-risk groups, a new dual-action treatment option, and how to switch between treatments.
keyPoints: The update has 52 recommendations: 40% Grade A, 46% Grade B and 14% Grade C, with none at the weakest grade.
Of 368 citations, about 70% were the highest or intermediate levels of evidence.
The diagnosis of osteoporosis is clarified, and patients are grouped by high-risk and very-high-risk features.
It adds a new dual-action therapy option and guidance on moving between treatments.

items.title: Physical exercise training interventions for children and young adults during and after treatment for childhood cancer
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether exercise programmes help children and young people with cancer. It included six small trials with 171 participants, all children having treatment for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. Some fitness measures, strength and bone density improved with exercise, but the evidence was low quality and the overall effects were not yet convincing. Only one study measured bone density, and it found a benefit.
keyPoints: Only one study measured whole-body bone mineral density, and it found a statistically significant benefit from exercise.
Some measures of fitness, flexibility and muscle strength were better in the exercise groups, but not all measures showed a difference.
No significant differences were found for fatigue, daily activity or adverse events, each assessed in one study.
The studies were small and all children had leukaemia, so more and larger studies including other cancers are needed.

items.title: Calcium intake and bone mineral density: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 59 randomised trials in people over 50 to see whether getting more calcium from food, or from supplements, changes bone density. Both approaches raised bone density by a small amount, roughly 0.6-1.8%, and the gains did not keep growing over time. The authors concluded the increases are unlikely to make a meaningful difference to fracture risk.
keyPoints: More calcium from food raised bone mineral density by about 0.6-1.0% at one year and 0.7-1.8% at two years at most sites measured, with no effect at the forearm.
Calcium supplements raised bone density by about 0.7-1.8% at all five sites, and the gain at later time points was similar to the gain at one year.
Results were similar for food versus supplements, calcium alone versus with vitamin D, higher versus lower doses, and low versus higher starting calcium intake.
The authors concluded these small, non-progressive increases are unlikely to lead to a clinically significant reduction in fracture risk.

items.title: Calcium plus vitamin D supplementation and the risk of fractures
items.summary: This large trial followed over 36,000 healthy postmenopausal women aged 50 to 79 for about 7 years. Half took calcium (1000 mg) with vitamin D3 (400 IU) each day and half took a placebo. The supplements gave a small boost to hip bone density but did not significantly lower the risk of hip fracture. They were linked to a higher chance of kidney stones.
keyPoints: Hip bone density was about 1 percent higher in women taking calcium plus vitamin D than in those taking placebo.
The supplements did not significantly reduce hip fractures, spine fractures or total fractures.
Kidney stones were more common in the calcium plus vitamin D group (hazard ratio 1.17).
When only women who kept taking the supplements as directed were counted, the hip fracture risk was lower (hazard ratio 0.71).

items.title: American Society of Breast Surgeons and Society of Breast Imaging 2025 Guidelines for the Management of Benign Breast Fibroepithelial Lesions
items.source: American Society of Breast Surgeons and Society of Breast Imaging
items.organisation: American Society of Breast Surgeons and Society of Breast Imaging
items.summary: Two US breast specialist societies wrote guidelines on how to manage benign (non-cancer) breast lumps called fibroepithelial lesions, which include fibroadenomas and benign phyllodes tumors. The guidelines are based on expert consensus and available evidence. They say many fibroadenomas confirmed by biopsy do not need to be removed, and that people can usually return to routine breast screening afterwards.
keyPoints: A biopsy-proven fibroadenoma without atypia only needs removal if it causes symptoms, the patient prefers it, it reaches a certain size, or it clearly grows over time.
Patients with a biopsy-proven, matching fibroadenoma do not need follow-up imaging and can return to age-appropriate screening.

Lesions suspected to be phyllodes tumors, including benign ones, need surgical removal of the whole mass; a second surgery for a positive margin is not required but may be considered if the mass was cut through or disease may remain.
After a benign phyllodes tumor is removed, no follow-up imaging is needed and age-appropriate screening can resume.

items.title: Screening for Breast Cancer: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force reviewed the evidence on breast cancer screening for women at average risk who are aged 40 or older. It recommends a mammogram every two years for women aged 40 to 74, and rates the overall benefit as moderate. For women 75 and older, and for extra scans such as ultrasound or MRI in women with dense breasts, it says there is not yet enough evidence to weigh the benefits against the harms.
keyPoints: Mammogram screening every two years is recommended for women aged 40 to 74 at average risk (B recommendation).
The Task Force has moderate certainty that this screening has a moderate net benefit.
Evidence is insufficient to judge the balance of benefits and harms of mammograms in women aged 75 and older.
Evidence is insufficient to judge extra screening with ultrasound or MRI for women with dense breasts and a normal mammogram.

items.title: Implants versus autologous tissue flaps for breast reconstruction following mastectomy
items.summary: This review looked at 35 non-randomised studies (over 57,000 women) comparing breast reconstruction after mastectomy using implants versus the woman's own tissue. Women who had their own tissue used reported somewhat better emotional and sexual well-being and more satisfaction with the reconstruction. Implant surgery may be shorter, but much of the evidence is low or very low quality, so firm conclusions are hard. The authors say no single technique is best for every woman.
keyPoints: Own-tissue reconstruction may give better psychosocial and sexual well-being than implants (low-certainty evidence).
Women with implants may be less satisfied with the reconstruction (low-certainty evidence).
Implants may lead to more long-term complications and a shorter operation, but the evidence is very uncertain.
No technique suits all women, and randomised trials are lacking to guide the choice.

items.title: Mammography in combination with breast ultrasonography versus mammography for breast cancer screening in women at average risk
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether adding a breast ultrasound scan to mammography helps find more breast cancer in women at average risk. It found that the combination detected more cancers and missed fewer, but it also caused more false alarms and more biopsies. No study checked whether adding ultrasound actually reduces deaths from breast cancer.
keyPoints: In the main trial (about 72,700 women), adding ultrasound found about 2 more breast cancers per 1000 women over two years (5 versus 3 per 1000), and cancers that appeared between screens were less common (high certainty).
Adding ultrasound led to about 37 more false-positive results and 27 more biopsies per 1000 women screened (high certainty).
In women with dense breasts, cohort studies also found more cancers detected with the combination; in women with non-dense breasts, cohort studies found no clear difference.
None of the studies looked at breast cancer deaths or overall deaths, so it is unknown whether finding more cancers saves lives.

items.title: Mammographic breast density and the risk of breast cancer: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled nine studies to see how breast density on a mammogram relates to breast cancer risk. Women with extremely dense breast tissue (called BI-RADS D) had about twice the risk of breast cancer compared with women with scattered dense tissue (BI-RADS B). The authors say this is lower than earlier estimates, which may be because newer digital mammograms and an updated density scale were used.
keyPoints: Extremely dense breasts (BI-RADS D) were linked to about a 2.11-fold higher breast cancer risk than scattered density (BI-RADS B).
After adjusting for age and BMI, the increased risk was about 1.83-fold.
This is a lower risk estimate than previously reported.
The difference may be explained by digital mammography and the 5th edition of the BI-RADS system.

items.title: Breastfeeding and Health Outcomes for Infants and Children: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review pulled together 29 earlier reviews and 145 newer studies on breastfeeding and children's health in developed countries. More breastfeeding was linked to a lower risk of several problems, including moderate-to-severe chest and tummy infections, ear infections, asthma, obesity, type 1 diabetes, childhood leukemia and infant death. The studies were observational, so they show links rather than proof of cause, and there were risks of bias.
keyPoints: More breastfeeding was linked to lower risk of moderate-to-severe respiratory and gut infections, ear infections, allergic rhinitis and asthma.
Links to lower risk were also seen for obesity, rapid weight gain, high systolic blood pressure, type 1 diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease, childhood leukemia and infant mortality.
No clear length of breastfeeding stood out as the most beneficial for any outcome.
There were few data on whether the type of breastfeeding or the source of breast milk changed the results.

items.title: Assessment of growth status and nutritional management of prematurely born infants after hospital discharge: A position paper of the ESPGHAN Nutrition Committee
items.journal: Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition
items.summary: This position paper from a European paediatric nutrition committee gives advice on feeding and growth checks for premature babies after they leave hospital. It is based on 101 published studies plus expert opinion where studies were lacking. It recommends regular growth checks, breastfeeding when possible, extra nutrition for babies who need to catch up, and starting solid foods based on the baby's development rather than a fixed age.
keyPoints: Weight, length and head size should be measured regularly after discharge to spot slow growth or undernutrition.
Breastfeeding is highly recommended for all preterm infants when feasible; babies needing to catch up may be given supplements such as human milk fortifier.
Solid foods should start when the baby reaches developmental milestones, rather than at a strict set age.
Vitamin D and iron supplements are recommended through at least 12 months corrected age, with regular ferritin (iron store) checks.

items.title: Immediate or early skin-to-skin contact for mothers and their healthy newborn infants
items.summary: This Cochrane review combined 69 trials (7290 mothers and babies) to see what happens when a healthy newborn is placed skin-to-skin on the mother's chest right after birth, compared with usual hospital care. Skin-to-skin contact probably helps more mothers breastfeed exclusively, both up to one month and from six weeks to six months. It also probably helps babies keep up their blood sugar and body temperature. Effects on the mother's blood loss and the time to deliver the placenta were unclear, and no trial met all the criteria for high quality.
keyPoints: Skin-to-skin contact probably increases exclusive breastfeeding from hospital discharge to one month (RR 1.36) and from six weeks to six months (RR 1.38), based on moderate-certainty evidence.
Babies probably have higher blood sugar levels, and slightly higher temperature (about 0.28 °C, not clinically meaningful), with skin-to-skin contact.
Babies may be more stable in heart and breathing function, but this evidence is low certainty from small studies.
Evidence on maternal blood loss and placenta delivery time was inconclusive, and no trials were done in low-income countries.

items.title: Frenotomy for tongue-tie in newborn infants
items.summary: This review looked at five small trials (302 babies under three months old) of frenotomy, a quick procedure that releases a tight tongue-tie, to see if it helps with breastfeeding. Mothers reported less nipple pain in the short term after their baby had the procedure. The results for how well babies fed were mixed, with no consistent benefit, and no serious problems were reported. The trials were small and had weaknesses, so the findings are uncertain.
keyPoints: Frenotomy reduced breastfeeding mothers' nipple pain in the short term.
There was no consistent improvement in how well babies breastfed; two trials showed no change and one showed improvement.
No serious complications were reported, but the number of babies studied was small.
No trial could say whether frenotomy leads to successful breastfeeding in the long term.

items.title: Breastfeeding in the 21st century: epidemiology, mechanisms, and lifelong effect
items.summary: This large review pulled together many studies on breastfeeding and health for babies and mothers, in both rich and poor countries. Breastfeeding was linked to fewer infections and bite problems in children, higher intelligence scores, and probably less overweight and diabetes. For mothers, it was linked to lower breast cancer risk and longer gaps between pregnancies. No link was found with asthma, allergies, blood pressure or cholesterol, and longer breastfeeding was linked to more tooth decay.
keyPoints: Breastfeeding protected children against infections and malocclusion (poorly aligned teeth) and was linked to higher intelligence, with probable reductions in overweight and diabetes.
No link was found with allergic conditions such as asthma, or with blood pressure or cholesterol; longer breastfeeding was linked to more tooth decay.
For mothers, breastfeeding protected against breast cancer, improved birth spacing, and might also protect against ovarian cancer and type 2 diabetes.
Near-universal breastfeeding could prevent an estimated 823,000 deaths in children under 5 and 20,000 breast cancer deaths each year.

items.title: Breastfeeding Challenges: ACOG Committee Opinion, Number 820
items.summary: This guidance from ACOG looks at common problems that can stop women from breastfeeding as long as they hoped. Many women stop early because of ongoing pain or nipple injury, and only about 25% of women in the United States breastfeed exclusively at 6 months. Care professionals are advised to take a careful history and examine the woman to find the exact cause of pain and choose the right treatment. Worries about medicines, and issues like limited paid leave or workplace barriers, can also lead to early weaning.
keyPoints: Breastfeeding is linked to lower risk of breast cancer, ovarian cancer, diabetes and hypertensive heart disease for the mother.
Pain or nipple injury is a common reason for early, unwanted weaning, so a focused history and exam is needed to find the cause and the right treatment.
Pain with breastfeeding may be linked to postpartum depression, so screening for postpartum depression is an important part of care.
Advice about medicines during breastfeeding should rely on current resources such as the LactMed database.

items.title: Oral galactagogues (natural therapies or drugs) for increasing breast milk production in mothers of non-hospitalised term infants
items.summary: This large review pooled 41 trials (about 3,000 mothers) of drugs and natural remedies, such as fenugreek, fennel and moringa, taken by mouth to boost breast milk. Drugs like domperidone and metoclopramide may increase milk volume a little, but the evidence is low quality. Natural remedies may help some babies' weight and milk volume, but the studies were so different and weak that the size of any benefit is very uncertain. Side effects, where reported, were minor.
keyPoints: Drugs such as domperidone, metoclopramide and sulpiride may increase milk volume (low-certainty evidence).
Natural remedies may help infant weight and milk volume in some studies, but the size of the effect is very uncertain.
Reported side effects were minor, such as tiredness, nausea, headache, dry mouth, and maple-syrup-smelling urine in mothers, but safety data were limited.
It is not known whether any remedy helps mothers keep breastfeeding longer, or whether one remedy works better than another.

items.title: Interventions for preventing mastitis after childbirth
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 10 trials with over 3,000 breastfeeding women to see what helps prevent mastitis (a painful breast inflammation) after childbirth. Probiotics, acupoint massage, and breast massage with low frequency pulse treatment may lower the chance of mastitis compared with placebo or routine care. For antibiotics, ointments, breastfeeding education and special cereal, results were uncertain. Most of the evidence is low quality, and a large probiotics trial has not shared its results, so the picture is incomplete.
keyPoints: Probiotics may reduce the risk of mastitis compared with placebo (low-certainty evidence).
Acupoint massage probably reduces both mastitis and breast pain compared with routine care (moderate-certainty evidence).
Breast massage with low frequency pulse treatment may reduce mastitis (low-certainty evidence).
Antibiotics, antibiotic ointments, specialist breastfeeding education and special cereal showed no clear benefit, but the evidence is too uncertain to be sure.

items.title: Resistance training in pregnancy: systematic review and meta-analysis of pregnancy, delivery, fetal and pelvic floor outcomes and call to action
items.summary: This review pooled 50 studies (nearly 48,000 pregnant people) to look at resistance training, such as exercising with weights or resistance bands, during pregnancy. Resistance training, on its own or as part of a mixed exercise programme, was linked to lower odds of gestational high blood pressure, gestational diabetes, mood problems around birth and very large babies. Most programmes mixed several types of exercise, so it is hard to know how much of the benefit came from resistance training itself. The authors say better-designed studies are needed.
keyPoints: Resistance training was linked to lower odds of gestational hypertension (OR 0.42) and gestational diabetes (OR 0.62).
It was also linked to lower odds of perinatal mood disorders (OR 0.48) and macrosomia, or a very large baby (OR 0.67).
About 90% of the studies used mixed exercise programmes, and the amount of resistance training was generally low to moderate.
Because the programmes were mixed and poorly described, the effect of resistance training alone is hard to pin down.

items.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 205: Vaginal Birth After Cesarean Delivery
items.summary: This American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists guideline looks at trying to give birth vaginally after a previous cesarean (called TOLAC, with a successful result called VBAC). It says VBAC can meet a woman's wish for vaginal birth and is linked to fewer complications for the mother and in later pregnancies. A trial of labor that does not succeed carries more risk than a successful VBAC or a planned repeat cesarean. Because of this, it is important to look at each woman's chance of success and personal risks when deciding if TOLAC is a good fit.
keyPoints: TOLAC is a planned attempt at vaginal birth after a previous cesarean, and a successful attempt is called VBAC.
VBAC is linked to lower maternal complications and fewer problems in future pregnancies.
A failed trial of labor is linked to more maternal and newborn complications than VBAC or an elective repeat cesarean.
Counseling should weigh the likelihood of VBAC and each woman's individual risks.

items.title: Continuous support for women during childbirth
items.summary: This Cochrane review combined 26 trials with nearly 16,000 women to see what happens when someone stays with a woman throughout labour, compared with usual care. Women with continuous support were more likely to have a spontaneous vaginal birth and less likely to have a caesarean birth. They also had shorter labours and were less likely to report negative feelings about their birth. Much of the evidence was rated low quality, and no harms were found.
keyPoints: Continuous support in labour increased spontaneous vaginal birth (average RR 1.08) and reduced caesarean birth (average RR 0.75), though this evidence was low quality.
Labours were about 0.69 hours shorter, and women were less likely to use pain relief medicines, have an instrumental birth (forceps or vacuum), or report negative feelings about their birth.
Babies were less likely to have a low five-minute Apgar score, with no clear effect on special care nursery admission or breastfeeding.
The review found no evidence of harms. Some subgroup results (such as a bigger caesarean reduction with a doula) were exploratory and should be read with caution.

items.title: Maternal caffeine consumption during pregnancy and offspring cord blood DNA methylation: an epigenome-wide association study meta-analysis
items.summary: Researchers looked at whether caffeine from coffee, tea and cola during pregnancy changes the way genes are switched on or off (DNA methylation) in babies at birth. They combined data from six European studies covering 3,725 mother-baby pairs. They found very few changes and little evidence that caffeine affects this process in the womb. The study may not have been large enough to spot very small effects, and the mothers drank only small amounts of caffeine.
keyPoints: Only one DNA methylation change was linked to total caffeine intake and one to cola intake, out of the whole genome.
This gives little evidence that caffeine in pregnancy changes babies' DNA methylation at birth.
Mothers in the study had low caffeine intake, so results might differ in people who drink a lot.
Current guidelines advise limiting caffeine to under 200 mg a day, though there is no clear proof of its effects on human development.

items.title: Systematic review of the potential adverse effects of caffeine consumption in healthy adults, pregnant women, adolescents, and children
items.summary: This systematic review looked at research published from 2001 to mid-2015 on whether caffeine causes harm in healthy adults, pregnant women, teenagers and children. After weighing study quality and consistency, it found that up to 300 mg of caffeine a day in healthy pregnant women is generally not linked to harm to reproduction or development. Information on children and teenagers was limited. The authors say more research is needed on people who may be more sensitive to caffeine.
keyPoints: Up to 300 mg of caffeine a day in healthy pregnant women is generally not associated with adverse reproductive and developmental effects.
Up to 400 mg a day in healthy adults is not associated with overt harm to the heart, behavior, bones, or reproduction and development.
Little data exists for children and teenagers; 2.5 mg per kg of body weight per day still seems an appropriate limit.
Future research should look at groups who may be at higher risk, such as people with existing health conditions.

items.title: Coffee, Caffeine, and Health Outcomes: An Umbrella Review
items.summary: This review pulled together results from many earlier studies on coffee and caffeine and a wide range of health outcomes. Coffee was linked to a probably lower risk of several cancers (breast, colorectal, endometrial), heart disease, Parkinson's disease and type 2 diabetes. Caffeine was linked to a probably higher risk of pregnancy loss, and to a rise in blood pressure in short-term trials. The authors concluded that coffee can be part of a healthful diet.
keyPoints: Coffee was linked to a probably lower risk of breast, colorectal, colon, endometrial and prostate cancers, cardiovascular disease, Parkinson's disease and type 2 diabetes.
Caffeine intake was linked to a probably increased risk of pregnancy loss in the observational studies reviewed.
In short-term trials, caffeine raised blood pressure and coffee raised blood fats, though the blood fat result varied a lot between studies.
The authors concluded that coffee can be part of a healthful diet.

items.title: Coffee consumption and health: umbrella review of meta-analyses of multiple health outcomes
items.summary: This large review pulled together results from 201 earlier studies of coffee and health outcomes in adults. For most outcomes, coffee drinking was linked to benefit more often than harm, with the biggest gains at three to four cups a day. In pregnancy the picture was different: high coffee intake, compared with low or none, was linked to low birth weight, preterm birth and pregnancy loss. These are links seen in observational studies, so they do not prove coffee is the cause.
keyPoints: High versus low or no coffee in pregnancy was linked to low birth weight (odds ratio 1.31), preterm birth (1.22 first trimester, 1.12 second trimester) and pregnancy loss (1.46).
Outside pregnancy, most other harmful links were largely explained away once smoking was accounted for.
Coffee seems generally safe at usual intakes in the general adult population, with most benefit seen at three to four cups a day.
Coffee drinking was also linked to fracture risk in women but not in men, and robust randomised trials are needed to tell if the links are causal.

items.title: Effects of restricted caffeine intake by mother on fetal, neonatal and pregnancy outcomes
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked for randomised trials testing whether cutting down caffeine in pregnancy changes outcomes for mothers and babies. Only two trials qualified, and only one gave usable results. In that trial, regular coffee drinkers (3+ cups a day) who switched to decaf in the second and third trimester had babies with similar birthweight, similar rates of preterm birth and similar rates of being small for gestational age. The evidence was low quality, so the review could not confirm or rule out a benefit of avoiding caffeine.
keyPoints: Only two trials met the review's criteria, and just one contributed data.
Cutting caffeine by about 182 mg a day (by switching to decaf) did not change birthweight, preterm birth or small-for-gestational-age rates in that trial.
Evidence for birthweight and preterm birth was low quality because of the small sample and wide confidence intervals.
The authors concluded there is not enough evidence to confirm or refute that avoiding caffeine affects pregnancy outcomes, and call for better double-blinded trials.

items.title: Oral antihypertensive treatment during pregnancy: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
items.source: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This review pooled 23 trials (3989 women) comparing three blood pressure medicines used in pregnancy: methyldopa, labetalol and nifedipine. Labetalol and methyldopa lowered the chance of severe high blood pressure compared with no treatment or placebo. Labetalol was linked to less preeclampsia and fewer preterm births than nifedipine, so it was modestly favoured. The trials were of low-to-moderate quality, so the results should be read with caution.
keyPoints: Labetalol and methyldopa reduced severe high blood pressure compared with placebo or no treatment.
Labetalol was linked to less preeclampsia and fewer preterm births than nifedipine.
For most other outcomes, the three medicines showed no significant differences.
The included studies were of low overall quality, so caution is advised.

items.title: Exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation for coronary heart disease
items.summary: This Cochrane review combined 85 trials with over 23,000 people who have coronary heart disease to see whether exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation helps. It found that rehab lowers the chance of a heart attack and of being admitted to hospital, and may slightly improve quality of life. Longer-term, it may also reduce deaths from heart causes. Fewer than 15% of participants were women, so the findings reflect mostly men.
keyPoints: Within 6 to 12 months, exercise-based rehab reduced the risk of heart attack (high certainty evidence) and of any hospital admission (moderate certainty evidence).
It likely makes a small reduction in deaths from any cause, and made little to no difference to bypass surgery or stent procedures.
Over longer follow-up, rehab may reduce deaths from heart disease and heart attacks.
Women were still a small share of trial participants (under 15%), so more trials representing women and everyday care are needed.

items.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 203: Chronic Hypertension in Pregnancy
items.summary: This is a practice guideline from ACOG, a US group of obstetricians and gynecologists, on chronic high blood pressure that is present before or early in pregnancy. It explains how this condition is defined and diagnosed, how it can affect a pregnancy and how pregnancy can affect it. It also reviews the evidence on ways to manage it. The abstract notes the condition is becoming more common and can raise health risks for mother and baby.
keyPoints: Chronic hypertension is present in about 0.9-1.5% of pregnant women and may cause significant health problems for the mother, baby and newborn.
The rate rose by 67% from 2000 to 2009, with the biggest rise (87%) among African American women.
The rise is largely linked to obesity and women being older at pregnancy, and the trend is expected to continue.
The guideline sets out criteria for diagnosing chronic hypertension and appraises the evidence for management options.

items.title: Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination for the prevention of cervical cancer and other HPV-related diseases: a network meta-analysis
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 60 randomised trials with over 157,000 people to see whether HPV vaccines are safe and prevent HPV-related disease. Vaccination lowered the risk of cervical pre-cancer and genital warts in young women, and no safety concerns showed up. The trials were too short for cancers to develop, so cervical cancer itself could not be measured, and there was no pre-cancer data for people vaccinated under age 15.
keyPoints: In females aged 15 to 25, HPV vaccination reduced cervical pre-cancer (CIN2+): by about 30% overall and by about 60% for the HPV types the vaccine targets (moderate certainty).
Anogenital warts were much less common after vaccination, about 25 fewer cases per 1000 people (high certainty), and fewer people needed treatment for HPV-related pre-cancer (moderate certainty).
Serious side effects were no more common in vaccinated groups than in control groups (high certainty).
No data were available on cervical cancer or other cancers, and none on pre-cancer outcomes for vaccination under age 15.

items.title: Global and regional estimates of genital human papillomavirus prevalence among men: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 65 studies covering about 44,800 men in 35 countries to estimate how common genital HPV infection is in men. Around 3 in 10 men had at least one genital HPV type, and about 2 in 10 had a high-risk type linked to cancer. Infection was most common in young adults, peaking at ages 25 to 29. The authors say men are an important source of HPV spread, so prevention plans should include them.
keyPoints: About 31% of men worldwide had any genital HPV, and 21% had a high-risk HPV type.
HPV-16 was the most common type (5%), followed by HPV-6 (4%).
Infection was highest between ages 25 and 29 and then levelled off or fell slightly.
Rates were similar across most world regions but about half as high in Eastern and South-Eastern Asia.

items.title: Cervical Cancer, Version 3.2019, NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology
items.journal: Journal of the National Comprehensive Cancer Network
items.summary: This is a guideline summary on cervical cancer from a US cancer expert group. It notes that most cervical cancers can be prevented through HPV vaccination, routine screening and treatment of precancerous changes. Even so, cervical cancer is still the fourth most common cancer in women worldwide, largely because screening is not good enough in many regions. The rest of the guideline covers how early and locally advanced cervical cancer is checked, staged and treated.
keyPoints: Most cervical cancers are preventable through HPV vaccination, routine screening and treatment of precancerous lesions.
Cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer in women globally.
Inadequate screening in many parts of the world is why it remains so common.
The guideline covers workup, staging and treatment of early stage and locally advanced disease.

items.title: Cytology versus HPV testing for cervical cancer screening in the general population
items.summary: This review pooled 40 studies of more than 140,000 women to compare HPV testing with cervical cytology (the smear test) for finding serious cervical changes (CIN 2+). HPV tests were better at picking up these changes, but they also flagged more women who did not need follow-up. A negative HPV test was more reassuring than a negative smear, because smears are more likely to miss real disease.
keyPoints: HPV testing found more cases of CIN 2+ than cytology (pooled sensitivity about 90% for the HC2 HPV test versus about 63% for conventional cytology and 73% for liquid-based cytology).
HPV tests were slightly less specific, so they lead to more unnecessary referrals.
A negative HPV test is more reassuring than a negative cytology result, which has a greater chance of being falsely negative and delaying treatment.
Results did not differ between women under and over 30, but longer-term studies are still needed to confirm the clinical impact.

items.title: Linked color imaging versus conventional white-light colonoscopy for the detection of colorectal polyps
items.summary: This review looked at whether a special colonoscopy imaging mode called linked color imaging (LCI), which boosts color contrast, finds more bowel polyps than standard white-light imaging. It combined 16 trials with about 12,800 adults having colonoscopy for screening, symptoms or follow-up checks. LCI found slightly more adenomas (a type of polyp that can turn into cancer) and more polyps overall, with no adverse events needing medical treatment reported. No trial measured whether this led to fewer bowel cancers appearing after colonoscopy.
keyPoints: LCI slightly increased the adenoma detection rate compared with standard white-light colonoscopy (high-certainty evidence).
LCI slightly increased the overall polyp detection rate and likely found more sessile serrated lesions and more adenomas per person (moderate-certainty evidence).
No adverse events needing medical treatment were reported with LCI (moderate-certainty evidence).
No study measured cancers appearing after colonoscopy, so the effect on cancer prevention is not yet known.

items.title: Metformin and Combined Oral Contraceptive Pills in the Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.source: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: This review pooled 36 randomised trials in women with PCOS to compare the combined pill, metformin, and both together. For excess hair growth (hirsutism), there was no difference between metformin and the pill, or between the pill and the combination. Metformin was better at lowering insulin and triglycerides, while the pill was better at improving male-type hormone measures. The authors conclude that the choice should be based on symptoms, and that combining both treatments gave some blood-test benefits.
keyPoints: Hirsutism did not differ between metformin and the combined pill, or between the pill alone and the pill plus metformin.
The combined pill was better than metformin for male-type hormone measures (free androgen index, SHBG and testosterone).
Metformin lowered insulin and triglycerides more than the pill did.
Pill plus metformin gave some better blood-test results than the pill alone, including insulin, insulin resistance, free androgen index and SHBG.

items.title: Guidelines of care for the management of acne vulgaris
items.source: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
items.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
items.summary: This 2024 guideline reviewed the evidence on treating acne and made 18 recommendations. Treatments with strong support include benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids, topical antibiotics and oral doxycycline. Combined oral contraceptive pills were given a conditional (weaker) recommendation as one acne option, alongside spironolactone and several other treatments.
keyPoints: Strong recommendations were made for benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids, topical antibiotics and oral doxycycline.
Combined oral contraceptive pills received a conditional recommendation for acne, meaning the evidence supports them less strongly than the first-line options.
Oral isotretinoin is strongly recommended for severe acne, acne causing psychosocial burden or scarring, or acne that has not responded to standard treatment.
Good practice advice includes combining topical treatments that work in different ways and limiting the use of antibiotics taken by mouth.

items.title: Combined oral contraceptive pill for primary dysmenorrhoea
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 21 trials (3723 women) to see how well combined birth control pills treat period pain that has no underlying pelvic cause. The pills reduced pain more than placebo, with a moderate size of benefit. They also caused more side effects, especially irregular bleeding, headaches and nausea. It was unclear whether the pills work better than anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs), because only one small study compared them.
keyPoints: Combined pills reduce period pain more than placebo or no treatment (high-quality evidence for the size of the pain reduction).
About 28% of women improved on placebo, versus roughly 37% to 60% of women using the pill.
Side effects were more common with the pill: irregular bleeding (high-quality evidence), plus headaches and nausea (moderate-quality evidence).
Taking the pill continuously (no break) may ease pain more than the standard regimen, but the evidence is low quality and long-term safety data are needed.

items.title: Evaluation and Treatment of Hirsutism in Premenopausal Women: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: This Endocrine Society guideline gives advice on checking for and treating unwanted excess hair growth (hirsutism) in women before menopause. For most women who want treatment, it suggests starting with the combined pill, and adding a medicine that blocks male-type hormones after 6 months if the response is not good enough. Hair removal methods such as laser can be added for extra cosmetic benefit.
keyPoints: Testing for high androgen (male-type hormone) levels is suggested for women with an abnormal hirsutism score, but not for women with regular periods and only local unwanted hair growth.
For most women, the combined estrogen-progestin pill is the suggested first medicine; an antiandrogen can be added after 6 months if the response is not good enough.
Antiandrogen medicines on their own are not recommended unless reliable contraception is also used.
Insulin-lowering drugs are suggested against, and laser or photoepilation is suggested for most women who choose hair removal.

items.title: Combined oral contraceptives: the risk of myocardial infarction and ischemic stroke
items.summary: This review pooled results from 24 observational studies to see whether women taking the combined pill have more heart attacks or strokes caused by blood clots. Pill users had about a 1.6-times higher relative risk than non-users, and the increase was similar for heart attack and for stroke. Pills with higher estrogen doses seemed to carry more risk, and the type of progestagen did not clearly change the risk.
keyPoints: Combined pill users had about a 1.6-fold higher risk of heart attack or ischemic stroke than non-users.
The increase was similar for heart attack (1.6) and ischemic stroke (1.7).
Risk seemed to rise with higher estrogen doses and was highest for pills with more than 50 micrograms of estrogen.
The risk did not vary clearly by progestagen type or generation; with clot data from other studies, a levonorgestrel plus 30 microgram estrogen pill appears the safest oral option.

items.title: U.S. Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use, 2024
items.summary: This is the 2024 update of the US guidance for health care providers on starting and using specific birth control methods. It was updated by the CDC after reviewing the scientific evidence and meeting with national experts. The goal is to remove unnecessary medical barriers to getting and using contraception and to support respectful, person-centred counselling without pressure.
keyPoints: Updated advice on which medications can be given for intrauterine device (IUD) placement.
Updated advice on managing bleeding changes while using a contraceptive implant.
New advice on testosterone use and the risk of pregnancy.
New advice on self-administering injectable contraception.

items.title: Progestin intrauterine devices versus copper intrauterine devices for emergency contraception
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether a hormonal coil (levonorgestrel IUD) can be used for emergency contraception as well as the copper coil, which is the most effective emergency option. Only one trial of 711 women met the review's criteria. The evidence was very uncertain about pregnancy rates, failed insertions, expulsions, removals and how acceptable women found each coil. The review cannot yet say whether the hormonal coil works as well as, better than, or worse than the copper coil for emergency use.
keyPoints: Only one trial (711 women) was found, with one month of follow-up.
Evidence on pregnancy rates, failed insertions, expulsion, removal and acceptability was very uncertain.
The copper coil may cause slightly more cramping, while the hormonal coil may cause slightly more bleeding and spotting days, but this evidence is also uncertain.
More studies are needed before the hormonal coil's effectiveness for emergency contraception can be confirmed.

items.title: Risk of thromboembolism in patients with COVID-19 who are using hormonal contraception
items.summary: This review looked for studies on whether hormonal contraception raises the risk of blood clots in people with COVID-19. It found no studies that directly compared clot risk between users and non-users. The few studies available suggest hormonal contraception did not clearly make COVID-19 more severe, but the evidence is very uncertain and of low quality.
keyPoints: No comparative studies were found on blood clot risk in people with COVID-19 who use hormonal contraception.
Combined hormonal contraception may have little to no effect on the odds of death or intubation in COVID-19, based on very low-certainty evidence.
Hospitalization odds may be slightly lower for combined hormonal contraception users with a BMI under 35, but this comes from one study and is very uncertain.
No large increase in COVID-19 severity was seen among hormonal contraception users, but better studies are needed.

items.title: 2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Management of Reproductive Health in Rheumatic and Musculoskeletal Diseases
items.summary: This guideline from the American College of Rheumatology gives advice on reproductive health for people with rheumatic and musculoskeletal diseases, including contraception, fertility treatment, menopause hormone therapy, pregnancy and medicines. It supports using safe and effective contraception to prevent unplanned pregnancy and planning pregnancy for a time when the disease is calm. The overall evidence specific to these conditions is low, so many recommendations are conditional and meant to be decided together with a doctor.
keyPoints: Safe and effective contraception is encouraged to prevent unplanned pregnancy in people with rheumatic and musculoskeletal diseases.
Pre-pregnancy counselling is advised so conception happens when the disease is quiet and medicines are pregnancy-compatible.
Reproductive health decisions should involve ongoing discussion between the patient, their rheumatologist and obstetrics/gynecology teams.
Many recommendations are conditional because the available evidence is limited or low level.

items.title: Postpartum practice: guidelines for clinical practice from the French College of Gynaecologists and Obstetricians (CNGOF)
items.source: French College of Gynaecologists and Obstetricians (CNGOF)
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.organisation: French College of Gynaecologists and Obstetricians (CNGOF)
items.summary: The French College of Gynaecologists and Obstetricians reviewed the research to make recommendations for care after birth, for mothers and babies. It recommends breastfeeding for at least 4-6 months, starting effective contraception by 21 days after birth, and avoiding combined hormonal contraception (containing oestrogen) before six weeks because of clot risk. It also covers pelvic floor exercises and notes that the months after birth can be emotionally hard, with postpartum depression the most common difficulty.
keyPoints: Exclusive and extended breastfeeding is recommended for at least 4-6 months, as it is linked to fewer illnesses and better cognitive development in children.
Effective contraception should start no later than 21 days after birth for women who do not want a closely spaced pregnancy.
Combined hormonal contraception is not recommended before six weeks after birth because of the higher risk of venous blood clots.
Pelvic floor exercises are recommended for urinary incontinence that persists at 3 months after birth, but not routinely for women without symptoms.

items.title: Combined hormonal versus nonhormonal versus progestin-only contraception in lactation
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 11 trials (1482 women) on whether hormonal birth control affects breastfeeding or infant growth. Most trials found no clear difference between groups in how long women breastfed, in milk composition, or in how babies grew. A few older studies suggested combined pills (with estrogen) may lower milk volume or breastfeeding duration, but results were often not well reported. Overall the evidence was limited and not consistent across methods.
keyPoints: Most trials found no significant difference in breastfeeding duration, breast milk composition or infant growth between contraceptive groups.
One combined pill trial showed lower milk volume than placebo, and an older pill trial reported shorter breastfeeding, though results were not always quantified.
Trials of the progestin-only pill, the hormonal IUD and the etonogestrel implant mostly showed no significant effect on breastfeeding.
The evidence was limited for any single method and results were not consistent across trials.

items.title: Timed intercourse for couples trying to conceive
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at seven trials with 2,464 women or couples to see whether timing sex around ovulation helps people conceive. Using urine ovulation tests probably increases the chance of a live birth and of a positive pregnancy test compared with having sex without tracking ovulation. For fertility awareness methods such as temperature or cervical mucus tracking, the evidence was too limited to say whether they help. The evidence ranged from moderate to very low quality.
keyPoints: Urine ovulation tests probably increase live birth: if the chance is 16% without tests, it is about 16% to 28% with them (moderate-quality evidence, one trial).
Urine ovulation tests probably also increase the chance of a clinical pregnancy or positive pregnancy test (moderate-quality evidence, four trials).
It is uncertain whether fertility awareness-based methods change live birth, pregnancy, time to pregnancy, stress, anxiety or depression, because the evidence was limited and low to very low quality.
The benefits seen were in women under 40 who had been trying for less than 12 months; no trials tested timing sex using ultrasound.

items.title: Effectiveness of Fertility Awareness-Based Methods for Pregnancy Prevention: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review pulled together 53 studies on how well fertility awareness-based methods prevent pregnancy. None of the studies were high quality, and the rest were moderate or low quality. Pregnancy rates varied a lot between methods and even within the same method, so the studies cannot be used to say that one method works better than another.
keyPoints: Of 53 studies, none were high quality, 21 were moderate quality and 32 were low quality.
In moderate-quality studies, typical-use pregnancy rates in the first year ranged from about 2 to 34 per 100 women, depending on the method and study.
Perfect-use rates were lower, from 0 to about 12 per 100 women in the first year.
Studies covered different groups of women, so the methods cannot be fairly compared with each other.

items.title: Interventions for fertility preservation in women with cancer undergoing chemotherapy
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at two ways to protect fertility in women having chemotherapy for cancer, mostly breast cancer: stimulating the ovaries to freeze eggs or embryos, and using GnRH agonist medicines to temporarily switch the ovaries off. GnRH agonists may greatly lower the chance that chemotherapy causes ovarian insufficiency (the ovaries stopping working properly), but the evidence is low certainty. For egg or embryo freezing with added protective drugs (letrozole or tamoxifen), there was no evidence on live births, ovarian insufficiency or survival. No studies compared the two approaches directly.
keyPoints: GnRH agonists may result in a large reduction in chemotherapy-related ovarian insufficiency in women with breast cancer (low-certainty evidence).
The effect of GnRH agonists on live birth is very uncertain, and they may make little or no difference to survival over 10 years (low certainty).
