For ovarian stimulation with letrozole or tamoxifen, there was no evidence on live birth or survival; there is probably little to no difference between the two drugs in the number of eggs retrieved.
No studies compared egg or embryo freezing directly with GnRH agonist suppression, and evidence for cancers other than breast cancer was too limited to draw conclusions.

items.title: Planned oocyte cryopreservation: a systematic review and meta-regression analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 10 studies of women who froze their eggs to protect against age-related fertility decline. About 11% of women came back to use their frozen eggs, and 28% of the women who returned had a live birth. Success was much higher when eggs were frozen at 35 or younger than at 40 or older. The authors say success rates are limited overall and that better-quality data are needed.
keyPoints: Across 8,750 women, about 11% returned to use their frozen eggs.
Live birth rate per woman was 28% overall, 52% if eggs were frozen at 35 or younger, and 19% at 40 or older.
About 78.5% of frozen eggs survived thawing.
Egg freezing is a feasible option for later conception, but the chance of a live birth falls as age at freezing rises.

items.title: Cleavage-stage versus blastocyst-stage embryo transfer in assisted reproductive technology
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 32 trials (5,821 women or couples) comparing IVF embryo transfer on day 5 to 6 (blastocyst stage) with transfer on day 2 to 3 (cleavage stage). In fresh transfers, blastocyst transfer was linked to higher live birth and clinical pregnancy rates. It was also linked to a higher chance that no embryo was available to transfer and to fewer spare embryos being frozen. The evidence for live birth was low quality, and it is still unclear whether the benefit holds when frozen embryo transfers are counted too.
keyPoints: Live birth after a fresh transfer was higher with blastocyst transfer: if 31% of women had a live birth with cleavage-stage transfer, about 32% to 41% would with blastocyst transfer (low-quality evidence).
Clinical pregnancy was also higher with blastocyst transfer, about 42% to 47% compared with 39% (moderate-quality evidence).
Having no embryo to transfer was more likely with blastocyst transfer (about 2% to 4% compared with 1%), and fewer women had spare embryos frozen (moderate and low-quality evidence).
The review is uncertain whether blastocyst transfer changes miscarriage or multiple pregnancy rates, or the total pregnancy rate across fresh and frozen transfers; more research is needed.

items.title: The role of assisted hatching in in vitro fertilization: a guideline
items.summary: This guideline from the American Society for Reproductive Medicine looked at assisted hatching, a lab step in IVF where a small opening is made in the outer shell of an embryo before transfer. It found moderate evidence that this step does not meaningfully raise live birth rates in fresh IVF cycles. There is not enough evidence to say whether it helps people with a poor outlook or those having frozen embryo transfers.
keyPoints: Moderate evidence shows assisted hatching does not significantly improve live birth rates in fresh IVF cycles.
Evidence is insufficient to show a benefit for patients with a poor prognosis.
Evidence is also insufficient to show a benefit in frozen embryo transfer cycles.
This guideline replaces the 2014 version.

items.title: Preparation of the Endometrium for Frozen Embryo Transfer: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This review looked at the different ways the womb lining can be prepared before a frozen embryo is transferred during IVF. Low-quality evidence suggests that natural cycle approaches may work better than hormone replacement treatment. The review also suggests that timing matters, and that progesterone levels can vary a lot between women even on the same dose. The authors say better-designed trials are urgently needed.
keyPoints: Low-quality evidence suggests natural cycle protocols (true or modified) may be better than hormone replacement treatment.
Suggested timing for a warmed blastocyst transfer is day 6 of progesterone start, day 6 after the LH surge, or day 7 after hCG, depending on the protocol.
Progesterone levels can differ markedly between women on the same dose and route, which may affect outcomes.
Well-designed trials comparing protocols on live birth and maternal and baby outcomes are urgently needed.

items.title: Endometrial preparation for women undergoing embryo transfer with frozen embryos or embryos derived from donor oocytes
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 31 trials (5,426 women) comparing ways to prepare the womb lining for frozen embryo transfer or transfer of embryos from donor eggs. The authors found not enough good evidence to say that any one method is best. Some small differences appeared, for example a stimulated cycle may give more clinical pregnancies than a fully medicated (programmed) cycle, and a natural cycle probably leads to fewer cancelled cycles. Most of the evidence was low or very low quality, so these results are uncertain.
keyPoints: Overall, there is insufficient evidence to recommend any one method of womb-lining preparation for frozen embryo or donor-egg transfers.
Stimulating the cycle (with FSH, letrozole or clomiphene) may improve clinical pregnancy rates compared with a programmed cycle (low-quality evidence).
A natural cycle probably reduces cycle cancellations compared with a programmed cycle, but the effect on live birth is uncertain.
Adding a GnRH agonist may improve live birth rates (low-quality evidence), while GnRH antagonists probably give better clinical pregnancy rates than agonists (moderate-quality evidence).

items.title: Risk factors for ectopic pregnancy occurrence: Systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: This review pooled 11 observational studies (25,051 women) to find out which factors are linked to ectopic pregnancy, where a pregnancy grows outside the womb. The strongest links were a past ectopic pregnancy, pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, abdominal or pelvic surgery, and previous tubal ligation. Smoking, older age, more than one partner, past miscarriage or abortion, earlier use of emergency contraception, and an intrauterine device were linked to a slightly higher risk. The authors suggest screening women who have the strong risk factors.
keyPoints: Strongest links to ectopic pregnancy: a past ectopic pregnancy (OR 9.03), abdominal or pelvic surgery (OR 5.60), previous tubal ligation (OR 5.59), pelvic inflammatory disease (OR 4.00) and infertility (OR 3.70).
Previous use of emergency contraception, an intrauterine device, smoking, older age and more than one partner showed only a slightly increased risk.
Oral contraceptive use was linked to a slightly lower risk, and condom use appeared to have very limited effect.
The authors suggest screening for ectopic pregnancy in women with the strong risk factors.

items.title: Interventions for emergency contraception
items.summary: This Cochrane review pulled together 115 trials with over 60,000 women to compare ways of preventing pregnancy after unprotected sex, including emergency contraception pills and the copper IUD. Levonorgestrel and mifepristone worked better than the older Yuzpe combination pills, and ulipristal acetate and mifepristone may work better than levonorgestrel. Nausea and vomiting were the main side effects, and some methods changed the timing of the next period. The quality of the evidence for pregnancy outcomes was moderate to high.
keyPoints: Levonorgestrel caused fewer pregnancies than the Yuzpe combination pills, with fewer side effects such as nausea and vomiting.
Ulipristal acetate was linked to fewer pregnancies than levonorgestrel, and mid-dose mifepristone (25 to 50 mg) was probably more effective than levonorgestrel.
Ulipristal acetate made a later-than-expected period more likely, and mifepristone caused period delay that seemed to depend on the dose.
The copper IUD and mifepristone showed no clear difference in pregnancy risk (low-quality evidence), and the copper IUD may cause more abdominal pain.

items.title: Diagnosis of Endometriosis
items.summary: This is a clinical practice guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists on how endometriosis should be evaluated and diagnosed. It covers the clinical, imaging and surgical steps of diagnosis for adults and adolescents who have symptoms that could point to endometriosis. The abstract does not list the specific recommendations. It notes that for adolescents the advice rests on limited evidence, data from adults and expert consensus.
keyPoints: The guideline gives recommendations on the clinical, imaging and surgical evaluation and diagnosis of endometriosis.
Recommendations are graded by strength and evidence quality, with ungraded Good Practice Points where evidence is lacking.
The advice also applies to adolescents unless stated otherwise.
For adolescents, recommendations draw on limited evidence, adult data and expert consensus.

items.title: Guideline No. 449: Diagnosis and Impact of Endometriosis - A Canadian Guideline
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline looks at how endometriosis is diagnosed and how much it affects people's lives. It says diagnosis can be supported by a detailed history, a physical exam and imaging tests, ideally with providers who have experience in endometriosis care. Surgery with lab testing can confirm the diagnosis, but it is not needed if imaging has already confirmed it. The guideline calls for earlier recognition and better education to cut delays in getting care.
keyPoints: Diagnosis can be made using a detailed history, examination and imaging tests with providers experienced in endometriosis care.
Surgery with pathology confirms endometriosis but is not required if imaging has already confirmed the diagnosis.
Earlier recognition is needed so people can get timely care and support.
Education for the public, patients, families, health care providers and administrators can help reduce delays in diagnosis and treatment.

items.title: The genetic basis of endometriosis and comorbidity with other pain and inflammatory conditions
items.summary: Researchers combined genetic data from over 60,000 women with endometriosis and about 700,000 women without it. They found 42 places in the genome linked to the condition, including genes involved in how pain is sensed. Endometriosis shared genetic links with other pain conditions such as migraine and back pain, and with inflammatory conditions such as asthma and osteoarthritis. The authors say more work is needed to turn this into new treatments.
keyPoints: 42 genome regions were linked to endometriosis, with the strongest effects seen in more advanced (stage 3/4) disease driven by ovarian endometriosis.
Some of the linked genes are involved in sensing and maintaining pain.
Endometriosis showed genetic overlap with 11 pain conditions, including migraine, back pain and chronic pain in several body sites.
It also overlapped genetically with inflammatory conditions such as asthma and osteoarthritis.

items.title: Effect of physical activity and exercise on endometriosis-associated symptoms: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at whether physical activity and exercise help with endometriosis symptoms such as pain. Only three small studies, with 109 women in total, were good enough to include. One study found less pain and one found lower stress, but the studies were too different and too limited to say whether exercise really helps.
keyPoints: Only three studies (two randomized trials and one without a control group) with 109 women were included.
Only one study found improved pain, and one showed lower stress levels.
The effect of exercise on endometriosis symptoms could not be determined because of major limitations in the studies.
Better-designed trials are needed that measure pain, quality of life and what patients think of the exercise.

items.title: Laparoscopic surgery for endometriosis
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 14 trials (1563 women) looking at keyhole (laparoscopic) surgery for endometriosis, a condition linked to pain and difficulty getting pregnant. Compared with a look-only keyhole operation, surgery probably increases the chance of an ultrasound-confirmed ongoing pregnancy. It is uncertain whether surgery reduces pain, and no trials reported live birth. Many of the studies were small or poorly reported, so the evidence for most outcomes is weak.
keyPoints: Laparoscopic surgery probably increases the rate of viable pregnancies confirmed by ultrasound compared with diagnostic laparoscopy only (moderate quality evidence).
It is uncertain whether surgery reduces overall pain, as the evidence was very low quality and based on very few women.
No studies looked at live birth, and there was not enough information on adverse events to draw conclusions about safety.
There was not enough evidence to say whether ablation or excision works better, or whether one heat tool is better than another.

items.title: Pre- and postsurgical medical therapy for endometriosis surgery
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 26 trials (3457 women) to see whether hormone-suppressing medicines work better when taken before surgery, after surgery, or both, for endometriosis. Taking medicine after surgery may lower the chance that the disease returns and probably increases pregnancy rates compared with surgery alone. For taking medicine before surgery, or comparing before with after, the evidence was too weak to draw conclusions. No trials looked at medicine both before and after surgery, and there was not enough data on serious side effects.
keyPoints: Hormone medicine after surgery may reduce disease recurrence within 12 months compared with surgery alone (low-quality evidence).
Hormone medicine after surgery probably increases pregnancy rates compared with surgery alone (moderate-quality evidence).
Evidence on medicine taken before surgery, or on before versus after, was uncertain (low to very low quality).
Not enough data to judge serious side effects, and no trials tested medicine both before and after surgery.

items.title: Physical exercise in pregnancy: benefits, risks and prescription
items.summary: This review pulled together the strongest published research (57 articles, including 32 meta-analyses and 16 randomized trials) on exercising during pregnancy. It found that regular exercise is linked to many benefits and was not linked to a higher risk of problems for the mother or baby. The authors say the type and amount of exercise should fit a woman's earlier fitness level, health history and the details of her pregnancy.
keyPoints: Exercise can help prevent gestational diabetes, excessive weight gain in pregnancy, hypertensive disorders, urinary incontinence and large babies (fetal macrosomia).
Exercise can also help prevent lower back and pelvic pain, anxiety and depression during pregnancy.
Exercise was not related to an increased risk of adverse outcomes for the mother or baby.
Following current exercise guidelines is enough to get the main benefits, and exercise type and intensity should be based on a woman's previous fitness level.

items.title: Physical Activity and Exercise During Pregnancy and the Postpartum Period: ACOG Committee Opinion, Number 804
items.summary: This guidance from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) looks at exercise during pregnancy and after birth. It says that for most women without pregnancy or medical complications, staying active or starting safe activity is safe and desirable. Women who were already active, even at vigorous levels, can generally keep going, though some routines may need small changes as the body changes.
keyPoints: Without pregnancy or medical complications, physical activity in pregnancy is safe and desirable, and women are encouraged to continue or start safe activities.
Women who were active before pregnancy, including vigorous aerobic activity, can continue during pregnancy and after birth.
Observational studies link exercise in pregnancy to less gestational diabetes, fewer cesarean births and assisted vaginal deliveries, and faster postpartum recovery.
Physical activity may help prevent postpartum depression, and some exercise routines may need adjusting for normal body changes in pregnancy.

items.title: Combined diet and exercise interventions for preventing gestational diabetes mellitus
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 23 trials with nearly 9,000 pregnant women to see whether combining healthy eating and exercise programmes helps prevent gestational diabetes. Women in the programmes had a possibly lower chance of gestational diabetes and caesarean birth, and gained a little less weight during pregnancy. There were no clear differences for pre-eclampsia, high blood pressure, large babies or baby deaths. The programmes in the trials varied a lot, so the review says its findings have limited ability to guide practice.
keyPoints: Diet and exercise programmes may reduce the risk of gestational diabetes slightly (moderate-quality evidence), though the result was borderline.
Women in the programmes gained about 0.9 kg less weight during pregnancy on average (moderate-quality evidence).
A possible small reduction in caesarean section was seen (moderate-quality evidence).
No clear differences were found for pre-eclampsia, high blood pressure, large-for-gestational-age babies or perinatal death (low to very low-quality evidence).

items.title: Bed rest in singleton pregnancies for preventing preterm birth
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether being prescribed bed rest, at home or in hospital, helps prevent early (preterm) birth in women at high risk. Only two studies qualified, and only one (1266 women) could be analysed. Early birth before 37 weeks was similar with bed rest (7.9%) and without it (8.5%). The authors found no evidence for or against bed rest, even though it is widely used.
keyPoints: Only two studies met the review's criteria, so the evidence is very limited.
In the one analysed study, preterm birth before 37 weeks was similar with bed rest (7.9%) and without (8.5%).
There is no evidence that bed rest at home or in hospital prevents preterm birth, and none showing it does not.
Because bed rest may have downsides for women, families and healthcare costs, the authors say pros and cons should be discussed with women at risk.

items.title: Fetal Movement Counting and Perinatal Mortality: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled five randomized trials covering about 468,000 pregnancies. It compared women taught to count their baby's movements with women who were not given this instruction. Teaching movement counting was not linked to a clear drop in baby deaths around the time of birth. It was weakly linked to slightly more preterm births, labor inductions and cesarean births.
keyPoints: Perinatal death was 0.54% with movement counting and 0.59% without, a difference that was not clearly significant (relative risk 0.92, 95% CI 0.85-1.00).
No clear differences were found in stillbirths, neonatal deaths, low birth weight, Apgar scores or NICU admissions.
Small increases were seen in preterm delivery (7.6% vs 7.1%), induction of labor (36.6% vs 31.6%) and cesarean delivery (28.2% vs 25.3%).
The authors concluded that instructing women to count movements is not associated with a clear improvement in pregnancy outcomes.

items.title: Planned early delivery versus expectant management of the term suspected compromised baby for improving outcomes
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at what to do at term (37 weeks or later) when a baby is suspected to be compromised, such as when growth is slow or fluid around the baby is low. It compared planning an early delivery with waiting and monitoring. Across three trials of 546 women, there were no clear differences in deaths, serious illness for babies or mothers, or development at two years. The trials only covered slow growth and low fluid, so the findings cannot be applied to every suspected problem, such as reduced baby movements.
keyPoints: No clear difference in perinatal death, major newborn illness, or disability at two years between early delivery and waiting.
Early delivery meant birth about 10 days earlier on average, more inductions, and more babies admitted to intermediate care nursery.
Caesarean rates, vaginal birth, pre-eclampsia and breastfeeding did not differ between the two approaches.
Only three trials were included, covering slow growth and low amniotic fluid; reduced fetal movement and abnormal heart tracings still need their own trials.

items.title: Risk of Recurrence and Reintervention After Uterine-Sparing Interventions for Symptomatic Adenomyosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 42 studies (5,877 women) to see how often symptoms or lesions come back after treatments that keep the womb in place for adenomyosis. Three options were looked at: surgery to remove the adenomyosis (adenomyomectomy), uterine artery embolization (blocking blood flow to the womb), and image-guided heat ablation. These treatments worked well overall and few women needed another procedure, but embolization had higher recurrence and reintervention rates. The women treated with embolization had larger wombs and larger adenomyosis, so the comparison may be unfair, and the authors say more randomized trials are needed.
keyPoints: Recurrence rates were about 12.6% after adenomyomectomy, 29.5% after uterine artery embolization and 10.0% after image-guided thermal ablation.
Reintervention rates were about 2.6% after adenomyomectomy, 12.8% after embolization and 8.2% after thermal ablation.
Embolization had higher recurrence and reintervention rates, but those patients had larger wombs and larger adenomyosis, so selection bias may explain some of the gap.
The included studies were single-arm studies, and larger randomized controlled trials are still needed.

items.title: Folic Acid Supplementation to Prevent Neural Tube Defects: Updated Evidence Report and Systematic Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force
items.summary: This review looked at newer studies on whether taking folic acid around pregnancy helps prevent neural tube defects, which are serious birth defects of the brain and spine. The studies suggested folic acid lowered the chance of these defects, and found no signs of harm for twin pregnancy, autism or cancer in the mother. The new findings matched what earlier reviews had found. Most of the evidence came from observational studies rather than trials.
keyPoints: One large cohort study found a lower risk of neural tube defects with folic acid taken before pregnancy, during pregnancy, or both.
The lower risk was seen only in the later study period (2006-2013), not the earlier one (1999-2005), and no other significant benefits were reported.
No study found significant harms linked to folic acid in pregnancy, including multiple births, autism or maternal cancer.
The new evidence agreed with previously reviewed evidence on benefits and harms.

items.title: Guideline No. 427: Folic Acid and Multivitamin Supplementation for Prevention of Folic Acid-Sensitive Congenital Anomalies
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline gives updated advice on folic acid and multivitamin supplements for women who could become pregnant, to help prevent neural tube defects and other folate-sensitive birth defects. A low daily dose of folic acid is recommended for all women who could become pregnant, before conception and throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding. A higher dose is advised only for women who have had a previous pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect or similar condition. The abstract does not give the specific doses or the certainty ratings.
keyPoints: All women who could become pregnant are advised to take a low daily dose of folic acid before conception and throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding.
High-dose folic acid is recommended only for women who have had a previous pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect or other folate-sensitive birth defect.
Folic acid, or folate from food plus a multivitamin, is linked to lower rates of neural tube defects, other birth defects and some pregnancy complications.
Women with complex risks (genetic, medical or surgical) may benefit from a personalised approach, possibly including folate blood testing.

items.title: Practice Bulletin No. 187: Neural Tube Defects
items.summary: This guideline from a leading obstetrics group explains neural tube defects, which are birth defects of the brain, spine or spinal cord. It notes that, unlike many other birth defects, these can be prevented in the first place with folic acid. It also says screening and diagnosis in pregnancy are widely available and that fetal surgery has improved outcomes for some babies.
keyPoints: Neural tube defects are the second most common major birth defect after heart defects.
Primary prevention of neural tube defects is possible with folic acid, unlike many other birth defects.
Prenatal screening and diagnosis for neural tube defects are widely available.
Outcomes depend on the level and extent of the defect; most babies with spina bifida survive after surgical repair, while anencephaly is not compatible with life.

items.title: Effects and safety of periconceptional oral folate supplementation for preventing birth defects
items.summary: This Cochrane review combined five trials with 7,391 women to see whether taking folic acid around the time of conception prevents birth defects. Daily folic acid, taken alone or with other vitamins and minerals, clearly reduced neural tube defects (serious defects of the baby's brain and spine), including in women who had a previous affected pregnancy. There was no clear effect, good or bad, on cleft lip or palate, heart defects, other birth defects or miscarriage, though the evidence for most of these was low quality.
keyPoints: Folic acid reduced neural tube defects by about two-thirds compared with no folic acid (risk ratio 0.31), based on high quality evidence.
The protective effect held for first-time and repeat (recurrence) neural tube defects, and was the same at 400 micrograms (0.4 mg) a day or higher, alone or with other vitamins.
No clear effect was found on cleft lip, cleft palate, heart defects or other birth defects, but the evidence was low quality.
Folic acid did not appear to raise the risk of miscarriage (moderate quality evidence).

items.title: Prevention of neural tube defects: results of the Medical Research Council Vitamin Study. MRC Vitamin Study Research Group
items.summary: This large trial followed 1817 women who had previously had a pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect (such as spina bifida). Women took folic acid, a mix of other vitamins, both, or neither around the time of conception. Neural tube defects were far less common in the folic acid groups: 6 cases compared with 21 in the groups without folic acid, a 72% protective effect. The other vitamins did not show a clear benefit, and no harm from folic acid was seen, though the study could not rule out rare or slight side effects.
keyPoints: Folic acid cut the risk of neural tube defects by 72% in women who had a previous affected pregnancy.
The mix of other vitamins (A, D, B1, B2, B6, C and nicotinamide) showed no significant protective effect.
No demonstrable harm from folic acid was found, but the study had limited ability to detect rare or slight side effects.
The authors recommended folic acid starting before pregnancy for women who have had an affected pregnancy, and diets with enough folic acid for all women who may have children.

items.title: Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine Consult Series #52: Diagnosis and management of fetal growth restriction: (Replaces Clinical Guideline Number 3, April 2012)
items.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
items.summary: This guideline from the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine explains how doctors should diagnose and manage fetal growth restriction, when a baby is measuring smaller than expected in the womb. It affects up to 10% of pregnancies. The guideline sets out how it is defined, which tests to offer, how closely to monitor the baby, and when to plan delivery. It does not cover food safety or fish in pregnancy.
keyPoints: Fetal growth restriction is defined as an ultrasound estimated weight or abdominal size below the 10th percentile for gestational age.
Once it is diagnosed, regular ultrasound Doppler checks of blood flow in the umbilical cord are recommended to watch for changes.
Timing of delivery depends on the Doppler results and how small the baby is, ranging from about 30-32 weeks up to 38-39 weeks.
Low-molecular-weight heparin, sildenafil and activity restriction are recommended against as treatments for fetal growth restriction.

items.title: Antioxidants for female subfertility
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 63 trials with 7760 women who were having trouble getting pregnant, to see whether antioxidant supplements taken by mouth help. Some results suggested higher live birth and pregnancy rates, but the quality of the evidence was low to very low, so we cannot be sure. No increase in miscarriage, multiple pregnancy, stomach upset or ectopic pregnancy was seen, though that evidence was also of low quality. A 2026 editorial note says nine included studies were retracted or flagged, but the editors found this did not meaningfully change the conclusions.
keyPoints: Antioxidants may improve live birth and clinical pregnancy rates compared with placebo or no treatment, but the evidence is very low to low quality.
No difference was found in miscarriage, multiple pregnancy, gastrointestinal problems or ectopic pregnancy, based on low-quality evidence.
Comparisons between different antioxidants, such as lower versus higher melatonin doses, showed no clear difference.
Overall, evidence supporting oral antioxidant supplements for subfertile women is limited.

items.title: Interventions to Prevent Perinatal Depression: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force reviewed ways to prevent depression during pregnancy and after birth, which affects as many as 1 in 7 women. It found convincing evidence that counseling, such as cognitive behavioral therapy and interpersonal therapy, helps prevent it. The Task Force is moderately certain this approach has a moderate benefit and little risk of harm. Evidence for other approaches, such as exercise, education or supplements, was too limited to judge.
keyPoints: Counseling such as cognitive behavioral therapy and interpersonal therapy is effective in preventing perinatal depression.
Women with past depression, current depressive symptoms, or risk factors like low income or young or single parenthood may benefit most.
Harms of counseling were judged to be no greater than small.
There was not enough evidence to judge the benefits and harms of other non-counseling approaches.

items.title: The AUA/SUFU/AUGS Guideline on Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause
items.summary: This guideline from US urology and gynaecology bodies reviews the evidence on genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM), the vaginal and urinary symptoms caused by falling estrogen around menopause. GSM is diagnosed from a person's symptoms, with or without physical findings, once other causes have been ruled out. Many hormonal and non-hormonal treatments have been studied, and low-dose vaginal estrogen has the strongest evidence. There was not enough information to say that one hormonal treatment is better than another.
keyPoints: GSM is diagnosed from symptoms, with or without physical changes, after other causes are ruled out.
Urinary symptoms of GSM can look like other common bladder conditions such as overactive bladder.
Local low-dose vaginal estrogen has the most robust evidence among the treatment options.
There is not enough evidence to favour one hormonal therapy over another, so treatment is chosen through shared decision-making based on patient goals and preferences.

items.title: Vaginal lasers for treating stress urinary incontinence in women
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether vaginal laser treatment helps women with stress urinary incontinence (leaking urine when coughing, sneezing or exercising). It combined nine trials with 689 women, comparing lasers with sham (pretend) treatment or with topical treatments such as oestrogen. Lasers may make little or no difference in the first year, and any small improvement in symptom scores may not be noticeable to patients. The evidence is very uncertain, and no major side effects were seen.
keyPoints: In the short term (under one year), vaginal lasers may make little to no difference to stress urinary incontinence compared with sham or topical treatments.
The small improvement seen in symptom questionnaire scores may not be big enough for patients to notice.
One small study suggested more women were continent after one to five years with laser, but the evidence is very uncertain.
No major adverse events were reported with lasers, sham treatment or topical oestrogen.

items.title: Clinical Practice Guidelines for Managing Genitourinary Symptoms Associated With Menopause
items.summary: This guideline looks at genitourinary syndrome of menopause, a group of vaginal and urinary symptoms caused by low estrogen after menopause. These include dryness, burning, pain with sex, urinary urgency, painful urination and repeat urinary tract infections. It says the symptoms can strongly affect wellbeing and quality of life, and it describes several treatment options.
keyPoints: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause is caused by low estrogen and includes genital dryness, burning or irritation, sexual discomfort, and urinary symptoms such as urgency, painful urination and recurrent UTIs.
The symptoms can have a profound effect on wellbeing, daily functioning and quality of life in postmenopausal women.
Vaginal moisturizers and lubricants are used to give symptom relief.

Hormonal treatments help thicken the vaginal lining and increase vaginal secretions, and pelvic floor physical therapy and behavioral therapies address pelvic floor tightness and psychosocial factors.

items.title: Local oestrogen for vaginal atrophy in postmenopausal women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 30 trials (6,235 postmenopausal women) of oestrogen put directly into the vagina as a ring, cream or tablet to treat vaginal atrophy, which causes dryness, itching and painful sex. The different forms worked about equally well when compared with each other. Compared with placebo (a dummy treatment), the oestrogen treatments improved symptoms, though the evidence was mostly low quality.
keyPoints: No clear difference in symptom relief was found between oestrogen ring, cream and tablets.
Vaginal oestrogen improved symptoms of vaginal atrophy more than placebo, based on low-quality evidence.
Oestrogen cream may be linked to a thickening of the womb lining compared with the ring, possibly because higher doses of cream were used.
Overall side effects did not clearly differ between the oestrogen forms or compared with placebo.

items.title: Effects of Dietary Approaches and Exercise Interventions on Gestational Diabetes Mellitus: A Systematic Review and Bayesian Network Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 39 trials involving 2,712 women with gestational diabetes to compare different diets and types of exercise. The DASH diet (rich in fruit, vegetables and whole grains) and low glycemic index diets were linked to better blood sugar control and lower baby birth weight. Resistance exercise and the DASH diet were also linked to less need for insulin. The certainty of the evidence was low or very low, so the authors say better-quality research is still needed.
keyPoints: The DASH diet and low glycemic index diets improved blood sugar control, though the certainty of evidence was very low to low.
The DASH diet and resistance exercise each reduced the need for insulin therapy.
Both diets lowered newborn birth weight, and the DASH diet was also linked to fewer large babies (macrosomia) and fewer cesarean births.
Exercise did not change infant outcomes; effects on babies were seen mainly with diet changes.

items.title: Antenatal dietary supplementation with myo-inositol for preventing gestational diabetes
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at seven trials (1319 pregnant women) of myo-inositol, a natural sugar-like supplement, to see if it helps prevent gestational diabetes. The trials suggest it may lower the chance of gestational diabetes, high blood pressure disorders in pregnancy and preterm birth. However, the studies were small, mostly done in Italy, and the certainty of the evidence was low to very low, so the results are uncertain.
keyPoints: Myo-inositol may reduce gestational diabetes (risk ratio 0.53) and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (risk ratio 0.34).
It may also be linked to fewer preterm births, and may make little to no difference to caesarean section rates.
The effect on large-for-gestational-age babies, weight gain in pregnancy and newborn low blood sugar was unclear.
The authors call for larger studies in more diverse groups of women, with long-term follow-up and checks for harms.

items.title: Induction of labour at or near term for suspected fetal macrosomia
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at four trials (1190 women) comparing induction of labour at or near term with waiting for labour to start, when a baby was thought to be very large (over 4000 g). Induction did not clearly change the chance of caesarean birth or instrumental delivery. It did lower the chance of shoulder dystocia and of broken bones in the baby, and babies were born a little smaller on average. The authors suggest the pros and cons of induction be discussed with parents.
keyPoints: Induction did not clearly change the risk of caesarean section or instrumental (forceps or vacuum) delivery.
Shoulder dystocia and birth fractures were less common with induction; about 60 inductions would be needed to prevent one fracture.
Scan estimates of baby weight are often inaccurate, so some women may worry or be induced unnecessarily.
One large trial saw more use of phototherapy for newborns after induction, and the trials were too small to show an effect on the rare nerve injury called brachial plexus injury.

items.title: Gestational diabetes mellitus and adverse pregnancy outcomes: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This large review pulled together 156 studies covering more than 7.5 million pregnancies to see how gestational diabetes relates to problems in pregnancy and for babies. After accounting for other factors, gestational diabetes was linked to higher chances of caesarean birth, preterm birth, larger babies and some newborn complications. For several other outcomes, such as stillbirth and shoulder dystocia, no clear difference was found. Only about a third of the studies had a low or medium risk of bias, and results varied between studies.
keyPoints: In studies where no insulin was used, gestational diabetes was linked to higher odds of caesarean section, preterm delivery, macrosomia (a very large baby) and a baby born large for gestational age.

In studies where insulin was used, gestational diabetes was linked to higher odds of a large-for-gestational-age baby, neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, newborn jaundice and neonatal intensive care admission.
No clear difference was found for stillbirth, neonatal death, shoulder dystocia, postpartum haemorrhage or instrumental delivery.
Differences between countries, screening methods and whether body mass index was adjusted for explained some of the variation between studies.

items.title: Macrosomia: ACOG Practice Bulletin, Number 216
items.summary: This guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists looks at babies who are expected to be born very large (macrosomia). It explains that as birth weight goes up, the chances of a difficult labor, shoulder dystocia (a baby's shoulder getting stuck), birth injury and lasting harm to the newborn also go up. It also covers how accurate the methods for estimating a baby's weight are, what their limits are, and how care can be managed when a large baby is suspected. It has been updated with newer research, including on preventing macrosomia.
keyPoints: The larger the baby's birth weight, the higher the chance of labor problems, shoulder dystocia, birth trauma and permanent injury to the newborn.
Methods for estimating a baby's weight before birth have limits in how accurate they are.
The guideline suggests how to manage a pregnancy when a very large baby is suspected.
It has been updated with recent research on preventing macrosomia.

items.title: Hyperglycemia and adverse pregnancy outcomes
items.summary: This large study followed about 25,500 pregnant women from nine countries who had a glucose drink test at 24 to 32 weeks of pregnancy. It looked at whether blood sugar levels lower than those that count as diabetes were still linked to problems for mothers and babies. Higher blood sugar was linked to larger babies and higher insulin-related markers in cord blood, and the risk rose steadily with no clear cut-off point.
keyPoints: Higher blood sugar in pregnancy, even below the level of diabetes, was linked to a higher chance of a baby with a birth weight above the 90th percentile.
Higher blood sugar was also linked to higher cord-blood C-peptide levels (a sign of the baby making extra insulin).
Links with caesarean delivery and newborn low blood sugar were weaker, and the same pattern was seen for other outcomes like early birth, shoulder dystocia and preeclampsia.
The researchers found no obvious blood sugar threshold where risks suddenly increased.

items.title: Interventions for treating urinary incontinence in older women: a network meta-analysis
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 43 trials with 8506 women aged 60 and over who have urinary incontinence (leaking urine). Treatments that train the pelvic floor muscles, with or without education or complementary therapies, looked the most helpful for cure and improvement, with bladder medicines also showing some benefit. However, the evidence was very low to low certainty because trials were small and often had weaknesses, so no firm conclusion about the single best treatment can be drawn.
keyPoints: Physical therapies, mainly pelvic floor muscle training, performed best for 'cure' and for 'cure or improvement' of incontinence in older women.
Adding education or complementary therapies to physical therapy may help further, but this rested on very few studies.
Bladder medicines (β3-adrenergic agonists and antimuscarinic drugs) also improved symptoms compared with control, and some medicine trials reported serious side effects.
No serious adverse events were reported for conservative treatments, but the evidence was too limited to say whether any treatment is safer than another.

items.title: Resistance training for postmenopausal women: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 12 small trials (452 women in total) looking at resistance (strength) training after menopause. Compared with no exercise, strength training of up to 16 weeks seemed to improve everyday physical function and bone density and to reduce hot flashes. No serious side effects were reported. The studies were small and had unclear to high risk of bias, so the evidence is low to very low certainty and better trials are still needed.
keyPoints: Compared with no exercise, resistance training seemed to improve functional capacity and bone mineral density and reduce hot flash frequency.
Compared with aerobic exercise, resistance training may reduce hot flash frequency and fat mass, with no clear difference in quality of life.
No serious adverse events were reported.
The certainty of the evidence was low to very low, so the effects are imprecisely estimated and higher-quality trials are needed.

items.title: Risk-Reducing Salpingo-Oophorectomy and the Use of Hormone Replacement Therapy Below the Age of Natural Menopause: Scientific Impact Paper No. 66 October 2021: Scientific Impact Paper No. 66
items.source: Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
items.organisation: Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
items.summary: This Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists paper looks at hormone replacement therapy (HRT) for women who have their ovaries and fallopian tubes removed to prevent ovarian cancer before the natural age of menopause. Removing the ovaries causes early menopause, which brings hot flushes, mood changes, bone thinning and a higher risk of heart disease. HRT is usually advisable up to about age 51 for women who have not had breast cancer. Research suggests HRT in early menopause does not raise breast cancer risk, including for BRCA1 and BRCA2 carriers.
keyPoints: HRT is usually advisable up to about age 51 (the average UK age of menopause) for women in early menopause after preventative surgery who have not had breast cancer.
Women with a womb are given estrogen plus progestogen to protect the womb lining; women without a womb are given estrogen only.
Unlike in older women, HRT in early menopause does not appear to increase breast cancer risk, including in BRCA1 and BRCA2 carriers after preventative surgery.
Non-hormonal medicines and behavioural therapy are options if HRT cannot be used, but they are less effective; regular exercise and a healthy lifestyle are also advised.

items.title: Management of urinary incontinence in postmenopausal women: An EMAS clinical guide
items.summary: This is a clinical guide from the European Menopause and Andropause Society (EMAS) on managing urinary incontinence (bladder leakage) after the menopause. Leakage becomes more common with age, affecting 38% to 55% of women over 60, yet few women seek help. The guide, based on a literature review and expert consensus, says treatment usually starts with lifestyle changes, pelvic floor exercises and bladder training, with other options available if these are not enough.
keyPoints: Urinary incontinence affects 38% to 55% of women over 60, but few seek care.
First-line management is lifestyle and behavior changes, pelvic floor exercises and bladder training.
Estrogens and other medicines can help urgency incontinence that does not improve with these measures.
Surgery, including midurethral slings, is described as safe and effective for stress incontinence in postmenopausal women.

items.title: Medical treatment of fibroids: FIGO best practice guidance
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: This international guidance from FIGO looks at medicines for uterine fibroids, which are common non-cancerous growths in the womb. Only a few drugs are officially approved for fibroids, mainly certain GnRH antagonists, and these medicines are mostly used before surgery because of side effects with long-term use. Other medicines, such as the combined pill, progestin tablets, the hormonal coil (LNG-IUS) and tranexamic acid, are not specifically approved for fibroids but can lighten heavy periods. This can ease symptoms and improve quality of life.
keyPoints: Only a few medicines are officially approved to treat fibroids, including some GnRH antagonists.
GnRH analogs are mainly used before surgery because of their long-term side effects.
Ulipristal acetate was heavily restricted because of safety concerns.
Combined pills, progestins, the LNG-IUS and tranexamic acid can reduce heavy bleeding from fibroids and improve quality of life.

items.title: Guideline No. 437: Diagnosis and Management of Adenomyosis
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline describes how adenomyosis (a condition where womb-lining tissue grows into the muscle wall of the uterus) is diagnosed and treated. It says ultrasound or MRI scans can be used to diagnose it. Treatment is matched to symptoms such as heavy periods, pain or trouble getting pregnant, and the guideline notes that options which preserve fertility are available. The abstract lists the options but does not give the detailed recommendations or how strong the evidence is.
keyPoints: Adenomyosis is common in women of reproductive age.
It can be diagnosed with transvaginal ultrasound or MRI.

Medicines that may be used include anti-inflammatory painkillers, tranexamic acid, combined contraceptive pills, the hormonal coil (levonorgestrel IUS), dienogest and other progestins, and GnRH analogues.
Other options include uterine artery embolization and surgery (endometrial ablation, removing adenomyosis tissue, or hysterectomy), and fertility-preserving options exist.

items.title: The Prevalence of Menstrual Cycle Disorders and Menstrual Cycle-Related Symptoms in Female Athletes: A Systematic Literature Review
items.summary: This review pulled together 60 studies of 6,380 female athletes not using hormonal contraceptives to see how common period problems and period-related symptoms are. Period problems were common, and painful periods (dysmenorrhoea) were the most frequent at about 1 in 3 athletes, though results varied a lot between studies. Most studies relied on athletes remembering their symptoms, and the authors say better, standardised ways of measuring problems like heavy bleeding are needed.
keyPoints: Painful periods were the most common period problem, affecting about 32% of athletes (range 7.8% to 85.6%).
Prevalence varied widely for every type of period disorder, including heavy menstrual bleeding, and little data existed on anovulation or luteal phase deficiency.
Mood-related symptoms appeared more common than physical ones, and more athletes reported symptoms in the first days of a period than before it.
Nine in ten studies relied on athletes recalling symptoms, and most studies were of moderate quality; the authors call for standard definitions and prospective tracking of cycles and symptoms.

items.title: Interventions for heavy menstrual bleeding; overview of Cochrane reviews and network meta-analysis
items.summary: This large review pulled together nine Cochrane reviews to compare treatments for heavy periods, which affect 2 to 5 in every 10 women of reproductive age. Among first-choice treatments, the hormone coil (LNG-IUS) reduced bleeding the most, followed by tranexamic acid and long-cycle progestogen pills. Among second-choice treatments, hysterectomy reduced bleeding the most, followed by endometrial ablation. Much of the evidence was low or very low certainty, so many treatments could not be confidently compared.
keyPoints: The levonorgestrel hormone coil (LNG-IUS) was the best first-line treatment for reducing menstrual blood loss, though the evidence was low certainty.
Tranexamic acid (an antifibrinolytic) probably reduces bleeding (moderate certainty), and long-cycle progestogens also reduced it (low certainty).
For second-line treatment, hysterectomy reduced bleeding the most, followed by endometrial ablation procedures.
No firm conclusions could be drawn on satisfaction with first-line treatments because the evidence was very low certainty.

items.title: Interventions to prevent or treat heavy menstrual bleeding or pain associated with intrauterine-device use
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 21 trials of medicines and other treatments for heavy bleeding or pain linked to using an IUD (coil) for contraception. Most trials were small, and the evidence was mostly low or very low quality, so the authors say the findings should be read with caution. Some treatments, such as vitamin B1 and mefenamic acid, showed possible benefits for heavy bleeding with the copper IUD, but these need more research.
keyPoints: In one trial of copper IUD users, vitamin B1 led to fewer pads used per day and fewer bleeding days than placebo (low-certainty evidence).
Mefenamic acid led to less blood loss than tranexamic acid in copper IUD users, though bleeding duration did not differ (low-certainty evidence).
Tolfenamic acid may help prevent heavy bleeding with a copper IUD (very low-certainty evidence), but may not prevent painful periods.
Ulipristal acetate did not clearly reduce bleeding with the levonorgestrel IUD, and may have increased the percentage of bleeding days when used for prevention.

items.title: International Menopause Society (IMS) recommendations and key messages on women's midlife health and menopause
items.summary: The International Menopause Society reviewed the research on midlife health and menopause and wrote new guidance for healthcare professionals. It covers hot flushes and night sweats, vaginal and urinary symptoms of menopause, early menopause (premature ovarian insufficiency), bone health, heart health and more. The abstract describes how the guidance was built but does not list the individual recommendations.
keyPoints: The guidance contains 342 recommendations (285 backed by research and 57 good practice points) and 40 key messages.
Topics include hot flushes and night sweats, genitourinary syndrome of menopause, premature ovarian insufficiency, osteoporosis, cardiometabolic health and dementia.
It covers menopause hormone therapy (estrogens, progestogens and combined treatments) and alternatives, and takes account of differences in care between countries.
A new section looks at sarcopenia (loss of muscle), which the authors say needs urgent attention.

items.title: Black cohosh extracts in women with menopausal symptoms: an updated pairwise meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 22 randomised trials with 2,310 menopausal women to see whether black cohosh extracts ease menopausal symptoms. Compared with placebo, black cohosh was linked to better overall symptoms, fewer hot flushes and fewer physical symptoms. It did not clearly improve anxiety or low mood. The authors describe the benefits as potential rather than certain.
keyPoints: Black cohosh extracts improved overall menopausal symptoms compared with placebo.
Hot flushes and physical (somatic) symptoms improved with black cohosh.
No clear improvement was found for anxiety or depressive symptoms.
Women stopped taking black cohosh at about the same rate as placebo.

items.title: Menopausal hormone therapy and women's health: An umbrella review
items.summary: This review pulled together results from 60 earlier systematic reviews on menopausal hormone therapy (MHT), covering many different health outcomes. In trials, MHT clearly reduced how often and how severe hot flushes and night sweats were, and it also lowered the risk of fractures. It was also linked to higher risks of stroke and blood clots, so the overall picture is a mix of benefits and harms. The authors say the quality of the evidence is only moderate to poor, and the review could not show how effects differ by dose, type, or when treatment starts.
keyPoints: In trials, MHT reduced the frequency of hot flushes and night sweats (risk ratio 0.43) and their severity (risk ratio 0.29).
MHT lowered the risk of fractures overall, and was also beneficial for vaginal dryness (vaginal estrogen) and sexual function.
MHT increased the risk of stroke and venous thromboembolism (blood clots), along with some other conditions such as gallbladder disease needing surgery.

Observational studies linked MHT to higher risks of breast and ovarian cancer, and estrogen-alone versus estrogen-plus-progestin therapy had opposite effects on some outcomes such as endometrial cancer.

items.title: Hormone replacement therapy after surgery for epithelial ovarian cancer
items.summary: This review looked at whether hormone replacement therapy (HRT) is safe and helpful for women who had surgery for epithelial ovarian cancer and then went through menopause. It found only three small trials with 350 women in total. HRT may slightly improve overall survival and may make little or no difference to the cancer coming back or progressing. The evidence is low or very low quality, so the results should be treated with caution.
keyPoints: HRT may slightly improve overall survival after surgery for epithelial ovarian cancer (low-certainty evidence).
HRT may make little or no difference to progression-free survival (low-certainty evidence).
Researchers are uncertain about effects on quality of life, breast cancer, stroke, mini-stroke and heart attack because the evidence was very low quality.
The evidence is too limited to show that HRT is very harmful in this group, and better trials are needed.

items.title: Progestogens or progestogen-releasing intrauterine systems for uterine fibroids (other than preoperative medical therapy)
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether progestogen pills or progestogen-releasing coils (intrauterine systems) help women before menopause who have uterine fibroids, which can cause heavy periods. Only four small studies (221 women) were found, and the evidence was very low quality, so it is uncertain whether these treatments reduce bleeding or raise haemoglobin compared with the contraceptive pill or other hormone treatments. Hot flushes were reported with goserelin acetate (55% of women) but not with the oral progestogens dienogest or desogestrel.
keyPoints: Four small trials (221 women) were included, and all evidence was very low quality.
It is uncertain whether the progestogen coil (LNG-IUS) reduces heavy bleeding or raises haemoglobin compared with the combined pill or norethisterone acetate.
There was not enough evidence to say whether the coil shrinks fibroids more than the combined pill.
Hot flushes (vasomotor symptoms) occurred in 55% of women on goserelin acetate but not in those on dienogest or desogestrel.

items.title: Treatment of Symptoms of the Menopause: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: This is a clinical practice guideline from the Endocrine Society on treating menopause symptoms. It found that menopausal hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for hot flushes and night sweats. For women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause starting, the benefits may outweigh the risks for most who have symptoms. Other options exist for vaginal symptoms and for women who prefer not to use hormones.
keyPoints: Menopausal hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for hot flushes, night sweats and other menopause symptoms.
Benefits may exceed risks for most symptomatic women under age 60 or within 10 years of menopause onset, and treatment should be tailored to each woman's health and preferences.
Women should be screened for heart disease and breast cancer risk before starting hormone therapy, and it is not recommended to prevent heart disease, breast cancer or dementia.
Low-dose vaginal estrogen and ospemifene treat genitourinary symptoms such as vaginal dryness, while moisturizers and lubricants are options for those avoiding hormones.

items.title: European society of endocrinology clinical practice guideline for evaluation and management of menopause and the perimenopause
items.summary: This is a clinical practice guideline from the European Society of Endocrinology on how menopause and the perimenopause should be assessed and managed. It covers women who go through menopause in middle age, women with premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) or early menopause, and women for whom hormones are not suitable, including those with or at high risk of breast cancer. It looks at the benefits and risks of hormone therapy, other treatments for symptoms, and whether hormone therapy helps prevent long-term disease. The abstract does not give specific findings or recommendations, so details need to be read in the full guideline.
keyPoints: About 25% of postmenopausal women are reported to have debilitating menopausal symptoms.
The guideline covers evaluation and management for midlife menopause, premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) and early menopause.
It discusses the benefits and risks of hormone therapy and other treatments, including options for women who cannot use hormones, such as those with or at high risk of breast cancer.
It also considers the debated question of whether menopausal hormone therapy can prevent chronic disease.

items.title: Hormone therapy in postmenopausal women and risk of endometrial hyperplasia or endometrial cancer
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 72 trials with about 40,000 postmenopausal women to see how different hormone therapy types affect the lining of the womb (endometrial hyperplasia, a thickening that can sometimes lead to cancer). Estrogen taken alone probably raises the chance of this thickening compared with placebo or with estrogen plus progestogen. Continuous combined therapy may make little or no difference compared with placebo, though the evidence is less certain. There were too few cases of womb cancer to draw any conclusions.
keyPoints: Estrogen on its own probably increases the risk of womb lining thickening compared with placebo, both at one year and after one year (moderate-certainty evidence).
Estrogen alone probably carries a much higher risk of womb lining thickening than estrogen combined with a progestogen taken continuously (moderate-certainty evidence).

Continuous combined estrogen plus progestogen may have little to no effect on this risk compared with placebo, while sequential combined therapy may raise the risk at one year (low-certainty evidence).
Womb cancer was too rare in the trials to draw meaningful conclusions, and evidence on progestogen dose comparisons was too limited to be clear.

items.title: A systematic review and critical appraisal of menopause guidelines
items.summary: Researchers searched for menopause guidelines published since 2015 and checked how good each one was. Of 26 documents, only five guidelines and one statement on non-hormonal treatments were of at least moderate quality. The best guidelines agreed that menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) is mainly for hot flushes and night sweats, and for low mood linked to menopause. Advice for women in perimenopause was limited.
keyPoints: The five higher-quality guidelines listed hot flushes and night sweats, disturbed sleep, joint and muscle pain, lower sexual desire and low mood as menopause-related symptoms.
Hot flushes and night sweats and menopause-related low mood were the only consistent reasons to use systemic hormone therapy.
No guideline recommended hormone therapy for memory or thinking symptoms, or to prevent other long-term diseases; some supported it for bone health but gave little specific guidance.

Non-hormonal options for hot flushes included a neurokinin 3B antagonist, certain antidepressants (SSRIs/SNRIs) and gabapentin; cognitive behavioural therapy and hypnosis were also seen as possibly helpful.

items.title: EULAR recommendations for women's health and the management of family planning, assisted reproduction, pregnancy and menopause in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus and/or antiphospholipid syndrome
items.summary: European rheumatology experts reviewed the evidence and agreed on advice for women with lupus (SLE) and/or antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) about family planning, pregnancy, fertility treatment and menopause. They say menopause hormone therapy and hormonal contraception can be used when the disease is stable or inactive and the risk of blood clots is low. Most women with these conditions can have successful pregnancies, and steps can be taken to lower the risks.
keyPoints: Menopause hormone replacement therapy can be used in patients with stable or inactive disease and a low risk of blood clots.
Family planning should be discussed as early as possible after diagnosis, and most women can have successful pregnancies.
Assisted reproduction can be used safely when disease is stable or inactive; those with antiphospholipid antibodies/APS should receive blood thinners and/or low-dose aspirin.
Cervical screening is similar to the general population, with extra care if taking immune-suppressing drugs, and HPV vaccination can be used when disease is stable.

items.title: Hormone therapy for preventing cardiovascular disease in post-menopausal women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 19 trials with over 40,000 post-menopausal women to see whether hormone therapy (taken by mouth) helps prevent heart disease. Overall it found little or no protective benefit for the heart, and a higher risk of stroke and blood clots. Women who started treatment less than 10 years after menopause had lower death and heart disease rates in a smaller analysis, but their clot risk was still higher.
keyPoints: Overall, hormone therapy did not reduce deaths, cardiovascular deaths, heart attacks, angina or the need for heart procedures (high quality evidence).
Hormone therapy raised the risk of stroke (about 6 extra cases per 1000 women) and blood clots in the veins (about 8 extra per 1000 women), plus lung clots (about 4 extra per 1000).
Among women who started less than 10 years after menopause, deaths and coronary heart disease were lower (moderate quality evidence), but blood clot risk was still higher.
Among women who started more than 10 years after menopause, there was little effect on death or heart disease, and higher risks of stroke and blood clots.

items.title: Risks and benefits of estrogen plus progestin in healthy postmenopausal women: principal results From the Women's Health Initiative randomized controlled trial
items.summary: This large trial followed over 16,000 healthy postmenopausal women aged 50-79 with a uterus for an average of 5.2 years. Half took a daily combined estrogen plus progestin pill and half took a placebo. The combined hormones raised the risk of heart disease, stroke, blood clots in the lungs and invasive breast cancer, while lowering the risk of colorectal cancer and hip fracture. The trial was stopped early because overall risks were judged to outweigh benefits, and the authors said this regimen should not be started or continued to prevent heart disease.
keyPoints: Compared with placebo, combined estrogen plus progestin raised the risk of heart disease (HR 1.29), stroke (HR 1.41), lung blood clots (HR 2.13) and invasive breast cancer (HR 1.26).
It lowered the risk of colorectal cancer (HR 0.63) and hip fracture (HR 0.66), and combined fractures overall.

The extra risk was small in absolute terms: per 10,000 women per year, about 7 more heart events, 8 more strokes, 8 more lung clots and 8 more breast cancers, versus 6 fewer colorectal cancers and 5 fewer hip fractures.
Overall risks exceeded benefits, deaths from all causes were not changed, and the regimen should not be used to prevent heart disease.

items.title: Infant formulas for the treatment of functional gastrointestinal disorders: A position paper of the ESPGHAN Nutrition Committee
items.journal: Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition
items.summary: The European paediatric gastroenterology and nutrition society (ESPGHAN) reviewed the evidence on special infant formulas sold for spit-up, colic and constipation in babies. These problems are common, usually normal in the early months, and often need no treatment. The evidence that special formulas help is limited, and the group says they should only be used on medical advice.
keyPoints: Spit-up, colic and constipation are common and usually normal in young babies, and typically do not need treatment or a switch to a special formula.
Breastfed babies with these problems should not be moved from breastfeeding to commercial formula.
Specialized formulas are not advised for colic because there is a lack of clinical evidence that they work.
Thickened formulas may be considered in specific cases of spit-up, and formulas with high β-palmitate and extra magnesium may be considered to soften stools in constipation.

items.title: Probiotics to prevent infantile colic
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether giving probiotics (helpful live bacteria) to newborns, or to mothers in pregnancy and then babies, can prevent infant colic. Six trials with 1886 babies compared probiotics with a placebo. There was no clear evidence that probiotics prevent colic from starting, but babies who had probiotics cried about 33 minutes less per day on average. The evidence was low certainty, so these results could change with more research.
keyPoints: No clear evidence that probiotics are better than placebo at preventing infant colic from developing.
Daily crying time was about 33 minutes shorter with probiotics, and about 44 minutes shorter with Lactobacillus reuteri.
No clear difference in serious side effects between probiotics and placebo.
All results were low-certainty, so the findings may change with further research.

items.title: Vitamin D for the management of asthma
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 20 placebo-controlled trials of vitamin D in children and adults with asthma, mostly mild to moderate asthma. Vitamin D did not reduce asthma attacks needing steroid tablets, and it did not improve asthma control or lung function. It also did not raise the rate of serious side effects. People with severe asthma or very low vitamin D levels were poorly represented, so those groups are still unclear.
keyPoints: Vitamin D did not reduce or increase the number of people having asthma attacks needing steroid treatment (high-quality evidence).
No benefit was found for asthma control scores, emergency visits or lung function, and results did not differ by age, dose or starting vitamin D level.
No effect on serious side effects was seen; reported reactions such as high urine calcium or stomach upset occurred in both vitamin D and placebo groups.
Too few people with severe asthma or very low vitamin D were studied, and one small trial of a different form (calcidiol) showed benefit, so more research is needed.

items.title: Skin-to-skin contact after birth: Developing a research and practice guideline
items.summary: This guideline used the World Health Organization process, including a systematic review and expert panel, to clarify how skin-to-skin contact should be done after birth. The panel gave a strong recommendation for immediate, continuous, uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact for all mothers and babies, after every type of birth. It reported high confidence in the evidence and said the practice does not need many resources. Delaying non-essential routine care so this contact can continue was found to be safe.
keyPoints: Immediate, continuous, uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact should be standard care for all mothers and babies after all modes of birth.
Babies weighing from 1000 g can have skin-to-skin contact, with experienced staff if help is needed.
Delaying non-essential routine care in favour of uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact is safe.
Skin-to-skin contact lets newborns move through their instinctive behaviours, and the practice is not resource intensive.

items.title: Vitamin D supplementation guidelines
items.source: Journal of Steroid Biochemistry and Molecular Biology
items.journal: Journal of Steroid Biochemistry and Molecular Biology
items.summary: This review compares vitamin D supplement guidelines from different agencies and scientific groups. Guidelines focused on bone health suggest aiming for a blood level of 20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L) with daily doses of 400-800 IU depending on age. Guidelines that also consider vitamin D's wider effects suggest a higher target of 30 ng/mL (75 nmol/L) and doses of 400-2000 IU a day. Side effects from taking supplements are described as rare and usually linked to extremely high doses taken for a long time.
keyPoints: Bone-focused guidelines suggest a blood level of 20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L) and 400-800 IU a day, depending on age.
Guidelines focused on wider effects suggest 30 ng/mL (75 nmol/L) and 400-2000 IU a day, depending on age, body weight, health status and ethnicity.
Food and sunlight alone are generally not enough to keep levels in the 30-50 ng/mL range all year round.
Harmful effects such as high blood calcium are rare and usually come from very high doses taken for a long time.

items.title: Early skin-to-skin contact for mothers and their healthy newborn infants
items.summary: This review pooled 46 trials (3,850 mothers and babies) that compared skin-to-skin contact straight after birth with usual hospital care for healthy newborns. Mothers who held their baby skin-to-skin were more likely to be breastfeeding one to four months later, and to be breastfeeding exclusively. The evidence for benefits to babies' body functions, such as blood sugar, was weaker, and many of the trials were small and had quality problems.
keyPoints: Mothers who had skin-to-skin contact were more likely to be breastfeeding one to four months after birth (moderate-quality evidence).
They were also more likely to breastfeed exclusively, both from discharge to one month and from six weeks to six months (moderate-quality evidence).
Babies who had skin-to-skin contact were more likely to breastfeed successfully at their first feed, and had higher blood sugar levels (low-quality evidence).
No differences were found between starting contact within 10 minutes of birth or later, or between shorter and longer contact times.

items.title: Guideline No. 447: Diagnosis and Management of Endometrial Polyps
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline explains how womb (endometrial) polyps should be diagnosed and managed. Polyps are common and can cause abnormal bleeding, difficulty getting pregnant, or bleeding after menopause. Options are watching and waiting, medication, or surgery, depending on symptoms, the chance of cancer and the patient's own choice. The abstract does not give the individual recommendations or how strong the evidence is.
keyPoints: Endometrial polyps are common and can cause abnormal bleeding, infertility or bleeding after menopause.
Polyps without symptoms often do not need treatment.
Management options are expectant (watchful waiting), medical or surgical, depending on symptoms, cancer risk and patient choice.
Medication can be used, but surgery is often needed.

items.title: The semen microbiome and its impact on sperm function and male fertility: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 55 observational studies (over 51,000 men) to see how bacteria in semen relate to sperm quality and male fertility. Several bacteria were linked to poorer sperm measures, while Lactobacillus appeared to be linked to better sperm quality. The authors say the evidence on fertility itself is inconclusive and more studies are needed.
keyPoints: Semen contains a rich and varied mix of bacteria in both fertile and infertile men.
Ureaplasma urealyticum was more common in infertile men and was linked to lower sperm concentration and poorer sperm shape.
Enterococcus faecalis, Mycoplasma hominis and Prevotella were linked to worse sperm measures, while Lactobacillus appeared protective.
Chlamydia trachomatis was not more common in infertile men and did not significantly affect semen parameters.

items.title: Semen quality and alcohol intake: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 15 studies covering 16,395 men to see whether alcohol intake affects semen quality. Drinking alcohol was linked to slightly lower semen volume and fewer sperm with normal shape. The differences were clearer for daily drinkers than for occasional drinkers, and moderate drinking did not seem to harm semen results. The authors say more research is needed before giving advice beyond avoiding heavy drinking.
keyPoints: Alcohol intake was linked to lower semen volume and a lower share of sperm with normal shape.
The effect was larger when comparing daily drinkers with occasional drinkers than when comparing never-drinkers with occasional drinkers.
Moderate drinking did not appear to harm semen parameters.
The only advice the authors support for now is to avoid heavy drinking, until studies show how changes in semen results affect pregnancy outcomes.

items.title: Fresh versus frozen embryo transfers in assisted reproduction
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled randomised trials comparing a 'freeze all' approach (freezing every embryo and transferring later) with the usual IVF/ICSI approach that includes a fresh embryo transfer. Overall chances of a live birth were probably about the same with either approach. Freezing all embryos may lower the risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), but may raise the risk of high blood pressure in pregnancy and of larger babies. The evidence was moderate to low quality, so findings should be read with some caution.
keyPoints: Cumulative live birth rate is probably little or no different between 'freeze all' and conventional fresh-transfer IVF/ICSI (moderate-quality evidence).
OHSS may be less common with 'freeze all' (about 1% versus 3%), based on low-quality evidence.
'Freeze all' may increase the risk of high blood pressure disorders in pregnancy, large-for-gestational-age babies and higher birth weight.
Time to pregnancy is likely shorter with a fresh transfer, since 'freeze all' delays embryo transfer; the evidence on miscarriage and multiple pregnancy was too uncertain to draw conclusions.

items.title: Fibroids and natural fertility: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review looked at whether fibroids (non-cancerous growths in the womb) make it harder to get pregnant without fertility treatment. Studies on IVF suggest some fibroids reduce the chance of an embryo implanting, but those results may not apply to natural conception. Looking at the studies on natural fertility, the reviewers found fibroids might interfere with getting pregnant, but the evidence is not strong enough to prove it.
keyPoints: Only a few studies have properly looked at fibroids and natural fertility, so the link between them has been insufficiently investigated.
Combining four studies, women who had trouble conceiving were more likely to have fibroids (odds ratio 3.54, 95% CI 1.55 to 8.11).
In the two most informative studies comparing time to pregnancy, the result was not clearly significant (odds ratio 1.93, 95% CI 0.89 to 4.18).
The authors say the evidence suggests, but does not demonstrate, that fibroids may interfere with natural fertility, and more research is urgently needed.

items.title: Preconception lifestyle advice for people with infertility
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at seven trials (2,130 people) testing whether lifestyle advice before conception helps people with infertility have a baby. Advice covering several topics may make little to no difference to the number of live births.
