The evidence was low to very low quality, so the review could not give clear guidance on what advice to offer.
keyPoints: Advice on a mix of lifestyle topics may make little to no difference to live births, based on low-quality evidence from one trial.
In women with infertility and obesity, weight advice may slightly lower BMI, but effects on live birth, miscarriage and pregnancy complications are uncertain.
Combined advice may make little to no difference to folic acid use, alcohol abstinence or smoking cessation in women.
No studies reported on adverse events or miscarriage for combined advice, and the evidence on safety was too weak for conclusions.

items.title: American Society of Hematology 2026 guidelines for diagnosis of iron deficiency
items.summary: The American Society of Hematology wrote new guidelines on how to diagnose iron deficiency, which is the most common vitamin and mineral deficiency and can lead to anemia if left untreated. A panel that included a patient representative reviewed the evidence and made 5 recommendations. These include blood ferritin (iron store) cut-offs for specific groups of people, aiming to spot iron deficiency even when anemia is not yet present, plus advice for people with inflammation. The authors also point out gaps in the research.
keyPoints: Iron deficiency is the most common micronutrient deficiency and can progress to anemia if untreated.
The guidelines recommend serum ferritin thresholds for specific populations to diagnose iron deficiency.
The goal is to diagnose iron deficiency whether or not anemia is present.
The guidelines give advice on diagnosing iron deficiency in people with inflammation.

items.title: Treatment for women with postpartum iron deficiency anaemia
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 33 trials with 4558 women to compare treatments for iron-low anaemia after childbirth: iron through a drip (intravenous), iron tablets, and blood transfusion. Intravenous iron probably eases tiredness slightly in the first weeks and causes much less constipation than tablets. Most of the evidence was low or very low quality, so many questions, such as rare serious reactions, are still uncertain.
keyPoints: Intravenous iron probably reduces tiredness slightly at 8 to 28 days compared with iron tablets, but probably makes little difference after four weeks.
Iron tablets probably cause a large increase in constipation compared with intravenous iron.

Intravenous iron may raise haemoglobin a little more than tablets, but results varied too much to combine; haemoglobin is an indirect measure, so decisions should rest on outcomes that matter to patients.
Effects on death, rare severe allergic reactions and breastfeeding are very uncertain or were not reported.

items.title: Nutrition-specific interventions for preventing and controlling anaemia throughout the life cycle: an overview of systematic reviews
items.summary: This large review pulled together 75 earlier reviews on ways to prevent or treat anaemia (low haemoglobin, often from low iron) at every age. Daily iron supplements may raise haemoglobin and lower the risk of anaemia and iron deficiency anaemia in babies, children, and pregnant and non-pregnant women. Iron-fortified foods also helped in several groups. Very few reviews looked at improving diet variety and quality, and the quality of evidence ranged from high to very low.
keyPoints: Daily iron supplements may raise haemoglobin and reduce anaemia and iron deficiency anaemia in infants, children, and pregnant and non-pregnant women.
In pregnancy, daily iron (with or without folic acid) raised haemoglobin and cut the risk of anaemia, while intermittent iron raised the risk of anaemia near term but caused fewer side effects.
Adding iron to foods such as flour, rice, salt and soy sauce raised haemoglobin and lowered anaemia risk in several reviews.
Few reviews tested diet-based approaches, and none looked at women aged 50 and over or at fortification or diet changes in non-pregnant women of reproductive age.

items.title: Hormone therapy for uterine and endometrial development in women with premature ovarian insufficiency
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at which hormone treatments best support the growth of the womb and womb lining in women whose ovaries stopped working before age 40 (premature ovarian insufficiency). Only three small trials, with 52 women in total, could be included. The evidence was very low quality, so the review could not say which hormone type, dose or route (oral or vaginal) works best.
keyPoints: Premature ovarian insufficiency means the ovaries lose function before age 40, often causing absent or irregular periods and low oestrogen.
Three small trials (52 women) compared oral versus patch oestrogen, low versus high oestradiol dose, and oral versus vaginal oestradiol with dydrogesterone.
The evidence was very low certainty, mainly because the studies were so small, so no clear conclusions could be drawn.
The authors call for larger, well-designed trials, including looking at pregnancy outcomes after donated eggs or embryos.

items.title: Functional Hypothalamic Amenorrhea: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: This is a clinical guideline from the Endocrine Society on functional hypothalamic amenorrhea (FHA), where periods stop because the brain's signals to the ovaries slow down. It is often linked to stress, weight loss, too much exercise, or a mix of these. The guideline says other causes must be ruled out first, and that care works best when doctors, dietitians and mental health professionals work together. Treatments for problems like bone loss and infertility are still being debated and studied.
keyPoints: FHA is a type of ongoing missed ovulation with no identifiable organic cause, often linked to stress, weight loss, excessive exercise, or a combination.
FHA is a diagnosis of exclusion, so doctors should check for other hormonal and body-wide causes first.
A team approach is needed, including medical care, dietary support and mental health support.
Bone loss and infertility are possible complications, and the best treatments for them are still under debate and investigation.

items.title: Ovarian surgery for symptom relief in women with polycystic ovary syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 22 trials (2278 women) of a keyhole operation called laparoscopic ovarian drilling for women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) who have irregular periods, unwanted hair growth or acne. The operation did not clearly improve period regularity or hair growth and acne compared with most medicines tested, such as metformin, clomiphene and letrozole. It caused fewer stomach side effects than metformin plus clomiphene. The quality of the evidence ranged from very low to moderate.
keyPoints: No clear evidence that ovarian drilling improves period regularity or hair growth and acne compared with most medical treatments.
Ovarian drilling caused fewer stomach side effects than metformin plus clomiphene (moderate-quality evidence).
Four to five punctures per ovary may work better for period regularity than two or fewer (low-quality evidence).
One small study found a benefit over gonadotrophin injections for regulating periods, but these are rarely used for this purpose.

items.title: Fertility-sparing treatment for atypical endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial cancer
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at ways to treat atypical endometrial hyperplasia (an overgrowth of the womb lining) and early womb cancer without removing the womb, for women who hope to have children. It found 12 studies with 904 women, but the evidence was low certainty and the studies had a high risk of bias. Adding metformin to progestin tablets may slightly improve how often the condition fully clears. A hormonal coil (levonorgestrel IUS) seemed about as effective as progestin tablets and may cause slightly less weight gain.
keyPoints: It is unclear which treatment, route or dose of progestin works best for fertility-sparing care, because the evidence is low certainty.
Adding metformin to progestin may slightly increase the chance of complete response, but may make little to no difference to live birth rate.
The levonorgestrel IUS (hormonal coil) may work about as well as oral progestin for complete response and may reduce severe weight gain slightly.
No studies gave evidence on overall survival, progression-free survival or quality of life.

items.title: Awareness, knowledge, and misconceptions of adolescents and young people regarding long-acting reversible contraceptives: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pulled together 40 studies of about 10,470 young people (aged 12-25) to see what they know about long-acting contraception such as coils (IUDs) and implants. Only about 65% had heard of at least one type. Many held mistaken beliefs, for example that these methods cannot be used by people who have never had a baby, or that they can cause infertility. The authors conclude that clinicians should specifically address these points when giving advice.
keyPoints: Only about 65% of young people were aware of at least one type of long-acting reversible contraceptive (LARC).
About 62% did not realise LARCs can be used by people who have never had a baby.
About 37% believed LARCs could cause infertility.
The authors say clinicians should counsel young people that LARCs suit those who have not had children and do not cause infertility.

items.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 201: Pregestational Diabetes Mellitus
items.summary: This is a guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists on caring for women who already have diabetes before they become pregnant. It explains how to counsel and manage women before and during pregnancy, including frequent monitoring and medication changes. The update also covers insulin pumps, oral diabetes medicines in pregnancy, and the option of long-acting reversible contraception (such as an IUD or implant) after the baby is born. The abstract notes that few well-designed studies exist, so many recommendations rest on expert and consensus opinion.
keyPoints: Diabetes that starts before pregnancy needs frequent monitoring and medication adjustment, and it carries risks for both mother and baby.
Women with pregestational diabetes can be counselled and managed before and during pregnancy using the updated guidance.
The update adds more on insulin pumps (continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion) and on oral diabetes medicines in pregnancy.
Long-acting reversible contraception is an option in the postpartum period for women with pregestational diabetes.

items.title: Practice Bulletin No. 186: Long-Acting Reversible Contraception: Implants and Intrauterine Devices
items.summary: This guideline from US obstetrician-gynecologists looks at long-acting reversible contraception (LARC), which means contraceptive implants and intrauterine devices (IUDs or coils). It describes them as the most effective reversible birth control methods. Because they do not need ongoing effort from the user, they work well over the long term, and fertility returns quickly once the device is removed.
keyPoints: Implants and IUDs (LARC) are the most effective reversible contraceptive methods.
Unlike many other methods, LARC does not require ongoing effort from the patient to work well long term.
Fertility returns rapidly after the device is removed.
The bulletin gives evidence-based recommendations on choosing patients for LARC and on starting and managing these methods.

items.title: Anti-adhesion therapy following operative hysteroscopy for treatment of female subfertility
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at treatments used after hysteroscopy (a procedure to treat problems inside the womb) to stop scar tissue forming, in women having fertility problems. Treatments included intrauterine devices, hormones and barrier gels. They may reduce scar tissue seen at a follow-up check, but no study measured live births and the evidence was low to very low quality. Whether these treatments improve pregnancy outcomes remains uncertain.
keyPoints: No study reported live birth, so the effect on having a baby is unknown.
Devices, hormones or gels may lead to fewer womb adhesions (scar tissue) at second-look hysteroscopy than no treatment or placebo (low-quality evidence).
There was not enough evidence to say whether these treatments change term delivery or ongoing pregnancy rates (very-low-quality evidence).
The authors conclude that the benefit of anti-adhesion treatment for reproductive outcomes remains uncertain and more research is needed.

items.title: Gonadotropins for ovulation induction in women with polycystic ovary syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at FSH injections (gonadotropins) used to trigger ovulation in women with PCOS who did not ovulate or get pregnant on clomiphene or letrozole. It pooled 15 trials with 2,348 women. Different types of FSH injections seemed to work about equally well, though the evidence was low or very low quality. In one larger trial, FSH injections probably led to more live births than carrying on with clomiphene, but may also raise the chance of miscarriage.
keyPoints: There may be little or no difference in live birth, multiple pregnancy, clinical pregnancy or miscarriage between recombinant FSH and urinary-derived FSH (low-certainty evidence).

For women who did not respond to clomiphene, FSH injections probably gave more live births (RR 1.24) and clinical pregnancies than continuing clomiphene (moderate-certainty evidence, one trial of 661 women), without more multiple pregnancies.
FSH injections may increase the miscarriage rate compared with continued clomiphene (low-certainty evidence).
It is uncertain whether any treatment differs in ectopic pregnancy or ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) risk; no women in the clomiphene comparison developed OHSS.

items.title: Aromatase inhibitors (letrozole) for ovulation induction in infertile women with polycystic ovary syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 41 randomised trials (6522 women) of letrozole for helping women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) ovulate. Compared with clomiphene-type drugs, letrozole led to more live births and more pregnancies when followed by timed intercourse. Rates of ovarian overstimulation, miscarriage and multiple pregnancy were similar between the treatments. Compared with a surgical option called laparoscopic ovarian drilling, the evidence was too weak to say which works better.
keyPoints: Live birth was more likely with letrozole than with clomiphene-type drugs (high-certainty evidence); for a woman with a 20% chance using clomiphene, the estimate with letrozole is 27% to 35%.
Clinical pregnancy rates were also higher with letrozole (high-certainty evidence).
Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, miscarriage and multiple pregnancy rates were similar between letrozole and clomiphene-type drugs (high-certainty evidence).
It is uncertain whether letrozole beats laparoscopic ovarian drilling for live birth, as the evidence was low or very low certainty.

items.title: ESHRE guideline: number of embryos to transfer during IVF/ICSI†
items.summary: This European guideline looked at when it might make sense to transfer two embryos instead of one during IVF or ICSI. It found that no single clinical or embryo factor on its own justifies choosing a double embryo transfer over an elective single embryo transfer. Double transfer raises the chance of twins or more, which brings higher risks such as preterm birth and low birthweight. Much of the evidence behind the recommendations is low or very low quality, so the guideline also lists areas that need more research.
keyPoints: No clinical or embryological factor alone justifies a double embryo transfer instead of an elective single embryo transfer.
Double embryo transfer is linked to more multiple pregnancies, which raises the risk of preterm birth, low birthweight and other problems for mother and babies.
Single embryo transfer is the approach preferred by international and national professional organisations to reduce these risks.
Of the evidence-based recommendations, 28% rest on moderate-quality evidence and most of the rest on low or very low-quality evidence.

items.title: Opening the black box: why do euploid blastocysts fail to implant? A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: Even when an embryo has the right number of chromosomes (found through PGT-A genetic testing), only about 50-60% implant. This large review pooled results from hundreds of studies to look at what else might explain why some of these embryos do not lead to a pregnancy. Lower embryo quality, slower development, older age, obesity and earlier repeated implantation failure were linked to poorer outcomes. Most studies were small or looked back at past cases, so the review rates the quality of the evidence as low or very low.
keyPoints: Lower embryo quality (such as a reduced inner cell mass or outer layer quality) and slower development were linked to lower chances of a live birth.
Women aged 38 or older had slightly lower live birth rates even with genetically tested embryos, and obesity was linked to lower live birth rates and more miscarriages.
Transferring a frozen-thawed embryo worked better than a fresh transfer after PGT-A, while repeated freezing and warming cycles may slightly lower success.
Most included studies were retrospective or small, so the evidence is low or very low quality and many causes of implantation failure remain unexplained.

items.title: Time-lapse systems for embryo incubation and assessment in assisted reproduction
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at time-lapse systems, which take pictures of embryos in the incubator during IVF, compared with the usual method of taking embryos out each day to check them under a microscope. It pooled nine trials with 2,955 couples. The review found not enough good-quality evidence to say whether time-lapse systems improve live birth, miscarriage or pregnancy rates. The evidence was low or very low quality, so the results should be read with caution. Time-lapse systems often add significant extra cost to treatment.
keyPoints: Nine trials with 2,955 couples were included, and the evidence was low to very low quality.
It is unclear whether time-lapse systems change live birth or ongoing pregnancy rates compared with conventional incubation.
One comparison suggested fewer miscarriages with time-lapse plus selection software, but this was very low-quality evidence.
The authors found too little good evidence to choose between time-lapse systems and conventional incubation.

items.title: The Impact of Minerals on Female Fertility: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This systematic review pulled together 39 studies on how minerals relate to female fertility, including in women using IVF. It found that minerals such as selenium, zinc and copper appear important for reproductive health, while exposure to toxic metals like cadmium and lead appears harmful. The authors say more research is needed before firm guidelines on supplement doses or blood levels can be set.
keyPoints: Selenium, zinc and copper were found to be important for maintaining reproductive health.
Exposure to toxic metals such as cadmium and lead was linked to harm to fertility.
The review looked at outcomes including egg quality, ovulation, embryo development, miscarriage and IVF results.
Further research is needed to refine guidelines for mineral supplementation and blood levels in women with fertility problems.

items.title: Vitamin D and in vitro fertilization: a systematic review
items.source: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.journal: Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics
items.summary: This review looked at 18 studies on whether vitamin D levels in the blood are linked to how well IVF works. Most studies (12) found no link, 5 found a positive link, and 1 found a negative link. The authors conclude the link between vitamin D and pregnancy rates after IVF is uncertain.
keyPoints: Of 18 studies, 5 found higher vitamin D linked to better IVF results, 12 found no link, and 1 found a negative link.
The link between vitamin D levels and pregnancy rates after IVF is uncertain.
Vitamin D might matter more for White than Asian patients, and for the number of follicles collected, but this is not settled.
Vitamin D may affect the immune system, which could play a role in embryo implantation and pregnancy.

items.title: Pain relief for women undergoing oocyte retrieval for assisted reproduction
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 24 trials (3,160 women) comparing different ways of easing pain during egg retrieval for IVF, including sedation, pain-relief drugs, a numbing injection near the cervix, acupuncture and general anaesthesia. No single method was clearly better than the others. Combining approaches, such as sedation with opioid pain relief plus a paracervical block or acupuncture, seemed to relieve pain better than one method alone. Most of the evidence was low or very low quality, and it was not enough to say whether any method changes pregnancy rates.
keyPoints: No single method or technique was shown to be better than the others for pain relief during and after egg retrieval.
Combining sedation and pain medicine with a paracervical block or acupuncture gave better pain relief than one approach alone.
There was not enough evidence to say whether any pain-relief method affects pregnancy rates.
All the methods reviewed were linked with high satisfaction, and women's preferences and local resources are worth considering.

items.title: The use of preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy: a committee opinion
items.summary: This committee opinion looks at preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy (PGT-A), a test that checks embryos for the wrong number of chromosomes during IVF. The committee says the value of PGT-A as a routine test for everyone having IVF has not been shown. Recent large randomized trials found that pregnancy outcomes after frozen embryo transfer were similar with or without PGT-A. Whether it lowers the chance of miscarriage is still unclear, and the studies have important limitations.
keyPoints: The value of PGT-A as a routine screening test for all IVF patients has not been demonstrated.
Some earlier single-center studies reported higher live-birth rates after PGT-A in patients with a favorable outlook.
Recent multicenter randomized trials in women with available blastocysts found similar overall pregnancy outcomes with frozen embryo transfer, with or without PGT-A.
Whether PGT-A reduces the risk of clinical miscarriage is unclear, and the studies have important limitations.

items.title: Endometrial injury in women undergoing in vitro fertilisation (IVF)
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 'endometrial scratching', a procedure that deliberately injures the womb lining before embryo transfer in IVF, to see if it improves pregnancy chances. Across 37 trials with 8,786 women, it is unclear whether scratching helps, makes no difference, or slightly lowers the chance of a live birth. It does not appear to change the chance of miscarriage. The procedure causes some pain and light bleeding.
keyPoints: The effect of endometrial injury on live birth and clinical pregnancy is unclear, with moderate-certainty evidence.
It probably makes little to no difference to the chance of miscarriage.
The procedure was mildly to moderately painful (about 4 out of 10) and usually caused minimal bleeding.
Current evidence does not support routine use of endometrial injury in women having IVF.

items.title: Evidence-based treatments for couples with unexplained infertility: a guideline
items.summary: The American Society for Reproductive Medicine reviewed 88 studies to guide treatment for couples whose infertility has no clear cause. Because the cause is unknown, treatment is based on trial and experience rather than a targeted fix. For most couples, the best first step is about 3 or 4 cycles of ovarian stimulation with oral medications plus intrauterine insemination (IUI), followed by IVF if that does not work.
keyPoints: Treatment of unexplained infertility is empiric, meaning it is based on what has worked in practice rather than on a known cause.
For most couples, the best initial treatment is typically 3 or 4 cycles of ovarian stimulation with oral medications and IUI.
IVF is recommended for couples who do not conceive with ovarian stimulation and IUI.
The guideline covers options such as clomiphene citrate, letrozole (an aromatase inhibitor), gonadotropins, timing of IUI, and IVF.

items.title: Conventional and modern markers of endometrial receptivity: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 163 studies of 88,834 women to see whether tests of the womb lining (the endometrium) can predict who will get pregnant. Things like lining thickness, ultrasound pattern and blood flow were linked to pregnancy, but none could predict it well enough to be used in routine care. Some newer molecular tests look promising, but more data are needed.
keyPoints: Lining thickness, ultrasound pattern, blood flow measures and some molecules were linked to clinical pregnancy.
These markers were poor at predicting who would get pregnant, so they are not recommended for clinical use yet.
Some modern molecular tests look promising, and further data are awaited.
The results may help manage couples' expectations during IUI and IVF.

items.title: Surgery for tubal infertility
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked for trials comparing surgery on blocked or damaged fallopian tubes with no treatment or with IVF, to see which gives more live births. The researchers found no suitable randomised trials. So it is still unknown whether tubal surgery works better or worse than IVF or waiting for women with tubal infertility.
keyPoints: No suitable randomised controlled trials were found, so no conclusions could be drawn.
How well tubal surgery works compared with IVF or no treatment, in terms of live births, remains unknown.
Estimated live birth rates after surgery range from 9% for severe tubal disease to 69% for mild disease, but these have not been tested rigorously against other options.
Large, well-designed trials are needed that also compare side effects and costs, and consider factors like age and how long a woman has been trying to conceive.

items.title: Global and regional causes of maternal deaths 2009-20: a WHO systematic analysis
items.summary: This WHO review looked at what causes women to die during pregnancy, birth and the weeks after, using data from 2009-20 around the world. The most common cause was severe bleeding (haemorrhage), followed by existing health problems made worse by pregnancy and high blood pressure disorders. Most deaths from bleeding and infection happened after the baby was born. The authors say effective treatments exist, so better access to quality care is the key need.
keyPoints: Worldwide, severe bleeding was the leading cause of maternal death (27%), followed by indirect causes (23%) and high blood pressure disorders (16%).
Bleeding deaths were most common in sub-Saharan Africa and in Western Asia and Northern Africa; high blood pressure deaths were highest in Latin America and the Caribbean.
Most deaths from bleeding and infection (sepsis) happened in the postpartum period, so care after birth matters as well as care during labour.
Data on maternal suicide and deaths after 42 days postpartum were very limited, with only 12 countries recording any maternal suicides.

items.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 209: Obstetric Analgesia and Anesthesia
items.summary: This is a guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) about pain relief and anesthesia during labor and delivery. It states that labor causes severe pain for many women, and that a woman's request for pain relief is a sufficient medical reason to provide it when there is no medical reason against it. It also says access to pain relief such as an epidural should not depend on a woman's health insurance or ability to pay.
keyPoints: Unless there is a medical reason not to, a woman's own request is enough of a reason to receive pain relief in labor.
A woman who asks for an epidural should not be denied it because of her health insurance status, and the methods a hospital offers should not depend on ability to pay.
Anesthesia services should be available to provide labor pain relief and surgical anesthesia in all hospitals that offer maternity care.
Trained labor nurses, under appropriate physician supervision, can help manage epidural pain relief so more women can benefit.

items.title: Epidural versus non-epidural or no analgesia for pain management in labour
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 40 trials with over 11,000 women to compare epidural pain relief in labour with other options, mostly opioid injections. Epidurals gave better pain relief and higher satisfaction, though the evidence for this was low quality. Epidurals did not change caesarean rates or long-term backache, and there was no clear effect on babies' Apgar scores or neonatal intensive care admissions. Epidurals were linked to more low blood pressure, fever, difficulty passing urine and longer labours.
keyPoints: Epidural analgesia probably reduces labour pain more than opioids and more women rated their pain relief as excellent or very good (low-quality evidence).
Assisted vaginal birth was more common with epidurals overall, but this difference was not seen in trials done after 2005.
No difference was found in caesarean section rates or long-term backache, and no clear differences in Apgar scores or neonatal intensive care admission.
Epidurals were linked to more low blood pressure, fever, urinary retention and longer labours, but less nausea, vomiting and breathing depression than opioids.

items.title: Labor Induction versus Expectant Management in Low-Risk Nulliparous Women
items.summary: This large trial looked at low-risk women having a first baby. Some were randomly chosen to have labour induced at 39 weeks, and others waited for labour to start on its own. Induction did not significantly reduce the chance of death or serious complications for the baby. It did lead to fewer caesarean births, 18.6% compared with 22.2%.
keyPoints: About 6,100 low-risk first-time mothers were randomly assigned to induction at 39 weeks or to waiting for labour to start naturally.
Serious problems for babies were 4.3% with induction and 5.4% with waiting, which was not a statistically significant difference.
Caesarean delivery was significantly lower with induction (18.6%) than with waiting (22.2%).

items.title: Midwife-led continuity models versus other models of care for childbearing women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 15 trials with over 17,000 women to compare midwife-led continuity care (seeing the same midwife or small team through pregnancy and birth) with other models of care. Women in midwife-led continuity care were less likely to have an epidural or spinal, an instrumental birth (forceps or vacuum), or an episiotomy, and more likely to have a spontaneous vaginal birth. They were also less likely to have a preterm birth or to lose a baby, and most studies found they were more satisfied with their care. The review found no worse outcomes for women or babies, and the main findings were graded as high quality.
keyPoints: Midwife-led continuity care meant fewer epidurals or spinals (RR 0.85), fewer instrumental births (RR 0.90) and fewer episiotomies (RR 0.84).
Women were slightly more likely to have a spontaneous vaginal birth (RR 1.05) and more likely to have no pain relief or anaesthesia during labour (RR 1.21).
There were fewer preterm births (RR 0.76) and fewer fetal losses and neonatal deaths overall (RR 0.84); the authors say these findings need further research.

There was no difference in caesarean births, intact perineum, postpartum haemorrhage or breastfeeding initiation; most studies reported higher satisfaction, and labour was about 30 minutes longer on average.

items.title: Dietary supplements for dysmenorrhoea
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 27 trials (3,101 women, mostly students in their late teens or early twenties) testing dietary supplements for painful periods. Some supplements, such as ginger, fenugreek, zinc, vitamin B1 and a few herbs, showed signs of reducing pain, but nearly all findings came from single, small trials. All the evidence was low or very low quality, and very little information on side effects was reported, so safety is unclear.
keyPoints: There is no high quality evidence that any dietary supplement works for painful periods.
Some supplements (for example ginger, fenugreek, zinc sulphate, vitamin B1 and zataria) showed possible pain reduction, but the evidence was very limited and low quality.
Vitamin E showed no benefit compared with placebo or no treatment.
Only 4 of 27 studies reported side effects in both groups, so evidence of safety is lacking.

items.title: Optimizing intrauterine insemination: A systematic review and meta-analysis of the effectiveness and safety of clinical treatment add-ons
items.summary: This review pooled 66 randomised trials (over 16,000 participants) of extra treatments added to standard intrauterine insemination (IUI). Using vaginal progesterone after insemination in cycles with fertility medication appeared to improve the chance of an ongoing pregnancy or live birth. Endometrial scratch and ovarian stimulation in the first half of the cycle also showed possible benefit, but the evidence for these is weaker. Most other add-ons made no clear difference, and the authors say more research is needed.
keyPoints: Vaginal progesterone for luteal phase support in stimulated IUI cycles significantly increased ongoing pregnancy or live birth (RR 1.37), with moderate to low certainty.
Endometrial scratch may increase pregnancy or live birth (RR 1.44), but the evidence is very uncertain.
Ovarian stimulation in the follicular phase (two studies) may increase success (RR 1.39), with low certainty.
The other add-ons studied showed no significant difference in the main outcomes.

items.title: Luteal phase support for women trying to conceive by intrauterine insemination or sexual intercourse
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 25 trials (5,111 women) testing luteal phase support, extra hormones given after ovulation, for women trying to conceive by intrauterine insemination (IUI) or intercourse. It is unclear whether vaginal progesterone raises the chance of a live birth or ongoing pregnancy. It may raise the clinical pregnancy rate, but the evidence is low quality and the effect on miscarriage is unclear. Other hormones and routes (oral, injected, GnRH agonist, hCG) did not clearly improve pregnancy outcomes, and the evidence for them is very uncertain.
keyPoints: Unclear whether vaginal progesterone increases live birth or ongoing pregnancy (low-certainty evidence).
Vaginal progesterone may increase clinical pregnancy rates in cycles with ovarian stimulation, but low-certainty evidence means this is not firm.
Effects on miscarriage and multiple pregnancy are uncertain for progesterone and the other treatments studied.
No trial tested luteal support in natural cycles, and oral progesterone, GnRH agonist and hCG showed no clear benefit (very low-certainty evidence).

items.title: Serum luteal phase progesterone in women undergoing frozen embryo transfer in assisted conception: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from studies of women having a frozen embryo transfer (FET) as part of fertility treatment. It looked at whether blood progesterone levels during the luteal phase (the time after transfer) were linked to pregnancy outcomes. Among women with levels below 10 ng/mL, higher progesterone was linked to more ongoing pregnancies or live births, more clinical pregnancies and fewer miscarriages. It is not clear whether levels at or above 10 ng/mL make a difference, and trials are still needed to show whether raising the dose of progesterone support helps women with low levels.
keyPoints: Below 10 ng/mL, higher blood progesterone was linked to more ongoing pregnancies or live births (RR 1.47) and more clinical pregnancies (RR 1.31).
Higher progesterone below 10 ng/mL was also linked to a lower risk of miscarriage (RR 0.62) in cycles using only vaginal progesterone and blastocyst embryos.
For levels of 10 ng/mL or above, results were uncertain because the studies differed a lot and had wide margins of error.
The authors suggest there may be a minimum progesterone level needed for implantation, and call for trials testing higher-dose luteal support in women with low levels.

items.title: European Association of Urology Guidelines on Male Sexual and Reproductive Health: 2025 Update on Male Infertility
items.summary: The European Association of Urology updated its 2025 guidelines on male infertility, covering how it is diagnosed, treated and followed up. The guidelines advise that every man seeking help for fertility problems should have a full urological check. They also recommend looking at the female partner at the same time, so a couple can decide together on timing and treatment.
keyPoints: All men seeking medical help for fertility problems should have a thorough urological assessment.
The female partner should be investigated in parallel, so couples can share decisions about timing and treatment.
Men with infertility or abnormal semen results should be counselled about the associated health risks.
The 2025 update adds new sections on exome sequencing (a genetic test) and probiotic treatment, and updates advice on diagnostic work-up.

items.title: The Association Between Male Viral Infections and Infertility: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 135 studies of 30,298 men of reproductive age to see how viral infections relate to male infertility. Men with HPV had more sperm DNA damage and lower sperm count, concentration, viability and normal shape than men without HPV. Hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV and COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2) were also linked to poorer semen quality. HPV and hepatitis B may also affect the results of fertility treatments such as IVF.
keyPoints: Men with HPV had higher sperm DNA fragmentation and lower sperm count, concentration, viability and normal morphology.
Hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV and SARS-CoV-2 were also linked to poorer semen quality.
Hepatitis B was linked to a lower fertilization rate in assisted reproduction.
HPV was linked to a lower clinical pregnancy rate and a higher miscarriage rate; HPV and adeno-associated virus were more common in men in fertility treatment.

items.title: Antioxidants for male subfertility
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 90 trials with over 10,000 men who had fertility problems to see whether antioxidant supplements help couples have a baby. Antioxidants may slightly raise the chances of pregnancy and live birth, but the evidence is low to very low certainty. When weaker studies were removed, the live birth benefit was no longer seen. The authors say the evidence is inconclusive and larger, better trials are needed.
keyPoints: Antioxidants may increase live birth rates, but this is based on very low-certainty evidence and disappeared when high-risk-of-bias studies were removed.
Antioxidants may increase clinical pregnancy rates, based on low-certainty evidence.
No clear difference in miscarriage was found, though few studies reported it.
Antioxidants may cause more mild stomach discomfort (about 2% on placebo versus roughly 2% to 7% on antioxidants).

items.title: EULAR recommendations for use of antirheumatic drugs in reproduction, pregnancy, and lactation: 2024 update
items.summary: European rheumatology experts updated their guidance on which arthritis and autoimmune medicines can be used when trying for a baby, during pregnancy and while breastfeeding. They reviewed the research and agreed 5 main principles and 12 recommendations. Several older medicines and all biologic medicines were judged compatible with breastfeeding, and some are considered compatible with pregnancy after an individual risk-benefit check.
keyPoints: Antimalarials, azathioprine, colchicine, cyclosporine, sulfasalazine and tacrolimus are considered compatible with pregnancy.
NSAIDs (anti-inflammatory painkillers) and glucocorticoids (steroids) should be used more cautiously during pregnancy.
All TNF inhibitor biologics can be used throughout pregnancy after an individual risk-benefit assessment, and other biologics may be used if needed.

For breastfeeding, compatible drugs include antimalarials, azathioprine, colchicine, cyclosporine, glucocorticoids, IVIG, NSAIDs, sulfasalazine and tacrolimus, and all biologics are considered compatible.

items.title: Evidence-based clinical practice guidelines for prevention, screening and treatment of peripartum depression
items.summary: This guideline pulled together 145 systematic reviews to make recommendations on preventing, screening for and treating depression during pregnancy and after birth. It recommends talking-based support for prevention, screening for depression in pregnancy and postpartum, and cognitive-behavioural therapy for treatment. Antidepressant medication is recommended for severe depression in pregnancy. Treatment choices should weigh severity, past history, risks and benefits for mother and baby, and the woman's own preferences.
keyPoints: Psychological and psychosocial support is strongly recommended to prevent depression in women with no symptoms and in women at higher risk.
Depression screening is strongly recommended during pregnancy and after birth.
Cognitive-behavioural therapy is strongly recommended for treating mild to severe peripartum depression.
Antidepressant medication is strongly recommended for severe depression in pregnancy, and electroconvulsive therapy for treatment-resistant or life-threatening severe depression.

items.title: Pain management for medical abortion before 14 weeks' gestation
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at ways to ease pain during medical abortion (mifepristone plus misoprostol) before 14 weeks. It found five studies, which were too different to combine. One study found that a high dose of ibuprofen reduced pain more than paracetamol. Most other findings came from small studies with low or very low certainty.
keyPoints: In one trial of 108 women, ibuprofen 1600 mg lowered pain scores by about 2 points out of 10 more than paracetamol 2000 mg (moderate-certainty evidence).
Paracetamol did not appear to cause more side effects or make the abortion less likely to be complete, but it eased pain less than ibuprofen 1600 mg.
Pregabalin 300 mg and ibuprofen 800 mg showed little to no clear pain benefit over placebo, and walking around or resting made little difference to pain (low to very low certainty).
Most results were low or very low certainty because studies were small and two had a high risk of bias; larger, high-quality trials are needed.

items.title: Paracetamol/acetaminophen (single administration) for perineal pain in the early postpartum period
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether a single dose of paracetamol (acetaminophen) eases pain around the vaginal opening and perineum in the first days after childbirth. It pooled 10 placebo-controlled trials, using data from 1301 women. More women had pain relief with paracetamol than with placebo, and fewer needed extra pain medicine. The trials were old (1970s to early 1990s) and the evidence was rated low certainty.
keyPoints: A single dose of paracetamol may give more women pain relief after vaginal birth than placebo.
Fewer women taking paracetamol may need additional pain relief.
There may be little or no difference in nausea or sleepiness, but this came from only one trial.
Side effects in babies were not studied, and the evidence is low certainty because the trials were old and varied.

items.title: Ovarian suppression for adjuvant treatment of hormone receptor-positive early breast cancer
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 15 trials of 11,538 premenopausal women with early hormone receptor-positive breast cancer. It looked at what happens when ovarian suppression (switching off the ovaries' oestrogen production) is added to other treatment. Adding it lowered the risk of dying and of the cancer coming back, and probably lowered the risk of cancer in the other breast. It also brought menopause-type side effects, including more hot flushes and possibly more low mood or anxiety, and may raise the risk of bone thinning.
keyPoints: Adding ovarian suppression reduced deaths (high-certainty evidence) and improved disease-free survival (high-certainty evidence).
The survival benefit was seen when it was added to observation, to tamoxifen, or to chemotherapy plus tamoxifen, but not when added to chemotherapy alone.
Hot flushes were more common with ovarian suppression (low-certainty evidence), and some studies reported more depression, anxiety or neuropsychiatric symptoms while others found no difference.
One study suggested a higher risk of osteoporosis (low-certainty evidence), and some women reported worse quality of life, such as vaginal dryness and night sweats.

items.title: Adjuvant gonadotropin-releasing hormone analogues for the prevention of chemotherapy-induced premature ovarian failure in premenopausal women
items.summary: This review pooled 12 trials of about 1,369 women having chemotherapy for cancers such as breast cancer, ovarian cancer or Hodgkin's lymphoma. It looked at whether taking a GnRH agonist (a hormone-suppressing medicine) alongside chemotherapy helps protect the ovaries from early menopause. Women who also took the medicine were less likely to develop premature ovarian failure, and more likely to get their periods back or keep them. The trials were at high or unclear risk of bias, and evidence on protecting fertility was not strong enough to draw conclusions.
keyPoints: Premature ovarian failure occurred in about 11% of women using a GnRH agonist with chemotherapy, versus about 25% with chemotherapy alone (moderate-certainty evidence).
Periods returned or continued more often with the agonist within 12 months, but there was no clear difference after 12 months (low-certainty evidence).
Pregnancy rates did not clearly differ between groups, and evidence on protecting fertility was insufficient.
Common side effects of GnRH analogues included hot flushes, vaginal dryness and mood swings, with no overall difference in side effects between groups.

items.title: Guidelines for the evaluation and treatment of perimenopausal depression: summary and recommendations
items.summary: Expert groups from the North American Menopause Society and a US depression network reviewed the research on depression during perimenopause, the years around the menopause transition. They found that most women who have a major depressive episode in this time have had depression before. Usual depression treatments such as antidepressants and talking therapy are the first choice. Estrogen is not approved for treating depression, but there is some evidence it can help, especially for women who also have hot flushes or night sweats.
keyPoints: Perimenopause is a time when women are more vulnerable to depressive symptoms and major depression, and most who have an episode have had depression before.

Depression in midlife often overlaps with menopause symptoms like hot flushes and poor sleep, so diagnosis involves checking menopause stage, other symptoms, life stresses and using validated screening tools.
Antidepressants and psychotherapy are the front-line treatments for perimenopausal depression.
Estrogen therapy is not approved for depression but may have antidepressant effects, particularly with hot flushes; data on estrogen plus progestin are sparse and inconclusive.

items.title: Hormonal Options for Perimenopause: A Clinician Toolkit
items.summary: This clinical perspective explains that perimenopause, the stage before menopause, looks different for every person and has no specific guidelines. Symptoms can include mood and thinking changes, irregular bleeding, poor sleep, hot flushes and sexual concerns. The article describes how hormonal contraceptives and other hormone-based options may be used, and notes that contraceptives do not suit everyone. It encourages choosing treatment through shared decision making between a patient and their clinician.
keyPoints: Perimenopause is a distinct stage from menopause and is defined in different ways.
It can bring mood and thinking changes, abnormal bleeding, sleep disruption, hot flushes and sexual concerns.
Hormonal contraceptives are often prescribed for perimenopause symptoms but are not always adequate or preferred.
Other hormonal options exist, and treatment can be tailored through shared decision making.

items.title: Nutritional interventions in treating menopause-related sleep disturbances: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 59 studies on whether changing what you eat or drink, or taking nutritional supplements, can help sleep problems linked to menopause. Most studies (37) found some sleep benefit, while 22 found none. The studies were quite different from each other and most were of low quality, so it is hard to draw firm conclusions. The authors say better-designed trials are needed.
keyPoints: 37 of 59 studies reported that a nutritional intervention improved some aspect of sleep; 22 found no benefit.
The improvements were mainly in sleep that women rated themselves (subjective sleep).
Most studies were of low methodological quality and varied widely in the interventions tested.
The authors call for more high-quality, adequately sized randomized controlled trials.

items.title: Hormone therapy for sexual function in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 36 trials (over 23,000 women, nearly all postmenopausal) that compared hormone therapy with placebo or no treatment for sexual function. Estrogen on its own probably gives a small improvement in sexual function, especially for lubrication, pain and satisfaction. For estrogen with progestogen, tibolone-type drugs and SERMs, the evidence is too weak to say whether they help. Many of the trials had a high risk of bias, and results varied a lot between studies.
keyPoints: Estrogen alone probably slightly improves overall sexual function in women with menopausal symptoms or early postmenopause, and in postmenopausal women generally (moderate-quality evidence).
The benefit was seen especially in lubrication, pain and satisfaction.
It is uncertain whether estrogen combined with progestogens helps, based on one small study with very low-quality evidence.
Evidence for synthetic steroids such as tibolone and for SERMs is very low quality, and current evidence does not suggest they improve sexual function.

items.title: Long-term hormone therapy for perimenopausal and postmenopausal women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 24 trials (45,660 women) to look at the long-term effects of taking hormone therapy for at least a year after menopause. Most of the results came from one large trial, mainly in women over 60. Combined oestrogen-plus-progestogen therapy probably raised breast cancer risk and may have raised stroke and blood clot risk, while oestrogen-only therapy probably raised stroke and gallbladder surgery risk. Both types probably lowered the risk of broken bones, and neither made much difference to heart attacks or other coronary events.
keyPoints: Combined hormone therapy probably makes little to no difference to coronary events but probably increases breast cancer risk (moderate-certainty evidence).
Combined therapy may increase stroke and venous thromboembolism (blood clots in the veins) risk (low-certainty evidence).
Oestrogen-only therapy probably makes little to no difference to coronary events or breast cancer, but probably increases stroke and gallbladder disease needing surgery.
Both types probably reduce the risk of all clinical fractures; the results come mostly from one trial of oral hormone therapy in mainly older women, so may not reflect current treatments.

items.title: Cardiovascular Changes in Menopause
items.summary: This review looked at published research from 1986 to 2019 on how menopause affects the heart and blood vessels. It found that menopause is linked to changes similar to cardiovascular ageing. Changes such as unhealthy blood fats, insulin resistance, fat redistribution and high blood pressure appear to add to the risk of heart and blood vessel disease. The abstract does not rate how strong the evidence is.
keyPoints: Menopause is associated with changes consistent with cardiovascular aging.
Dyslipidemia (unhealthy blood fats), insulin resistance, fat redistribution and high blood pressure contribute to higher cardiovascular risk.
Atherosclerosis (artery narrowing) appears to result from risk factors becoming stronger around the perimenopausal period.
Oxidative stress and levels of L-arginine and ADMA may also affect blood vessel function in menopause.

items.title: AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF CLINICAL ENDOCRINOLOGISTS AND AMERICAN COLLEGE OF ENDOCRINOLOGY POSITION STATEMENT ON MENOPAUSE-2017 UPDATE
items.source: American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists and American College of Endocrinology
items.organisation: American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists and American College of Endocrinology
items.summary: This 2017 position statement from two US endocrinology societies updates their earlier menopause guidance after reviewing newer trials. None of the earlier recommendations were changed. It covers when hormone therapy may suit symptomatic women, how the type of estrogen and progesterone matters, and what can be used instead of hormones.
keyPoints: Whether to use menopausal hormone therapy should depend on a woman's heart disease risk factors, her age, and how long since her menopause.
Estrogen given through the skin may carry a lower risk of blood clots, and possibly stroke and coronary artery disease, than estrogen taken by mouth.
If progesterone is needed, micronized progesterone is considered the safer choice.
Hormone therapy is not recommended to prevent diabetes, and for women who already have diabetes the decision should be individualized, taking account of age and metabolic and heart risk factors.

items.title: Acute and preventive treatment of menstrual migraine: a meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 26 randomized trials of treatments for menstrual migraine, a type of migraine linked to the monthly cycle that is often more severe and harder to treat. Triptans, with or without other pain relievers, worked better than placebo for relieving attacks and for prevention. Sumatriptan and lasmiditan gave the best pain relief during an attack, while frovatriptan and two newer injectable drugs (galcanezumab and erenumab) helped most with prevention.
keyPoints: Sumatriptan and lasmiditan were the most effective first-line treatments for an acute menstrual migraine attack, with better pain relief at 2 and 24 hours.
Frovatriptan was the more effective triptan for preventing menstrual migraine from coming back.
The CGRP antibody drugs erenumab and galcanezumab reduced the number of headache days per month more than triptans.

items.title: Migraine treatment: Position paper of the French Headache Society
items.summary: The French Headache Society updated its migraine treatment advice to reflect new drugs and new safety data. Newer preventive medicines that block a pain-related protein called CGRP can now be offered as a first choice, although national reimbursement is limited to people with severe migraine. The paper also says topiramate should no longer be a first-choice preventive for women who could become pregnant, because of possible harm to a baby's brain development if exposed in the womb.
keyPoints: CGRP-targeting preventive treatments (monoclonal antibodies and gepants) can be offered as first-line treatment, based on efficacy and safety.
French reimbursement covers these only for severe migraine, at least eight headache days a month, after two earlier preventive treatments have failed.
Topiramate is formally contraindicated in pregnancy because pharmacovigilance data suggest a possible effect on neurodevelopment in children exposed in utero.
In women of childbearing age topiramate needs extreme caution: effective contraception, no alternative available and annual follow-up, as with valproate.

items.title: A scoping review of hormonal clinical trials in menstrual cycle-related brain disorders: Studies in premenstrual mood disorder, menstrual migraine, and catamenial epilepsy
items.summary: This review looked at 85 studies of hormone treatments for three conditions linked to the menstrual cycle: premenstrual mood disorder, menstrual migraine and cycle-related epilepsy. Hormone treatments have been tested most often for premenstrual mood disorder and least for epilepsy. Combined birth control pills containing drospirenone showed promising results for both premenstrual mood disorder and menstrual migraine. The review did not give an overall certainty rating.
keyPoints: Hormone treatments were tested in 56 trials for premenstrual mood disorder, 21 for menstrual migraine and 8 for cycle-related epilepsy.
Combined oral contraceptives containing drospirenone showed promising results for both premenstrual mood disorder (PMDD) and menstrual migraine.
Drugs that switch off ovulation (GnRH agonists) were supported by a meta-analysis for premenstrual mood disorder, but were tested in only two menstrual migraine trials.
Menstrual migraine research has focused heavily on estrogen-based treatments, while epilepsy research has focused on progesterone in the second half of the cycle.

items.title: Antiphospholipid syndrome in pregnancy: a comprehensive literature review
items.summary: This review looked at antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), an autoimmune condition that can cause blood clots and problems in pregnancy, including repeated miscarriage. It brought together studies on how APS works, how it is diagnosed and how it is treated in pregnancy. The review found that low-dose aspirin and heparin help reduce miscarriage rates, and that hydroxychloroquine may help in higher-risk cases. The authors say treatment should be tailored to each person and that more research is needed.
keyPoints: APS affects about 0.5% of people and is a leading contributor to recurrent pregnancy loss, preeclampsia and poor fetal growth.
Evidence supports low-dose aspirin and heparin to reduce miscarriage rates.
Hydroxychloroquine has shown promise for improving live birth rates and reducing preterm delivery in high-risk cases.
Newer treatments, such as TNF-alpha inhibitors and nitric oxide modulators, may help in cases that do not respond to usual treatment, but more research is needed.

items.title: Autologous platelet-rich plasma for assisted reproduction
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether putting a woman's own platelet-rich plasma (PRP) into the womb or ovaries helps IVF or ICSI treatment work better. It combined 12 trials with 1069 women. The evidence was very low quality, so it is not clear whether PRP improves live birth or reduces miscarriage. One small trial also hinted at a higher chance of preterm birth.
keyPoints: The review is uncertain whether PRP in the womb or ovaries improves outcomes of assisted reproduction.
Only 1 of 12 trials was at low risk of bias, and that trial found no clear effect on live birth or miscarriage.
When all trials were pooled, womb PRP looked linked to more live births and clinical pregnancies, but the certainty was very low.
One trial of 120 women suggested womb PRP may increase the risk of preterm delivery (low-certainty evidence), and most trials gave little or no safety data.

items.title: Progestogens for preventing miscarriage: a network meta-analysis
items.summary: This Cochrane review combined seven randomised trials (5,682 women) to see whether progesterone-type medicines (progestogens) help prevent miscarriage. For most women with early pregnancy bleeding or a history of repeated miscarriages, these medicines probably make little or no difference to the chance of a live birth. The exception was vaginal progesterone for women with early bleeding who had already had one or more miscarriages, where live births increased slightly, with no clear rise in side effects. Evidence on other progestogens, such as dydrogesterone, is still too limited to be sure.
keyPoints: Progestogens probably make little or no difference to live birth rates for women with early pregnancy bleeding (threatened miscarriage) or recurrent miscarriage.
Vaginal micronized progesterone increased live births for women with early pregnancy bleeding and one or more previous miscarriages (high-certainty evidence).
Vaginal progesterone showed likely no difference in congenital abnormalities or adverse drug events compared with placebo.
Effects of dydrogesterone, oral progesterone and 17-α-hydroxyprogesterone remain uncertain because of limited or very low-certainty evidence.

items.title: Obesity in Pregnancy: ACOG Practice Bulletin, Number 230
items.summary: This is a guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) on obesity in pregnancy. It notes that obesity is the most common medical condition in women of reproductive age, and that its effects on pregnancy are often overlooked. It says care should start before pregnancy and continue through the postpartum period, and can involve other professionals such as nutritionists.
keyPoints: Obesity is the most common medical condition in women of reproductive age.
Managing obesity takes long-term approaches, from public health measures to individual nutrition, behavior or surgical options.
Care should begin before pregnancy and continue through the postpartum period.
Nutritionists and other health professionals can support the obstetric care team.

items.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 200: Early Pregnancy Loss
items.summary: This guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists covers early pregnancy loss, which is the loss of a pregnancy inside the womb during the first trimester. It reviews how doctors can tell whether an early pregnancy is viable or not. It also describes the options for managing a loss, which are waiting for it to pass naturally, taking medicine, or having a surgical procedure.
keyPoints: Early pregnancy loss means losing a pregnancy in the womb during the first trimester, and it is common in clinical practice.
Doctors use a range of diagnostic tools to tell a viable pregnancy from a nonviable one.
Patients should be offered the full range of management options: expectant, medical and surgical.

items.title: The Management of Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy and Hyperemesis Gravidarum (Green-top Guideline No. 69)
items.source: Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
items.organisation: Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
items.summary: This is a 2024 guideline from the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists on managing nausea and vomiting in pregnancy and the severe form called hyperemesis gravidarum. It recommends starting with well-studied first-line anti-sickness medicines, with other medicines added if these do not work. It also covers how severity is measured, how fluids are given in hospital, and vitamin B1 (thiamine) supplements for women who are vomiting a lot.
keyPoints: Validated scoring tools such as PUQE and HELP can be used to judge how severe the nausea and vomiting is; ketones in the urine should not be used to judge dehydration or severity.
First-line medicines (antihistamines, phenothiazines, and doxylamine/pyridoxine) have good safety and effectiveness data and should be offered first when medicine is needed.

If first-line medicines do not work, ondansetron or metoclopramide can be used as second-line options; ondansetron is linked to a very small increase in the absolute risk of cleft lip or palate when used in the first trimester, which should be weighed against the risks of poorly controlled hyperemesis.
Women admitted with vomiting or very low food intake should be given thiamine, and combinations of anti-sickness drugs can be used if one drug is not enough.

items.title: AGA Clinical Practice Update on Pregnancy-Related Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease: Expert Review
items.summary: This American Gastroenterological Association expert review gives practical advice on stomach, bowel and liver conditions in pregnancy. For nausea and vomiting, it says treating symptoms early may help stop them turning into hyperemesis gravidarum (severe pregnancy sickness). The advice comes from published studies and expert opinion, not a formal systematic review, so the statements are not rated for evidence quality.
keyPoints: Early treatment of nausea and vomiting of pregnancy may reduce progression to hyperemesis gravidarum.
Treatment starts with diet and lifestyle measures, then vitamin B6 and doxylamine, hydration and adequate nutrition.
Ondansetron, metoclopramide, promethazine and intravenous glucocorticoids may be needed in moderate to severe cases.
For constipation in pregnancy, options include dietary fiber, lactulose and polyethylene glycol-based laxatives.

items.title: Interventions for treating hyperemesis gravidarum
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 25 trials (2052 women) of treatments for hyperemesis gravidarum, the severe form of pregnancy sickness. Most comparisons came from single small studies, and the evidence was mostly low or very low quality. No one treatment stood out as clearly better than the others, though some medicines differed in side effects such as drowsiness.
keyPoints: There is little high-quality, consistent evidence supporting any one treatment for hyperemesis gravidarum.
Metoclopramide caused more drowsiness and dry mouth than ondansetron, with no clear difference in how well they eased nausea or vomiting.
Promethazine caused more drowsiness, dizziness and dystonia than metoclopramide in one study.
Corticosteroids did not clearly shorten hospital stays, but fewer women needed to be readmitted in four studies.

items.title: Interventions for nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 41 trials (5449 women) of treatments for nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy, including acupressure, acupuncture, ginger and vitamin B6. The authors found a lack of high-quality evidence to support any one treatment. Ginger may help, and three recent studies favoured ginger over placebo, but results were limited and not consistent. This does not mean the treatments don't work, only that the evidence is not strong enough to be sure.
keyPoints: No single treatment for early-pregnancy nausea and vomiting has strong, high-quality evidence behind it.
Ginger products may be helpful, but the evidence was limited and not consistent.
Acupuncture showed no significant benefit, and evidence for acupressure was limited.
Evidence for vitamin B6, doxylamine-pyridoxine and other anti-sickness drugs in mild or moderate cases was limited, and there was little information on side effects.

items.title: ESHRE guideline: ovarian stimulation for IVF/ICSI: an update in 2025†
items.summary: This is the 2025 update of the ESHRE guideline on ovarian stimulation for IVF/ICSI. It gives 121 recommendations on every step of stimulation, from pre-treatment checks to preventing a complication called ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), and also covers fertility preservation and egg freezing. The authors say much of the evidence behind the recommendations is of low or very low quality, and several newer treatments are not well studied yet.
keyPoints: The guideline covers pre-stimulation evaluation, pituitary suppression and stimulation, monitoring, triggering egg maturation, luteal support and OHSS prevention.
It includes 17 recommendations on fertility preservation, including elective egg freezing and egg donation.
Of the evidence-based recommendations, none rested on high-quality evidence, 6 on moderate, 36 on low and 148 on very low-quality evidence.
For several newer treatments the evidence was too limited, so the guideline advises against them or says they should only be used in research.

items.title: In vitro maturation in subfertile women with polycystic ovarian syndrome undergoing assisted reproduction
items.summary: This Cochrane review compared in vitro maturation (IVM), where eggs are collected early and matured in the lab, with standard IVF or ICSI in women with PCOS. It found four trials with 810 women. IVM greatly lowered the risk of moderate or severe ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) but raised the chance of miscarriage in pregnancies that were confirmed. The effect on live birth and pregnancy rates is very uncertain.
keyPoints: IVM greatly reduced moderate or severe OHSS compared with standard IVF (high-certainty evidence); about 3.5% with IVF versus roughly 0% to 2.4% with IVM.
IVM increased miscarriage per clinical pregnancy compared with IVF (high-certainty evidence); about 20.1% with IVF versus roughly 20.4% to 40.4% with IVM.
The effect on live birth and clinical pregnancy is very uncertain (very low-certainty evidence).
There was probably little to no difference in preterm birth, and the effect on birth defects was uncertain (low-certainty evidence).

items.title: Cycle regimens for endometrial preparation prior to frozen embryo transfer
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 32 trials (6,352 women) comparing different ways to prepare the womb lining for a frozen embryo transfer: natural cycles, hormone therapy cycles, and cycles using drugs to trigger ovulation. Across the comparisons, no approach clearly gave more live births or fewer miscarriages than another. Much of the evidence was low or very low quality, so the results are uncertain.
keyPoints: No cycle regimen was clearly better or safer than another for live birth or miscarriage rates.
Natural cycle versus hormone therapy with GnRHa suppression probably made little or no difference to live birth or multiple pregnancy (moderate-certainty evidence).
Most other comparisons were low or very low certainty, with wide ranges consistent with possible benefit or harm.
The review notes that important outcomes were often not reported and studies were small.

items.title: Evidence-based guideline: unexplained infertility†
items.summary: This European guideline looked at how to diagnose and treat couples whose fertility tests all come back normal (unexplained infertility). It makes 52 recommendations. The first treatment suggested is intrauterine insemination (IUI) combined with ovarian stimulation (medicines that help the ovaries release eggs). Most recommendations rest on very low or low quality evidence, so advice may change as better studies appear.
keyPoints: Unexplained infertility is diagnosed only after standard checks of both partners find no clear problem.
First-line treatment is IUI combined with ovarian stimulation.
Of 40 evidence-based recommendations, none had high-quality evidence, one had moderate, nine low and 31 very low quality evidence.
Many extra tests and treatments have not been properly tested, and recommendations may be revised as new studies appear.

items.title: Clinical evidence of growth hormone for infertile women with diminished ovarian reserve undergoing IVF: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 10 randomised trials (852 women) of adding growth hormone during ovarian stimulation for IVF in women with diminished ovarian reserve, meaning fewer eggs than expected. Women who received growth hormone had more clinical pregnancies, more eggs retrieved and better embryo results. They also needed fewer days and lower doses of fertility medication, and fewer cycles were cancelled. The trials were at high risk of bias because of blinding, and the authors say better-designed trials are needed to confirm the results.
keyPoints: Growth hormone was linked to a higher clinical pregnancy rate (RR 1.63) and more eggs retrieved.
It was also linked to higher fertilization and embryo implantation rates, more good-quality embryos, and fewer cancelled cycles.
Women using growth hormone needed fewer days and a lower total dose of stimulation medication.
The trials had a high risk of bias in blinding, so the authors call for well-designed trials to verify the findings.

items.title: The Role of Lifestyle Interventions in PCOS Management: A Systematic Review
items.summary: This systematic review looked at how lifestyle changes affect women with PCOS. It covered eating patterns, exercise and behavioural support. The review reports that these changes improved insulin sensitivity, hormone balance and body measures, and may lower long-term risks of metabolic and heart disease. The abstract does not rate the quality of the evidence.
keyPoints: Several eating patterns, including low glycemic index, Mediterranean, high-fibre and anti-inflammatory diets, improved insulin sensitivity and hormonal balance.
Aerobic and resistance exercise improved insulin sensitivity, helped weight loss and improved metabolic and reproductive outcomes.
Behavioural and education programmes can improve awareness, adherence to treatment and help with the mental health side of PCOS.
Lifestyle changes may also reduce long-term risks of metabolic and cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Inositol for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis to Inform the 2023 Update of the International Evidence-based PCOS Guidelines
items.source: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: This review pooled 30 trials (over 2,000 women) to see whether inositol, a supplement that may help the body respond to insulin, helps with PCOS. It found some possible benefits for certain blood sugar and metabolic measures, and possibly for ovulation with D-chiro-inositol, but little or no effect on other outcomes. Overall the authors say the evidence is limited and inconclusive.
keyPoints: Myo-inositol or D-chiro-inositol may help some metabolic measures, and D-chiro-inositol may help ovulation, but inositol may have no effect on other outcomes.
Metformin may improve waist-hip ratio and hirsutism more than inositol, with likely no difference in reproductive outcomes.
Myo-inositol likely causes fewer stomach and gut side effects than metformin, and these are usually mild and short-lived.
The evidence is limited and inconclusive, so decisions about inositol should weigh the uncertainty alongside personal values and preferences.

items.title: Statins for women with polycystic ovary syndrome not actively trying to conceive
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether statins (cholesterol-lowering medicines) help women with PCOS who are not trying to get pregnant. It found six small trials with 396 women in total, using simvastatin or atorvastatin for six weeks to six months. The evidence was of very low certainty, so researchers could not say whether statins improve periods, excess hair growth, acne or testosterone levels. The trials that checked for side effects reported no significant differences between groups.
keyPoints: Six small trials (396 women) tested statins in PCOS, and all main results were very low-certainty evidence.
It is uncertain whether statins improve menstrual regularity, hirsutism (excess hair), acne or testosterone levels compared with placebo, metformin or the pill.
No trials reported whether statins restore spontaneous ovulation.
Trials that recorded side effects found no significant differences between groups.

items.title: Lifestyle changes in women with polycystic ovary syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 15 small trials (498 women) of lifestyle changes such as exercise, diet and behavioural support in women with PCOS, compared with little or no treatment. Lifestyle changes may lower a hormone measure called the free androgen index, and may lead to small drops in weight and body mass index. The review is unsure about effects on glucose tolerance. No trials looked at live birth, miscarriage or menstrual regularity, and most of the evidence was low quality.
keyPoints: Lifestyle intervention may improve the free androgen index (a measure of male-type hormones) in women with PCOS.
It may reduce weight by about 1.7 kg and BMI by about 0.3 kg/m2 on average.
The effect on glucose tolerance is uncertain.
No studies reported live birth, miscarriage or menstrual regularity, and most trials were at risk of bias.

items.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 194: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
items.summary: This is a clinical guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists on polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). It describes PCOS as a condition with high levels of male-type hormones, irregular or absent ovulation, and polycystic ovaries. The cause is still unknown, so treatment mostly targets symptoms. The guideline also notes that PCOS can lead to longer-term health effects, which should be considered when planning treatment.
keyPoints: PCOS is defined by high androgen (male-type hormone) levels, ovulation problems, and polycystic ovaries.
The cause of PCOS is not known, and treatment is mostly based on symptoms and experience.
PCOS can raise the risk of diabetes and heart disease over time.
These long-term metabolic risks should be taken into account when choosing long-term treatment.

items.title: Impact of postpartum exercise on pelvic floor disorders and diastasis recti abdominis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 65 studies (about 21,000 women) to see how exercise in the first year after birth affects pelvic floor problems and the gap between the tummy muscles (diastasis recti). Pelvic floor muscle training lowered the odds of urinary leaking and pelvic organ prolapse compared with no training. Tummy muscle exercises reduced the gap between the abdominal muscles, though this evidence was lower quality. For other outcomes, such as bowel leakage and sexual function, the evidence was limited.
keyPoints: Pelvic floor muscle training reduced the odds of urinary incontinence by 37% (moderate certainty evidence, 7 trials).
Pelvic floor muscle training reduced the odds of pelvic organ prolapse by 56%, based on one trial of 123 women (moderate certainty).
Abdominal muscle training reduced the distance between the tummy muscles more than no exercise (low certainty evidence).
Evidence on anal incontinence, sexual function and the risk of diastasis recti was limited.

items.title: Clinical practice guideline for acupuncture and moxibustion: Female urinary incontinence
items.summary: This is a clinical practice guideline from the World Federation of Acupuncture-moxibustion Societies on using acupuncture and moxibustion (heat treatment with burning herbs) for urinary incontinence in women.
