The group made ten recommendations, and nearly all were 'conditional', which generally means the supporting evidence is not strong enough for firm advice. The guideline also describes treatment protocols taken from randomized trials.
keyPoints: Urinary incontinence is common in women but often under-reported and under-treated, and it can seriously affect quality of life.
The guideline made ten recommendations on acupuncture and moxibustion; nine were conditional for the treatment and one was conditional for either the treatment or the comparison.
It describes one conventional needle protocol, two deep-needling protocols on lower back acupoints, and four moxibustion protocols.
The recommendations were developed using GRADE methods and an expert panel vote (modified Delphi).

items.title: Pelvic floor muscle training for preventing and treating urinary and faecal incontinence in antenatal and postnatal women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 46 trials (10,832 women) to see whether pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) prevents or treats leaking urine or stool during pregnancy and after birth. Women who were not leaking at the start and did structured PFMT in pregnancy were less likely to report urine leakage in late pregnancy and in the months after birth. For women who already had leakage, and for leakage of stool, the evidence was too uncertain to say whether PFMT helps. Many trials were small or at risk of bias, and few followed women beyond 12 months.
keyPoints: Women without leakage who did PFMT in pregnancy probably had less urine leakage in late pregnancy (moderate-quality evidence) and slightly less at 3 to 6 months after birth (high-quality evidence).
For women who already leaked urine, there was no clear evidence that PFMT reduced leakage, and the evidence was low or very low quality.
There was no clear evidence that PFMT changed stool (faecal) incontinence, and starting PFMT only after birth for all women was not likely to reduce urine leakage.
Almost no side effects were reported; two women in one small trial stopped because of pelvic floor pain.

items.title: Pelvic Organ Prolapse: ACOG Practice Bulletin, Number 214
items.summary: This is a practice guideline from ACOG and the American Urogynecologic Society on pelvic organ prolapse, a common and non-cancerous condition in women. Prolapse can cause a vaginal bulge or pressure and problems with passing urine, bowel movements or sex, which may affect quality of life. The guideline reviews what is known about prolapse and sets out how it should be diagnosed and managed based on the best available evidence. The abstract does not list the specific treatment recommendations or rate the certainty of the evidence.
keyPoints: Pelvic organ prolapse is a common, benign condition in women.
It can cause vaginal bulge and pressure, bladder and bowel problems, and sexual difficulties.
Women in the US have a 13% lifetime risk of having surgery for prolapse.
Symptoms are most common at ages 70-79, and cases are expected to rise by about 50% by 2050.

items.title: Pelvic floor muscle training versus no treatment, or inactive control treatments, for urinary incontinence in women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 31 trials with 1817 women to see whether pelvic floor muscle training helps with leaking urine, compared with no treatment or inactive treatments. Women who did the training were much more likely to report being cured or improved, and they leaked less often and lost less urine. Side effects were rare and minor. Most trials were small, with follow-up mostly under 12 months, so long-term benefits are still unclear.
keyPoints: Women with stress incontinence who did pelvic floor training were about 8 times more likely to report cure (56% versus 6%), rated high-quality evidence.
Training reduced leakage by about one episode in 24 hours and led to less urine lost on short pad tests.
Women who did the training were also more satisfied and had better sexual outcomes; adverse events were rare and minor.
The authors suggest pelvic floor training could be part of first-line, non-surgical care, but long-term effects need more research.

items.title: FIGO best practice recommendations for the mental health of women at menopausal age
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: The International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) reviewed the evidence on mental health around the menopause and issued best practice recommendations. Anxiety and low mood are common during perimenopause, and they can affect quality of life. Treatment can be tailored to the person and may include lifestyle changes, talking therapy, or medicines such as hormone therapy. Experts rated eight of the 13 questions as strong recommendations.
keyPoints: Symptoms of anxiety and depression are common during perimenopause, but menopause-related mental health problems are often overlooked, especially in low- and middle-income countries.
Primary care providers need training to spot symptoms early, and psychological support should be part of menopause care.

Treatment should be individualised and may include lifestyle changes, cognitive-behavioural therapy and hormone therapy; transdermal estradiol is preferred for mood swings, particularly in women with metabolic risks.
Escitalopram and venlafaxine help depressive symptoms and hot flushes in women with major depressive disorder, and mindfulness, exercise and therapy have shown benefits.

items.title: Hormone Therapy for the Primary Prevention of Chronic Conditions in Postmenopausal Persons: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force reviewed whether taking hormone therapy (estrogen with progestin, or estrogen alone after a hysterectomy) can prevent long-term conditions like heart disease, cancer, osteoporosis and fractures in women after menopause. It found, with moderate certainty, that there is no net benefit overall. It recommends against using hormone therapy for this purpose. This advice applies to women without menopause symptoms who are considering hormones only to prevent disease, not to treat symptoms such as hot flushes.
keyPoints: The Task Force recommends against combined estrogen and progestin to prevent chronic conditions in postmenopausal women (D recommendation).
It also recommends against estrogen alone to prevent chronic conditions in women who have had a hysterectomy (D recommendation).
For both types of hormone therapy, the evidence showed no net benefit, with moderate certainty.
The advice is for women without symptoms who are considering hormones purely for prevention.

items.title: Dehydroepiandrosterone for women in the peri- or postmenopausal phase
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 28 trials with 1273 women in perimenopause or after menopause to see whether DHEA (a hormone precursor) helps menopausal symptoms. DHEA did not improve quality of life and was linked to more acne and other male-hormone-type side effects than placebo. It was unclear whether it eases symptoms like hot flushes, though it may slightly improve sexual function. The overall quality of the studies was moderate to low.
keyPoints: DHEA did not improve quality of life compared with placebo (moderate quality evidence).
DHEA was linked to more androgenic side effects, mainly acne, than placebo (moderate quality evidence).
It is uncertain whether DHEA reduces menopausal symptoms because trial results were inconsistent.
DHEA may slightly improve sexual function compared with placebo.

items.title: Treatment and Management of Mental Health Conditions During Pregnancy and Postpartum: ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 5
items.summary: This is a clinical practice guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG). It looked at the evidence on how safe and how well psychiatric medicines work for depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder and acute psychosis during pregnancy and breastfeeding. It gives recommendations on treating and managing these conditions, with a focus on medication, and rates each recommendation by strength and evidence quality. Where evidence was missing or too limited, it gives good practice points instead of formal recommendations.
keyPoints: The guideline covers treatment of depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder and acute postpartum psychosis in pregnancy and the first year after birth.
It reviews the safety and effectiveness of psychiatric medicines during pregnancy and lactation.
Each recommendation is classified by strength and quality of evidence.
Where evidence was inadequate or absent, ungraded good practice points give guidance instead.

items.title: Interventions for fear of childbirth including tocophobia
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at seven trials (1357 women) testing non-drug approaches such as education, cognitive behavioural therapy, group discussion, peer education and art therapy for high or severe fear of childbirth, including tocophobia. These approaches may lower fear scores slightly, but the drop may be too small to make a real difference. They probably reduce caesarean births and the number of women preferring a caesarean, and made little or no difference to depression scores. The evidence is limited, so the effect on fear itself is uncertain.
keyPoints: Non-drug interventions may reduce fear of childbirth scores, but the reduction may not be clinically meaningful (low-certainty evidence).
They probably reduce the number of women having a caesarean section (moderate-certainty evidence).
They probably mean fewer women prefer a caesarean birth (moderate-certainty evidence).
There may be little or no difference in depression scores, and epidural use may increase slightly (low-certainty evidence).

items.title: Mapping global prevalence of depression among postpartum women
items.summary: This large review pulled together 565 studies from 80 countries to find out how common depression is after childbirth. About 17% of women worldwide were found to have postpartum depression, though rates varied a lot between regions. It was lower in wealthier, more developed countries and highest in Southern Africa.
keyPoints: Around 17% of women worldwide had postpartum depression, and the authors say this is roughly one in five women.
Rates were much higher in some regions, such as Southern Africa (about 40%), and lower in high-income countries.
Rates differed with factors like social support, partner care, violence, financial difficulties, life stress, smoking, alcohol and living conditions.
The authors say the many causes call for attention and action from health professionals, health authorities and the wider community.

items.title: Worldwide prevalence of dysmenorrhea: a systematic review and meta-analysis across 70 countries
items.summary: Researchers pooled results from 336 studies across 70 countries to estimate how common period pain (dysmenorrhoea) is. About 7 in 10 women (71.3%) reported period pain, and it was more common in some places and groups, such as university students. The studies varied a lot from one to the next, and the authors rated the certainty of the evidence as very low, so the exact numbers should be treated as rough estimates.
keyPoints: The pooled worldwide prevalence of period pain was 71.3%.
Pain with no underlying cause (primary dysmenorrhoea) was estimated at 73%, and pain linked to another condition (secondary dysmenorrhoea) at 35%.
Period pain was reported more often in Central America (89.6%), Sri Lanka (97.7%), among adults (73.3%) and at universities (78.4%).
Results differed greatly between studies and the certainty of evidence was very low.

items.title: Guideline No. 345: Primary Dysmenorrhea
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline reviews how to assess and treat primary dysmenorrhea, which is period pain with no underlying cause found. It says this pain is common but often undertreated, even though effective, low-cost treatments exist. Treatments include anti-inflammatory pain medicines (NSAIDs) and hormonal contraceptives, and they can be started without a pelvic exam or waiting for a firm diagnosis.
keyPoints: Primary dysmenorrhea is common and often undertreated or dismissed, despite effective treatment being widely available at minimal cost.
Treatment includes non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and hormonal contraceptives.
Treatment can be provided without a pelvic examination or invasive procedures and should not be delayed pending a definitive diagnosis.
Treating the pain may improve quality of life and reduce time away from school or work; untreated persistent pain may develop into a chronic pain syndrome.

items.title: Exercise for dysmenorrhoea
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether regular exercise eases period pain (primary dysmenorrhoea) in women with moderate-to-severe pain. It found 12 trials with 854 women. Low-quality evidence suggests exercise may reduce period pain by a noticeable amount, around 25 points on a 100-point pain scale. The evidence is low quality, so more research is needed.
keyPoints: Exercise may reduce period pain intensity by about 25 mm on a 100 mm pain scale compared with no treatment (low-quality evidence).
The benefit was seen with exercise of about 45 to 60 minutes, three or more times a week, whatever the intensity (stretching, yoga, core work, Zumba or aerobic training).
Evidence on side effects, overall period symptoms, quality of life and exercise compared with anti-inflammatory painkillers was too limited to draw conclusions.
It is unclear if the benefits last after exercise stops or whether they apply to women over 25.

items.title: No. 345-Primary Dysmenorrhea Consensus Guideline
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This is a Canadian clinical guideline on primary dysmenorrhea, which means period pain with no underlying cause found. It reviewed trials and studies published between 2005 and 2016 to update advice on how the pain is investigated and treated. The guideline notes that this pain is common and often undertreated, and that effective treatment is widely available at low cost. Treating it may improve quality of life and reduce time lost from school or work.
keyPoints: Primary dysmenorrhea is period pain with no identified underlying cause, and it is common.
It is frequently undertreated, even though effective therapy is widely available at minimal cost.
Treatment can improve quality of life and reduce time lost from school or work.
The guideline updates the 2005 advice using evidence from 2005 to 2016.

items.title: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for dysmenorrhoea
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 80 trials (5,820 women) of anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) for period pain with no underlying cause. NSAIDs relieved pain much better than placebo and appeared to work better than paracetamol. They also caused more side effects, such as stomach and nervous system effects. The evidence was mostly low quality, and it is not clear whether any one NSAID is best or safest.
keyPoints: NSAIDs were more effective than placebo for period pain: if 18% of women on placebo got moderate or excellent relief, about 45% to 53% on NSAIDs would.
NSAIDs caused more side effects than placebo: if 10% on placebo had side effects, about 11% to 14% on NSAIDs would, with more stomach and neurological effects.
NSAIDs appeared to work better than paracetamol, though only three trials were available.
There was not enough evidence to say which individual NSAID is safest or most effective, and COX-2-specific NSAIDs showed no clear advantage.

items.title: Effect of nutritional interventions on the psychological symptoms of premenstrual syndrome in women of reproductive age: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This review looked at 31 randomized trials (3,254 women aged 15 to 50) testing diet changes and supplements for the mood and emotional symptoms of premenstrual syndrome (PMS). Vitamin B6, calcium and zinc were the ones that most consistently helped. For many other options, such as vitamin D, magnesium and soy, there was not enough evidence to say either way. Almost all of the trials had a risk of bias, so the findings are not yet conclusive.
keyPoints: Vitamin B6, calcium and zinc consistently showed positive effects on psychological PMS symptoms.
There was not enough evidence for vitamin B1, vitamin D, whole grains, soy isoflavones, fatty acids, magnesium, multivitamins or PMS-specific diets.
Only 1 of the 31 trials had a low risk of bias.
More consistent, better-designed and clearly reported research is needed before firm nutrition advice can be given.

items.title: The prevalence of premenstrual dysphoric disorder: Systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 44 studies (about 50,000 people) to estimate how common premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) is. When PMDD was confirmed by tracking symptoms daily over two cycles, about 3.2% of people had it. When it was only a provisional diagnosis, the figure was higher at 7.7%. The authors say studies using provisional diagnosis probably overestimate how common PMDD is.
keyPoints: Confirmed PMDD (symptoms tracked prospectively over two cycles) had a pooled prevalence of 3.2%.
Provisional PMDD diagnosis gave a higher estimate of 7.7%, which is likely to be artificially high.
In community-based samples with confirmed diagnosis, prevalence was 1.6%.
Results varied a lot between studies, by region, type of sample, and how PMDD was diagnosed.

items.title: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors for premenstrual syndrome and premenstrual dysphoric disorder
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 34 randomised trials comparing SSRI antidepressants (such as fluoxetine, sertraline and paroxetine) with placebo in women with PMS or PMDD. SSRIs probably reduce premenstrual symptoms, and seem to work better when taken every day than when taken only in the two weeks before a period. They also probably cause more side effects than placebo, most commonly nausea, weakness or low energy, and sleepiness. About two thirds of the studies were funded by drug companies and publication bias is suspected, so the results should be read with some caution.
keyPoints: SSRIs probably reduce overall self-rated premenstrual symptoms compared with placebo (moderate-certainty evidence).
Taking SSRIs continuously was probably more effective than taking them only in the luteal phase (the two weeks before a period).
SSRIs probably increase side effects, including nausea, weakness or low energy, sleepiness, insomnia, sexual problems and dry mouth.
68% of included studies were pharmaceutical-funded and publication bias is suspected, so findings should be interpreted with caution.

items.title: Oral contraceptives containing drospirenone for premenstrual syndrome
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled five trials (858 women, mostly with PMDD, the severe form of PMS) testing combined pills with drospirenone and ethinylestradiol against placebo. The pill may ease overall premenstrual symptoms and reduce the effect of symptoms on work, social life and relationships, with small to moderate benefits. It may also cause more side effects than placebo, such as breast pain and nausea. The evidence was mostly low quality, and the placebo also helped many women.
keyPoints: Drospirenone pills may improve overall premenstrual symptoms and day-to-day functioning (productivity, social activities, relationships) in women with PMDD, with small to moderate effects.
The pill may lead to more side effects overall and more people stopping because of them; it probably causes more breast pain and may cause more nausea and bleeding between periods.
The effect on premenstrual mood symptoms is uncertain, and no serious rare side effects such as blood clots were reported in the trials.
It is not known whether benefits last beyond three cycles, whether the pill helps women with milder symptoms, or whether it beats other combined pills.

items.title: Factors Associated with the Prevalence and Severity of Menstrual-Related Symptoms: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.source: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.summary: This review pooled results from 77 studies to find which factors are linked to period pain (primary dysmenorrhea) and premenstrual syndrome (PMS). Period pain was more common with a family history of it, stress, low body weight, irregular cycles, short sleep and late bedtimes. Smoking was linked to more severe period pain and to PMS. These are links between factors and symptoms, so they do not prove one causes the other.
keyPoints: Having a family history of period pain was linked to much higher odds of period pain (OR 3.80).
Stress, sleeping under 7 hours, going to bed after 23:01, irregular cycles and a BMI under 18.5 were each linked to more period pain.
Low BMI (under 18.5) and smoking were linked to more severe period pain.
Smoking was linked to a higher chance of premenstrual syndrome (OR 1.86).

items.title: Guideline No. 451: Asymptomatic Endometrial Thickening in Postmenopausal Women
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline looks at what to do when an ultrasound shows a thickened womb lining in a woman after menopause who has no bleeding. It aims to avoid unnecessary tests and procedures while still checking women who may be at risk of womb cancer. The guideline's public summary says that without bleeding, a lining thinner than 11 mm is rarely a serious problem, but it should still be looked at by a health care provider.
keyPoints: A thickened womb lining found on ultrasound in a postmenopausal woman with no bleeding is often not serious.
Without bleeding, a lining under 11 mm is rarely a serious problem but should still be evaluated by a health care provider.
The aim is to avoid unnecessary invasive tests while selectively investigating women at risk of endometrial cancer.
Fewer unnecessary procedures could mean less anxiety, pain and risk of complications.

items.title: Association of Endometrial Cancer Risk With Postmenopausal Bleeding in Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 129 studies to look at how often bleeding after menopause is linked to womb (endometrial) cancer. Around 9 in 10 women with endometrial cancer had bleeding after menopause. But only about 1 in 11 women with bleeding after menopause were found to have the cancer, so most cases have other, non-cancer causes.
keyPoints: About 91% of women with endometrial cancer had bleeding after menopause, whatever the stage of the cancer.
About 9% of women with bleeding after menopause were found to have endometrial cancer.
The risk ranged from 7% to 12% depending on hormone therapy use, and from 5% in North America to 13% in Western Europe.
Checking women who have bleeding after menopause could catch as many as 90% of endometrial cancers, but most of these women will not have cancer.

items.title: Short-term and long-term effects of tibolone in postmenopausal women
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 46 randomised trials (about 20,000 women) of tibolone, a synthetic hormone medicine used for menopause symptoms. Tibolone eased hot flushes and night sweats better than placebo but not as well as standard combined hormone therapy. It caused more unscheduled vaginal bleeding than placebo, but less than combined hormone therapy. Much of the evidence on long-term safety was low or very low quality.
keyPoints: Unscheduled vaginal bleeding was more likely with tibolone than placebo: if 18% of women on placebo had bleeding, an estimated 31% to 44% of women on tibolone would (moderate-quality evidence).
Compared with combined hormone therapy, tibolone had less unscheduled bleeding: if 47% on combined therapy had bleeding, an estimated 18% to 27% on tibolone would (moderate-quality evidence).
Tibolone was more effective than placebo but less effective than combined hormone therapy for hot flushes and night sweats.
In women with a history of breast cancer, tibolone raised the risk of the cancer coming back, and it may raise stroke risk in women over 60.

items.title: Breastfeeding interventions for preventing postpartum depression
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 10 trials (1573 women) testing whether support with breastfeeding could help prevent postpartum depression. Psychosocial breastfeeding support (such as counselling and emotional support around feeding) may lower the chance of postpartum depression in the first one to three months, and may help women breastfeed for longer. However, the evidence is low quality and based on very few small studies, so the results are uncertain. No harms from the interventions were reported, but it is unclear whether harms were actually measured.
keyPoints: Psychosocial breastfeeding support may reduce postpartum depression one to three months after the programme, but this came from one small study (82 women) and is low-certainty evidence.
Psychosocial support may increase how long women breastfeed in the long term (low-certainty evidence).
The effect on depression symptom scores, anxiety and exclusive breastfeeding is very uncertain, and 'alternative' relaxation-type interventions showed no clear benefit.
No adverse events were reported, but most studies may not have measured them; larger, better-run trials are needed.

items.title: Prevalence and correlates of perinatal depression
items.summary: This study pulled together 128 earlier reviews to give a global picture of depression during pregnancy and after birth. On average, about 1 in 4 women (26-29%) were affected, whether during pregnancy or after the baby arrived. Rates looked higher when women filled in questionnaires than when they had a structured interview, and higher in some vulnerable groups. The included reviews were all of medium-to-high quality, but the authors say the original research behind them could still be improved.
keyPoints: Average prevalence was 26.3% for perinatal depression, 28.5% for depression in pregnancy and 27.6% for postnatal depression.
Rates were higher with self-report questionnaires (27.4%) than with structured interviews (17.0%), and higher in potentially vulnerable groups (32.5%) than in the general population (24.5%).

Factors linked with perinatal depression included past mental illness, stressful life events, low social support, a history of abuse, relationship conflict, the baby blues, child care stress, long-term health conditions, preeclampsia, gestational diabetes, second-hand smoke and poor sleep.
The authors call for more standardised ways of assessing and diagnosing perinatal depression and for better-designed studies.

items.title: Prevalence and Risk Factors of Postpartum Depression in Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 27 studies including more than 133,000 women to estimate how common postpartum depression is and what raises the risk. About 14 in 100 women were affected, with rates ranging from about 5% to 26% depending on the country. Having gestational diabetes, depression in pregnancy, or a past history of depression was linked to a higher chance of postpartum depression. The authors note that high-quality reviews on this topic are limited, and results varied a lot between studies.
keyPoints: Pooled prevalence of postpartum depression was 14.0% across all studies, and it varied by country from 5.0% to 26.32%.
Gestational diabetes, depression during pregnancy, and a history of depression were linked to higher risk.
Having a baby boy was also linked to higher risk, though the abstract does not explain why.
Knowing these risk factors may help healthcare staff screen for and support women with postpartum depression.

items.title: Antidepressant treatment for postnatal depression
items.summary: This Cochrane review pulled together 11 trials (1016 women) of antidepressant treatment for depression in the first year after birth. Most trials tested SSRIs, a common type of antidepressant, for 4 to 12 weeks. SSRIs may work better than placebo (dummy pills) for improving or clearing depression, but the evidence is low or very low certainty because the trials were small and many women dropped out. No harm to children, including breastfed babies, was noted, but information on this was limited.
keyPoints: SSRIs may help more than placebo: 55% versus 43% responded and 42% versus 27% reached remission, though these gains were not firmly certain.
Women taking SSRIs and placebo stopped treatment at similar rates (27% in both groups).
Many women had side effects, but no trial found a difference in side effects between treatment groups.
Evidence is too limited to compare antidepressants with talking therapies or other treatments, or to judge safety for babies; the authors call for larger, longer trials.

items.title: ACOG Committee Opinion No. 757: Screening for Perinatal Depression
items.summary: This is a guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists on checking for depression during pregnancy and after birth. Perinatal depression happens during pregnancy or in the first 12 months after delivery and affects about one in seven women. The guideline recommends that care providers screen for depression and anxiety at least once in the perinatal period using a standard, validated questionnaire, and check mood again at the postpartum visit.
keyPoints: Perinatal depression affects about one in seven women, during pregnancy or in the first 12 months after delivery.
Care providers are advised to screen for depression and anxiety symptoms at least once during pregnancy or after birth using a validated tool.
A full check of mood and emotional well-being, including screening for postpartum depression and anxiety, is recommended at the postpartum visit.
Screening alone can help, but starting treatment or referral to mental health care gives the most benefit.

items.title: Immediate versus delayed postpartum insertion of contraceptive implant and IUD for contraception
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether getting a contraceptive implant or an IUD (a small device placed in the womb) right after birth works better than waiting until a later visit. It combined 16 trials: 5 on implants and 11 on IUDs. More people ended up with an implant or IUD when it was offered right after birth. However, IUDs placed straight after birth were more likely to come out on their own, and immediate implants may be linked with more bleeding and other side effects in the first six weeks.
keyPoints: Immediate insertion probably means more people start an implant (moderate-certainty evidence) or an IUD (moderate-certainty evidence) than waiting for a later visit.
IUDs placed immediately after birth may be more likely to be expelled (come out) by six months than IUDs placed later (low-certainty evidence).
Immediate implants may be linked with more prolonged bleeding and other side effects in the first six weeks (low-certainty evidence).
Hormonal implants and IUDs placed right after birth may have little or no negative effect on breastfeeding.

items.title: Society of Family Planning Guidelines: Postplacental insertion of intrauterine devices
items.summary: This guideline reviewed the evidence on having an intrauterine device (IUD) fitted within 10 minutes after the placenta is delivered, after either a vaginal or cesarean birth. It found this is safe and does not cause more complications than having an IUD fitted later. The IUD is more likely to come out on its own (expulsion) when fitted straight after birth, especially after a vaginal birth, though rates vary widely between studies.
keyPoints: Fitting an IUD within 10 minutes of delivering the placenta is safe and has no higher risk of complications than fitting it later.
Most studies find the IUD is more likely to be expelled after fitting straight after birth than after later fitting.
Expulsion is more common after vaginal delivery than after cesarean delivery, but rates vary widely and the reasons are unclear.
It may help most people who are unlikely to come back for a postpartum visit, if a replacement is available when an IUD comes out and the risks and benefits are explained.

items.title: Lactational amenorrhoea method for family planning
items.summary: This review looked at the lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM), where a mother uses full breastfeeding and the absence of periods as a form of birth control after having a baby. Across the studies, pregnancy rates at six months were low, ranging from about 0% to 7.5%. Women who were fully breastfeeding and had no periods but used no method had similarly low rates, and the review found no clear difference between the two groups. It is uncertain whether LAM support actually makes periods stay away for longer.
keyPoints: In controlled studies of LAM users, pregnancy rates at six months were 0.45% and 2.45%, and one study reported 5%.
Fully breastfeeding women with no periods who used no contraception had pregnancy rates of about 0.9% to 1.2% at six months.
No clear difference in pregnancy rates was found between women supported to use LAM and similar women using no method.
How long periods stayed away varied a lot between populations, so it is uncertain whether LAM extends this time.
keywords: can i get pregnant while breastfeeding

items.title: Adolescent Pregnancy Guidelines
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline sets out how to care for pregnant teenagers before, during and after birth. For the period after birth, it recommends that contraception be discussed before delivery, with a focus on long-acting reversible methods, to reduce the high rate of repeat pregnancy in this group. It also recommends breastfeeding support and postpartum programs, including screening for postpartum depression.
keyPoints: Postpartum care should include a focus on contraception, especially long-acting reversible methods, to lower high repeat-pregnancy rates in adolescents.
Talking about contraception should begin before delivery.
Postpartum programs should support young parents, increase breastfeeding, screen for postpartum depression and lengthen the time between pregnancies.
STI testing is recommended after birth, and breastfeeding should be recommended with enough support to help teens keep going.

items.title: Pelvic floor training to prevent stress urinary incontinence: A systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at seven randomised trials with 1,401 pregnant women to see whether pelvic floor muscle training can prevent leaking urine when coughing, sneezing or exercising (stress urinary incontinence). The authors found that, when done with a suitable method, this training can prevent or help cure the problem. Starting early in pregnancy seemed to help bladder control after birth. The abstract does not rate how strong the evidence is.
keyPoints: Stress urinary incontinence is common after birth, affecting 30 to 47% of women in the first 12 months.
Pelvic floor muscle training, applied with the appropriate method, can prevent or cure stress urinary incontinence.
Starting the training early in pregnancy had positive effects on bladder control after delivery.
The review covered 7 randomised trials with 1,401 pregnant women.

items.title: Pelvic floor muscle training for prevention and treatment of urinary and faecal incontinence in antenatal and postnatal women
items.summary: This Cochrane review combined 38 trials with nearly 9,900 women to see whether pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) helps prevent or treat leaking urine or stool around pregnancy and birth. For women who were not leaking before, starting a structured PFMT programme early in pregnancy may lower the chance of urine leakage in late pregnancy and in the months after birth. It is still unclear whether PFMT works as a treatment once leaking has started, or whether it helps with leaking stool. Many trials were small or had weaknesses, so much of the evidence is low or very low quality.
keyPoints: Women who were continent and did PFMT in pregnancy may have about 62% less urinary incontinence in late pregnancy (low-quality evidence) and about 29% less at 3 to 6 months after birth (moderate-quality evidence).
Whether PFMT treats urinary incontinence that has already started, in pregnancy or after birth, is uncertain (very low-quality evidence).
For faecal incontinence, antenatal PFMT made little or no difference in late pregnancy, and effects after birth are uncertain.
Apart from two reports of pelvic floor pain, trials reported no harmful effects of PFMT.

items.title: Insulin for the treatment of women with gestational diabetes
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 53 trials (7381 women) to see how insulin compares with oral diabetes medicines for treating gestational diabetes when diet and lifestyle changes are not enough. Insulin and oral medicines had similar effects on most key outcomes for mothers and babies. Women treated with insulin had more hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, but pre-eclampsia and caesarean birth rates were not clearly different. The evidence ranged from very low to moderate quality, and long-term outcomes were poorly reported.
keyPoints: Insulin and oral anti-diabetic medicines had similar effects on key health outcomes for mothers and babies.
Insulin was linked to a higher risk of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (moderate-quality evidence), but no clear difference in pre-eclampsia, caesarean birth or later type 2 diabetes.
No clear differences were found for babies born large, newborn low blood sugar, or later childhood adiposity and neurosensory outcomes.
The choice of treatment may come down to doctor or maternal preference, availability or how severe the gestational diabetes is.

items.title: The Effects of Exercise during Pregnancy on Gestational Diabetes Mellitus, Preeclampsia, and Spontaneous Abortion among Healthy Women-A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.source: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
items.summary: This review pooled results from randomized trials of exercise during pregnancy in healthy women. Exercise lowered the risk of gestational diabetes, and the type, intensity and supervision of exercise did not seem to matter. Overall, exercise did not clearly lower the risk of pre-eclampsia, though mind-body exercise and low-intensity exercise looked helpful in smaller subgroup checks. Exercise did not increase adverse events, but the authors say more high-quality studies are needed on pre-eclampsia.
keyPoints: Across 18 trials, exercise compared with no exercise was linked to about a one-third lower risk of gestational diabetes (RR 0.66).
Any type or intensity of exercise seemed equally effective for gestational diabetes prevention.
Across nine trials, exercise did not clearly reduce pre-eclampsia (RR 0.65, range 0.42 to 1.03), but mind-body and low-intensity exercise looked beneficial in subgroup analyses.
No effect of exercise on withdrawal from studies or adverse events was found, and the authors conclude exercise in pregnancy is beneficial and safe; no studies reported on spontaneous abortion.

items.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 202: Gestational Hypertension and Preeclampsia
items.summary: This is a practice guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists on gestational hypertension and preeclampsia. The abstract describes how common and serious these conditions are: preeclampsia affects about 2-8% of pregnancies worldwide, and high blood pressure disorders are a leading cause of death for mothers and babies. The guideline is meant to guide how doctors diagnose and manage these conditions. The abstract does not give the specific diagnosis or treatment recommendations.
keyPoints: Preeclampsia is estimated to affect 2-8% of pregnancies worldwide.
High blood pressure disorders cause about 16% of maternal deaths in high-income countries and about 26% in Latin America and the Caribbean.
In the US, the rate of preeclampsia rose by 25% between 1987 and 2004.
The condition is costly: an estimated $2.18 billion in the US in 2012 within the first year after delivery, with much of the cost tied to premature births.

items.title: Antiplatelet agents for preventing pre-eclampsia and its complications
items.summary: This Cochrane review combined 77 trials (about 40,000 pregnant women) that tested antiplatelet medicines, mostly low-dose aspirin, in women at risk of pre-eclampsia. Aspirin led to small-to-moderate benefits: fewer cases of pre-eclampsia, fewer preterm births, fewer small babies and fewer baby deaths. It probably slightly raised the chance of heavy bleeding after birth and may marginally raise the chance of placental abruption. Overall the authors concluded that outcomes improved and the medicine appears safe at these doses.
keyPoints: Antiplatelet agents reduced pre-eclampsia by 18% (about 16 fewer cases per 1000 women treated), with high-quality evidence.
Preterm birth before 37 weeks fell by 9% (about 16 fewer per 1000 treated), and fetal or neonatal death fell by 14% (about 5 fewer per 1000 treated).
Aspirin probably slightly increased postpartum bleeding over 500 mL and may marginally increase placental abruption (moderate-quality evidence).
Almost all women started treatment after 12 weeks, so it is unclear if starting earlier would help more.

items.title: Omega-3 fatty acid addition during pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 70 trials with nearly 20,000 pregnant women to see what happens when omega-3 fatty acids (from supplements or food, such as fish oil) are added during pregnancy. Women who took omega-3 had fewer babies born before 37 weeks and fewer born before 34 weeks, based on high-quality evidence. Pregnancies were probably more likely to go past 42 weeks, and babies were slightly less likely to have low birthweight. Evidence on pre-eclampsia and on longer-term outcomes for mothers and children was weaker.
keyPoints: Preterm birth before 37 weeks was lower with omega-3 (13.4% vs 11.9%), and birth before 34 weeks was also lower (4.6% vs 2.7%), both with high-quality evidence.
Pregnancies going past 42 weeks were probably more common with omega-3 (1.6% vs 2.6%), and there may be a small increase in larger-than-expected babies.
Low birthweight was less common, and perinatal death and neonatal care admissions were possibly reduced.
Pre-eclampsia may be slightly reduced, but this evidence was low quality; few differences were seen in children's development, mostly based on low or very low quality evidence.

items.title: Aspirin versus Placebo in Pregnancies at High Risk for Preterm Preeclampsia
items.summary: This trial looked at whether taking low-dose aspirin during pregnancy lowers the chance of preterm pre-eclampsia (pre-eclampsia leading to delivery before 37 weeks) in women at high risk. Over 1,700 women were randomly given either 150 mg of aspirin a day or a placebo, from 11-14 weeks until 36 weeks of pregnancy. Preterm pre-eclampsia happened in 1.6% of the aspirin group compared with 4.3% of the placebo group. There were no significant differences in newborn problems or other side effects between the groups.
keyPoints: Preterm pre-eclampsia occurred in 1.6% of women taking aspirin versus 4.3% of those taking placebo.
The women studied were at high risk and took 150 mg of aspirin daily from 11-14 weeks until 36 weeks of pregnancy.
No significant differences were found between groups in newborn adverse outcomes or other adverse events.
Most women took their tablets as planned, and the results held up when women who dropped out were accounted for.

items.title: Clinical risk factors for pre-eclampsia determined in early pregnancy: systematic review and meta-analysis of large cohort studies
items.summary: Researchers pooled 92 large studies covering over 25 million pregnancies to find which things known by 16 weeks of pregnancy raise the chance of pre-eclampsia. Having had pre-eclampsia before, chronic high blood pressure, pregestational diabetes, a BMI above 30 before pregnancy, and fertility treatment were all linked with higher risk. Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome had the highest rate of pre-eclampsia. The authors say these factors, alone or together, might help identify women at high risk early in pregnancy.
keyPoints: Prior pre-eclampsia carried the biggest increase in relative risk (about 8 times higher).
Chronic high blood pressure was second: about 16% developed pre-eclampsia, with about 5 times the relative risk.
Pregestational diabetes (about 11%), prepregnancy BMI over 30 (about 7%) and assisted reproductive technology (about 6%) were also clear risk factors.
These findings can help build tools to predict pre-eclampsia and guide who is offered aspirin in pregnancy.

items.title: American Thyroid Association 2026 Guidelines for Thyroid Disease in Preconception, Pregnancy, and Postpartum
items.summary: The American Thyroid Association updated its guidelines on thyroid disease before, during and after pregnancy, replacing the 2017 version. The guidelines cover thyroid testing, iodine, thyroid antibodies, underactive and overactive thyroid, thyroid nodules and cancer, and thyroid problems after birth. The authors say much of the evidence is low-to-moderate quality, so the guidelines reflect current best practice and expert agreement rather than certainty.
keyPoints: The guidelines give evidence-based advice on thyroid care for women with infertility, in pregnancy, and after birth or while breastfeeding.

Topics include thyroid function testing, iodine supplements, thyroid autoimmunity, hypothyroidism, hypothyroxinemia, hyperthyroidism and Graves' disease, thyroid nodules and cancer, and postpartum thyroid problems.
Where research was limited, the task force wrote Good Practice Statements based on expert consensus.
The authors note that much of the underlying evidence is of low-to-moderate quality and that care should be individualised.

items.title: ACOG Committee Opinion No. 762: Prepregnancy Counseling
items.summary: This guidance from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists explains why talking with a health professional before pregnancy is useful. The aim is to improve health before conception and lower risks for the woman, the baby and the newborn. It suggests this kind of counseling should be offered to anyone who may want to become pregnant and repeated at several points during the reproductive years.
keyPoints: Anyone planning a pregnancy should be offered counseling, whatever their sexual orientation or gender identity, and whether or not they are using contraception.
Long-term conditions such as diabetes, high blood pressure, mental health conditions and thyroid disease should be well managed before pregnancy.
Counseling can cover use of alcohol, nicotine and drugs, screening for sexually transmitted infections, genetic conditions and intimate partner violence, and the best gap between pregnancies.
Taking folic acid before pregnancy is encouraged to reduce the risk of neural tube defects.

items.title: Preconception care for diabetic women for improving maternal and infant health
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked for good-quality trials testing whether preparing for pregnancy (preconception care) helps women with type 1 or type 2 diabetes and their babies. It found only three small trials, all in adolescent girls with diabetes at US clinics, testing an education programme. None of them reported on the main health outcomes for mothers or babies, so the review could not say whether preconception care improves health. The authors say more high-quality research is needed.
keyPoints: Only three trials (254 adolescent girls with diabetes) were found, with unclear to high risk of bias.
The trials did not report on main outcomes such as birth complications, caesarean section, or birth defects in babies.
One trial found a slightly higher score for starting preconception conversations with healthcare providers, but the result was uncertain.
There is not enough trial evidence to judge the effects of preconception care for women with diabetes on mothers and infants.

items.title: Vitamin D for the Prevention of Disease: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
items.summary: The Endocrine Society reviewed trials of vitamin D given to people without a known need for it, to see whether it lowers disease risk. For pregnant people, it suggests vitamin D supplements because of their potential to lower the risk of pre-eclampsia, stillbirth, preterm birth, small babies and newborn death. It also suggests against routine blood testing of vitamin D in most people, and says the best dose is still unclear.
keyPoints: Vitamin D supplements are suggested in pregnancy because they may lower the risk of preeclampsia, intra-uterine mortality, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth and neonatal mortality.
Vitamin D is also suggested for children aged 1 to 18 (rickets and respiratory infections), adults over 75, and people with high-risk prediabetes.
Routine blood testing of 25(OH)D is not suggested for the general population, including people with obesity or dark skin, because no trial evidence supports it.
The best dose is unclear because the trials used very different doses, and food alone rarely supplies enough, so fortified foods plus supplements can be used.

items.title: Antioxidants and Fertility in Women with Ovarian Aging: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.summary: This review pooled 20 randomized trials with 2617 women who had ovarian aging (a lower number or quality of eggs) and were having fertility treatment. Women who took antioxidant supplements had more eggs retrieved, more high-quality embryos, needed less fertility medication, and had higher clinical pregnancy rates. Coenzyme Q10 appeared to work best, especially in women under 35 with a low egg reserve. The authors describe antioxidants as an effective and safe add-on treatment, with lower doses working better.
keyPoints: Antioxidants increased the number of eggs retrieved and the rate of high-quality embryos, and lowered the dose of fertility medication needed.
Clinical pregnancy rates were higher with antioxidant use.
Coenzyme Q10 tended to work better than melatonin, myo-inositol and vitamins.
The best CoQ10 regimen for pregnancy rate was 30 mg a day for 3 months before the ovarian stimulation cycle, with the clearest benefit in women under 35 with diminished ovarian reserve.

items.title: Vitamin D supplementation for women during pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether taking vitamin D during pregnancy, alone or with calcium and other vitamins, improves health for mothers and babies. After a stricter check of study trustworthiness, only 10 studies remained, so most findings are very uncertain. Vitamin D alone may lower the risk of severe bleeding after birth and of low birthweight, but each of these rests on few studies and the evidence is low quality.
keyPoints: For pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes and preterm birth, the evidence on vitamin D alone is very uncertain.
Vitamin D alone may reduce severe bleeding after birth, but only one study reported this (low-certainty evidence).
Vitamin D alone may reduce low birthweight, but a possible increase in risk cannot be ruled out (low-certainty evidence).
Vitamin D with calcium, or with other vitamins and minerals, gave very uncertain or uncertain results; the authors call for larger, higher-quality trials.

items.title: Daily oral iron supplementation during pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 57 trials with almost 49,000 pregnant women to see what daily iron tablets do during pregnancy. Iron probably or possibly lowers the chance of anaemia and iron deficiency by the end of pregnancy. Babies were probably a little less likely to be born with low birthweight. For most other outcomes there was little or no difference, or the evidence was too uncertain to say.
keyPoints: Daily iron may reduce anaemia (4.0% vs 7.4%) and iron deficiency at term (44% vs 66%), based on low-certainty evidence.
Iron probably reduces iron-deficiency anaemia at term (5.0% vs 18.4%), based on moderate-certainty evidence.
Iron probably lowers the chance of a low-birthweight baby (5.2% vs 6.1%), but there was probably little to no difference in preterm birth.
The evidence on side effects and on severe anaemia was very uncertain, and no trials reported malaria or infection during pregnancy.

items.title: The global prevalence of premature ovarian insufficiency: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from many studies to estimate how common premature ovarian insufficiency (POI, when the ovaries stop working normally before age 40) is around the world. It found that about 3.5% of women are affected. Rates were higher in some groups and regions, and the authors recommend more public awareness and health education about POI.
keyPoints: The global overall prevalence of POI among women was 3.5%.
POI was most common after medical treatment causes (11.2%) and with autoimmune causes (10.5%).
By region, prevalence was highest in North America (11.3%), then South America (5.4%).
It was higher in developing countries (5.3%) than in developed countries (3.1%), and the trend over 20 years was upward, though not statistically significant.

items.title: Anti-Müllerian hormone for the diagnosis and prediction of menopause: a systematic review
items.summary: This review looked at 41 studies (over 28,000 women) to see whether a blood test for anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), which reflects how many egg follicles remain in the ovaries, can help diagnose or predict menopause. Lower AMH for a woman's age was linked with menopause coming earlier, but the test could not pinpoint when menopause would happen, especially in younger women. Very low or undetectable AMH may help spot premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) earlier in young women with a family history or missing periods.
keyPoints: Lower age-specific AMH levels were generally linked with an earlier age at menopause.
AMH alone could not predict age at menopause precisely; estimates for women under 40 ranged from 2 to 12 years.
The test predicted menopause better as women got older and menopause was closer.
Undetectable or extremely low AMH may help with early diagnosis of POI in young women with a family history of POI or with absent periods.

items.title: Hormone replacement therapy for women previously treated for endometrial cancer
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether hormone replacement therapy (HRT) is safe and helpful for women who have been treated for endometrial cancer. Only one trial (1,236 women) could be included, and it closed early, so it was too small to give firm answers. Cancer came back in 2.3% of women taking oestrogen and 1.9% of women taking placebo, a difference that could easily be due to chance. The reviewers say the evidence is very limited and of very low certainty.
keyPoints: Only one randomised trial was found, and it stopped early, so there is not enough high-quality evidence to guide women considering HRT after endometrial cancer.
In that trial, cancer recurrence was 2.3% with oestrogen versus 1.9% with placebo, and new breast cancer was rare in both groups (very low-certainty evidence).
The available evidence, including non-randomised studies, does not suggest significant harm if HRT is used after surgery for early-stage endometrial cancer.
No information exists on HRT after higher-stage (FIGO stage II and above) disease; use should be individualised to a woman's symptoms, preferences and the uncertainty of the evidence.

items.title: Diagnostic accuracy of ultrasound screening for fetal structural abnormalities during the first and second trimester of pregnancy in low-risk and unselected populations
items.summary: This large review pooled 87 studies covering over 7 million pregnancies to see how well ultrasound scans find structural problems in the baby (such as problems with the heart, spine or organs). A scan at 11 to 14 weeks found most lethal problems but only about 4 in 10 problems overall. Having a scan in both the first and second trimesters found more problems than a single second-trimester scan, but this comparison is based on very low-certainty evidence because no studies compared the two approaches directly.
keyPoints: A first-trimester scan found about 91% of lethal anomalies (moderate-certainty evidence) but only about 38% of all structural anomalies (low-certainty evidence).
Scanning in both trimesters found about 84% of structural anomalies, compared with about 51% for a single second-trimester scan.
False alarms were rare with all approaches, roughly 0.1% to 0.2% of pregnancies without an anomaly.
Most of the evidence on first-trimester and two-stage scanning comes from single specialist hospitals, so results may not apply to everyone.

items.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 196: Thromboembolism in Pregnancy
items.summary: This guideline from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists covers blood clots (thromboembolism) in pregnancy. Pregnant and postpartum women have a four to five times higher risk of clots than women who are not pregnant, and most of these clots are in the veins. Clots in the veins are one of the leading causes of maternal death in the United States. The guideline covers risk factors, diagnosis, treatment and prevention, and has been updated on screening for clot risk and on managing blood-thinning medicine around delivery.
keyPoints: Pregnant and postpartum women have a fourfold to fivefold higher risk of thromboembolism than nonpregnant women.
About 80% of clots in pregnancy are venous, affecting 0.5 to 2.0 per 1,000 pregnant women.
Venous thromboembolism accounts for 9.3% of maternal deaths in the United States.
The bulletin covers risk factors, diagnosis, treatment and prevention, including screening for clot risk and anticoagulation around delivery.

items.title: Routine ultrasound in late pregnancy (after 24 weeks' gestation)
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 13 trials with almost 35,000 women to see whether routine ultrasound scans after 24 weeks help women with low-risk or unselected pregnancies. Women who had a routine late scan did not have better outcomes than those who did not. There were no clear differences in baby deaths around birth, preterm birth, induction of labour or caesarean section. Little is known about long-term effects on children or about how the scans affect mothers' emotional wellbeing.
keyPoints: Routine ultrasound after 24 weeks did not improve outcomes for mothers or babies in low-risk or unselected pregnancies.
No difference was found in perinatal death, preterm birth before 37 weeks, induction of labour or caesarean section.
There is little or no data on mothers' psychological effects, preterm birth before 34 weeks, or child neurodevelopment at age two.
The evidence for the main outcomes was rated moderate or high quality.

items.title: Management of preterm labor: Clinical practice guideline and recommendation by the WAPM-World Association of Perinatal Medicine and the PMF-Perinatal Medicine Foundation
items.source: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics, Gynecology, and Reproductive Biology
items.summary: This is a practice guideline from two international perinatal medicine groups on how preterm labor (labor starting too early in pregnancy) should be managed. It aims to help health professionals diagnose preterm labor more accurately. It also covers giving the right treatments at the right time, and avoiding unnecessary or excessive interventions. The abstract does not give specific recommendations or rate the strength of the evidence.
keyPoints: The guideline aims to improve how accurately preterm labor is diagnosed.
It supports timely, appropriate use of tocolytics (medicines that slow contractions), antenatal corticosteroids and magnesium sulphate.
It aims to help avoid unnecessary or excessive interventions.
It is based on expert consensus and the scientific literature, and is not meant to set a legal standard of care.

items.title: Multifetal Gestations: Twin, Triplet, and Higher-Order Multifetal Pregnancies: ACOG Practice Bulletin, Number 231
items.summary: This ACOG practice bulletin reviews twin, triplet and higher-order pregnancies and how they are managed. Multiple pregnancies have become more common over recent decades, linked to women conceiving at older ages and to fertility treatment. Preterm birth is described as one of the most serious complications, and the abstract says that none of the interventions tried so far to prolong these pregnancies has made a substantial difference.
keyPoints: Twin births in the US rose 76% from 1980 to 2009, then fell 4% between 2014 and 2018.
Older maternal age at conception and assisted reproductive technology are the two main reasons multiple pregnancies have become more common.
Multiple pregnancies carry higher risks of fetal anomalies, preeclampsia, gestational diabetes and preterm birth.
Preterm birth is one of the most consequential complications, and no tested intervention has substantially prolonged these pregnancies.

items.title: Antenatal corticosteroids for accelerating fetal lung maturation for women at risk of preterm birth
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 27 trials (over 11,000 women) of steroid injections given before an expected preterm birth to help the baby's lungs mature. Babies of women who received a single course were less likely to die around the time of birth or to develop breathing problems (respiratory distress syndrome). The steroids probably also lowered the risk of bleeding in the baby's brain and of developmental delay in childhood. The review found little to no difference in serious maternal outcomes such as infection of the womb lining, though the evidence there is less precise.
keyPoints: Antenatal corticosteroids reduced perinatal death (about 15% lower risk) and neonatal death (about 22% lower risk), based on high-certainty evidence.
They reduced respiratory distress syndrome in newborns by about 29%, also high-certainty evidence.
They probably reduce bleeding in the baby's brain (IVH) and developmental delay in childhood, with moderate-certainty evidence.
There was probably little to no difference in maternal death, chorioamnionitis or endometritis, but the wide margins of error leave possible benefit or harm open.

items.title: Antibiotics for asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at 15 trials with over 2000 pregnant women who had a urine infection with no symptoms (asymptomatic bacteriuria). Women given antibiotics may have fewer kidney infections (pyelonephritis), fewer preterm births and fewer low birthweight babies than those given a placebo or no treatment. However, the evidence was low certainty, because most of the trials had problems in how they were done, so confidence in these results is limited.
keyPoints: Antibiotics may reduce the risk of kidney infection (pyelonephritis) in pregnancy; this was low-certainty evidence.
Antibiotics may reduce preterm birth and low birthweight babies, also based on low-certainty evidence.
Results were inconclusive for serious newborn problems, and side effects for mothers were rarely described.
Only one of the 15 trials was at low risk of bias; more research is needed on who is most likely to benefit.

items.title: Progestin-only contraception and thrombosis: An updated systematic review
items.summary: This review pulled together 33 studies on whether progestin-only birth control is linked to blood clots. The DMPA injection (Depo-Provera) was generally linked to a higher risk of clots in the veins (VTE), but not clots in the arteries such as heart attack or stroke. Other progestin-only methods, including hormonal coils (levonorgestrel IUDs), implants and progestin-only pills, did not generally show a higher risk. The certainty of the evidence was low or very low, so these findings are uncertain.
keyPoints: Risk of vein clots (VTE) was generally higher with DMPA than with no use, both in the general population and in women with conditions linked to clotting.
DMPA was not generally linked to arterial clots such as heart attack or stroke.
Levonorgestrel IUDs, implants and progestin-only pills were generally not linked to higher clot risk.
Evidence was limited for many individual conditions, and certainty was low or very low for all outcomes.

items.title: Gynecologic Considerations for Adolescents and Young Women With Cardiac Conditions: ACOG Committee Opinion Summary, Number 813
items.summary: This ACOG guidance looks at birth control and pregnancy planning for teenagers and young women who have heart conditions. Because pregnancy can carry serious health risks for people with heart disease, it advises that starting birth control should not be put off over safety worries. For some heart conditions, a progestin-only method is a reasonable starting choice while the safety of estrogen-containing methods is checked with the patient's heart doctor.
keyPoints: Starting contraception should not be delayed because of worries about possible contraindications, since pregnancy can cause serious health problems in people with heart conditions.
For valvular heart disease, cardiomyopathy or hypertension, it is reasonable to start a progestin-only method until an estrogen-containing method is confirmed safe with the patient's cardiologist.
Contraceptive counseling should be patient-centered, free of coercion, and suited to the person's age and health literacy.
Future pregnancies should be planned with maternal-fetal medicine and cardiology specialists, and anyone continuing a pregnancy should be referred to a pregnancy heart team.

items.title: Maternal sleep during pregnancy and adverse pregnancy outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 41 studies to see whether how long pregnant women sleep is linked to pregnancy complications. Women who slept for a short time had a higher risk of gestational diabetes, and long sleep was also linked to gestational diabetes and caesarean birth. Short or long sleep was not clearly linked to high blood pressure in pregnancy, preterm birth, low birthweight or small babies. These studies show an association, which does not prove that sleep itself causes these outcomes.
keyPoints: Short sleep in pregnancy was linked to about 1.8 times the risk of gestational diabetes.
Long sleep was also linked to a higher risk of gestational diabetes and of caesarean section.
No significant link was found between short or long sleep and gestational hypertension, preterm birth, low birthweight or small for gestational age.
The authors suggest sleep should be routinely screened in pregnancy care.

items.title: Association of Supine Going-to-Sleep Position in Late Pregnancy With Reduced Birth Weight: A Secondary Analysis of an Individual Participant Data Meta-analysis
items.summary: This study looked at 1,760 women in late pregnancy (28 weeks or more) and asked which position they usually went to sleep in. Babies born to the 57 women who usually went to sleep on their back were about 144 g lighter on average than babies of women who did not. Going to sleep on the back was also linked to a higher chance of the baby being small for gestational age by one growth standard. The authors say the link is plausible and could be changed, but this type of study shows an association, not proof of cause.
keyPoints: Women who usually went to sleep on their back in the last 1 to 4 weeks had babies about 144 g lighter on average (3410 g vs 3554 g).

Going to sleep on the back was linked to about a 3-fold higher chance of a small-for-gestational-age baby by INTERGROWTH-21st standards, but the result was not statistically significant by customized standards.
Only 3.2% of the women reported usually going to sleep on their back.
The authors suggest encouraging women in the third trimester to settle to sleep on their side could help optimise birth weight.

items.title: Do psychosocial sleep interventions improve infant sleep or maternal mood in the postnatal period? A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
items.summary: This review pooled nine trials (1,656 mothers) of sleep-focused support programs offered to new parents. Mothers reported their babies slept a little longer at night after these programs, but the babies still woke up just as often. Mothers' mood improved slightly, but this result may have been affected by publication bias, so it needs more research to confirm.
keyPoints: Sleep-focused programs were linked to a small increase in the amount of night-time sleep mothers reported for their babies.
There was no clear evidence that the programs reduced how often babies woke at night.
Maternal mood improved slightly, but this finding could be influenced by publication bias.
More research is needed to know whether better infant sleep leads to better maternal mood.

items.title: Interventions for Tobacco Smoking Cessation in Adults, Including Pregnant Persons: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
items.summary: The US Preventive Services Task Force reviewed the evidence on ways to help adults, including pregnant people, stop smoking. It found with high certainty that behavioural support, such as counselling, helps pregnant people quit and improves pregnancy outcomes. There was not enough evidence to judge whether stop-smoking medicines or e-cigarettes are safe and helpful for quitting during pregnancy.
keyPoints: Smoking in pregnancy raises the risk of miscarriage, birth defects, sudden infant death syndrome and weaker lung function in childhood.
Behavioural support to quit smoking has a substantial benefit for pregnant people, with high certainty.
Evidence on stop-smoking medicines in pregnancy is insufficient because few studies exist, so benefits and harms cannot be balanced.
Evidence on e-cigarettes as a way to quit is insufficient for adults, including pregnant people, because well-designed trials are missing.

items.title: Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines, 2021
items.summary: This is the CDC's updated guideline on how to treat and prevent sexually transmitted infections (STIs), replacing the 2015 version. It was updated after experts met in 2019. It covers changes to treatment for gonorrhea, chlamydia and trichomoniasis, plus pelvic inflammatory disease, bacterial vaginosis and other infections. It is written to help health care providers, and the abstract does not rate how strong the evidence is.
keyPoints: Treatment recommendations were updated for gonorrhea, chlamydia and trichomoniasis.
Metronidazole was added to the recommended treatment for pelvic inflammatory disease, and there are new alternative options for bacterial vaginosis.
More risk factors now count for syphilis testing in pregnant women, and one-time testing for hepatitis C is recommended.
The guideline also updates advice on HPV vaccination, Mycoplasma genitalium, and two-step blood testing for genital herpes.

items.title: Population-level impact and herd effects following the introduction of human papillomavirus vaccination programmes: updated systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: This review pooled results from 65 studies in 14 high-income countries, covering about 60 million people, to see what happened after HPV vaccination programmes began. Within 5-9 years, HPV infections, genital warts and precancerous cervical changes (CIN2+) all dropped, especially in girls and young women. Genital warts also fell in boys and men, which points to a 'herd effect' (protection spreading beyond those vaccinated). Programmes that vaccinated several age groups and reached more people had bigger effects.
keyPoints: After 5-8 years of vaccination, HPV 16 and 18 infections fell by 83% in girls aged 13-19 and by 66% in women aged 20-24.
Genital wart diagnoses fell by 67% in girls aged 15-19, and also fell in boys aged 15-19 (48%) and men aged 20-24 (32%).
Precancerous cervical changes (CIN2+) fell by 51% in screened girls aged 15-19 and by 31% in women aged 20-24 after 5-9 years.
Programmes with multi-age vaccination and high coverage had greater direct and herd effects.

items.title: School-based interventions for preventing HIV, sexually transmitted infections, and pregnancy in adolescents
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at eight large trials (over 55,000 students) of school programmes meant to prevent HIV, other sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and teenage pregnancy. Classroom sex education programmes on their own did not show a clear effect on HIV, herpes, syphilis or pregnancy. Programmes that gave cash payments to keep girls in school may have lowered herpes infection and pregnancy, but the evidence is limited and more trials are needed.
keyPoints: Education-only school programmes showed no clear effect on HIV, herpes, syphilis or the number of young women who were pregnant.
Monthly cash incentives to stay in school were linked to lower herpes infection and fewer pregnancies in young women, based on low or very low certainty evidence.
Free school uniforms alone did not show a clear herpes benefit, but uniforms combined with sexual health education reduced herpes infection in one trial (low certainty).
The authors say adolescents still need services that include contraceptive choices and condoms, and that schools may be a good place to offer them.

items.title: Congenital Hypothyroidism: A 2020-2021 Consensus Guidelines Update-An ENDO-European Reference Network Initiative Endorsed by the European Society for Pediatric Endocrinology and the European Society for Endocrinology
items.summary: This is an updated set of European expert guidelines on congenital hypothyroidism, a condition where a baby is born with an underactive thyroid. The experts reviewed the research on newborn screening, diagnosis and treatment. They recommend starting the right dose of levothyroxine (thyroid hormone medicine) straight away once the condition is found, with regular follow-up checks.
keyPoints: Newborn screening helps find congenital hypothyroidism early, and the guidelines support its benefits.
Once diagnosed, treatment with correctly dosed levothyroxine should start immediately.
Frequent follow-up and blood tests keep thyroid hormone levels in the target range, with attention to brain development and senses such as hearing and vision.
People with the condition should have a well-planned move from children's to adult care.

items.title: 2016 American Thyroid Association Guidelines for Diagnosis and Management of Hyperthyroidism and Other Causes of Thyrotoxicosis
items.summary: The American Thyroid Association updated its 2011 guidelines on diagnosing and treating an overactive thyroid (hyperthyroidism) and other causes of too much thyroid hormone (thyrotoxicosis). An expert panel reviewed the research and rated how strong each recommendation is and how good the evidence behind it is. The guideline covers treatment options such as radioactive iodine, antithyroid medicines and surgery, and includes advice for pregnant patients, children and teenagers.
keyPoints: The guideline gives 124 evidence-based recommendations for caring for people with thyrotoxicosis.
It covers Graves' disease treatment with radioactive iodine, antithyroid drugs or surgery, and treatment of toxic nodules and goiter.
It includes updated advice on managing hyperthyroidism in pregnancy, as well as in children, adolescents and people with Graves' eye disease.
Choosing a treatment depends on the exact cause, other health conditions and patient preference.

items.title: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy: ACOG Practice Bulletin, Number 223
items.summary: This is a clinical guideline from ACOG, a major US group of obstetricians and gynecologists, on thyroid disease in pregnancy. It explains that both an overactive thyroid (thyrotoxicosis) and an underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism) are linked to poorer pregnancy outcomes. It also notes concern about how overt thyroid disease in the mother may affect the baby's development, and that some thyroid medicines can cross the placenta and reach the baby's thyroid. The updated guidance covers how thyroid disease is diagnosed and managed in pregnancy, and adds a new management flowchart.
keyPoints: Both overactive and underactive thyroid are linked to adverse pregnancy outcomes.
Overt maternal thyroid disease raises concern about fetal development.
Medicines that act on the mother's thyroid can cross the placenta and affect the baby's thyroid.
The updated bulletin covers diagnosis and management and includes a new clinical algorithm.

items.title: Thyroxine replacement for subfertile women with euthyroid autoimmune thyroid disease or subclinical hypothyroidism
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether levothyroxine (thyroid hormone) helps women having fertility treatment who have mildly underactive thyroid (subclinical hypothyroidism) or thyroid antibodies with normal thyroid levels. It combined four trials with 820 women. In women with thyroid antibodies but normal thyroid function, thyroxine made little difference to live birth or miscarriage rates. The evidence was low or very low quality, so the authors could draw no clear conclusions.
keyPoints: In women with subclinical hypothyroidism, one small trial (64 women) suggested thyroxine may improve live birth rates, but the evidence was low quality.
In women with thyroid antibodies and normal thyroid function, thyroxine may make little difference to live birth or miscarriage rates (two trials, 686 women, low-quality evidence).
Side effects and pregnancy complications were rarely reported, and preterm births were similar between groups where they were reported.
The authors could draw no clear conclusions because the evidence was of very low to low quality.

items.title: Screening and subsequent management for thyroid dysfunction pre-pregnancy and during pregnancy for improving maternal and infant health
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether testing all pregnant women for thyroid problems, instead of only those thought to be at higher risk or no one, leads to better health for mothers and babies. Two large trials (26,408 women) were included. Testing everyone found and treated more women with an underactive thyroid, but it did not clearly change rates of pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, miscarriage, or children's IQ at age three. The authors say more research is needed.
keyPoints: Testing all pregnant women found about three times as many cases of underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism) as testing only higher-risk women, and more women received thyroid medication.
