No clear differences were seen in pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, miscarriage, or fetal and newborn death between screening approaches.
Screening everyone for hypothyroidism did not clearly change the chance of a child having an IQ below 85 at three years.
Data were missing for several outcomes, including side effects of screening and treatment, so more trials are needed.

items.title: Updates to Recurrent Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infections in Women: AUA/CUA/SUFU Guideline (2025)
items.summary: This is a 2025 update to a urology guideline on women who get repeat urinary tract infections (UTIs) that are not caused by other health problems. It aims to cut unneeded antibiotic use, lower antibiotic resistance and side effects, and improve women's quality of life. The update adds more non-antibiotic options for preventing UTIs and shows that a negative urine test can help rule out a UTI. It also shifts away from relying on germ detection alone toward a clinician's judgement about the risks and benefits of antibiotics for each woman.
keyPoints: There are now more non-antibiotic options to help prevent repeat UTIs.
A negative urinalysis (urine test) is better understood as a way to rule out a UTI.
Decisions about antibiotics rely less on detecting germs and more on a clinician weighing each woman's individual risks and benefits.
The guideline aims to reduce inappropriate antibiotic use, antibiotic resistance and antibiotic side effects.

items.title: Cranberries for preventing urinary tract infections
items.summary: This Cochrane review combined 50 trials with nearly 9,000 people to see whether cranberry products help prevent urinary tract infections (UTIs). Overall, cranberry products reduced the risk of symptomatic UTIs confirmed by a lab test. The benefit was seen in women who get repeat UTIs, in children, and in people prone to UTIs after a medical procedure. There was little or no benefit shown in pregnant women, older people living in care homes, or adults with bladder-emptying problems, though the evidence for these groups was low certainty.
keyPoints: Cranberry products reduced the risk of symptomatic, lab-confirmed UTIs overall (moderate certainty evidence).
Cranberry probably reduced UTIs in women with recurrent UTIs, in children, and in people prone to UTIs after a medical intervention.
There may be little or no benefit in pregnant women, elderly people in care, or adults with neuromuscular bladder problems (low certainty evidence).
Compared with antibiotics, cranberry may make little or no difference; stomach side effects probably did not differ from placebo or no treatment.

items.title: Prevention and Control of Seasonal Influenza with Vaccines: Recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices - United States, 2025-26 Influenza Season
items.source: MMWR. Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
items.journal: MMWR. Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report
items.summary: This US report sets out the 2025-26 flu vaccine recommendations from the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices. It recommends a yearly flu vaccine for everyone aged 6 months and older who has no reason to avoid it. A new recommendation for the 2025-26 season is that children up to age 18, pregnant women and all adults receive only single-dose flu vaccines that are free of the preservative thimerosal.
keyPoints: Yearly flu vaccination is recommended for everyone aged 6 months and older without a contraindication.
New for 2025-26: children aged 18 or under, pregnant women and all adults should receive only single-dose vaccines free of thimerosal as a preservative.
Several vaccine types are expected to be available, including inactivated, recombinant and live attenuated (nasal) vaccines.
The report also notes the approval of FluMist for self- or caregiver administration and Flublok for ages 9 and up.

items.title: Respiratory syncytial virus vaccination during pregnancy for improving infant outcomes
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled six trials with nearly 18,000 pregnant women to see whether an RSV vaccine given in pregnancy protects babies. RSV is a common virus that can cause serious chest infections in infants. The vaccine roughly halved the number of babies hospitalised with lab-confirmed RSV. It had little or no effect on birth defects or poor growth in the womb, but there may be a small signal for more preterm births that needs further study.
keyPoints: Maternal RSV vaccination reduced infant hospitalisation with lab-confirmed RSV disease (about 11 fewer per 1000 infants), based on high-certainty evidence.
There was little or no effect on congenital abnormalities (high certainty) and likely little or no effect on poor growth in the womb (moderate certainty).
Preterm birth may be somewhat more likely after vaccination (8 more per 1000 infants), but the evidence is very uncertain and needs further investigation.
Evidence on stillbirth, maternal death and infant death is low or very low certainty, with little or no effect seen so far.

items.title: COVID-19 vaccine and pregnancy outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.source: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.journal: International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
items.summary: This review pooled results from observational studies that compared pregnant women who had a COVID-19 vaccine with those who did not. Babies of vaccinated women were no more likely to be smaller than expected for their age in the womb. Vaccinated women also had a slightly lower rate of premature delivery and fewer cases of non-reassuring fetal monitoring.
keyPoints: No difference was found in the chance of having a baby small for gestational age between vaccinated and unvaccinated pregnant women.
Vaccinated pregnant women had a slightly reduced rate of premature delivery.
Vaccinated women also had a reduced chance of non-reassuring fetal monitoring.
The studies reviewed were observational, not randomised trials.

items.title: Prevention of Pertussis, Tetanus, and Diphtheria with Vaccines in the United States: Recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP)
items.summary: This report pulls together the US vaccine advisory committee's existing advice on preventing whooping cough (pertussis), tetanus and diphtheria. It adds no new recommendations. For pregnancy, it advises a dose of the Tdap vaccine in every pregnancy, given between 27 and 36 weeks, even if the woman has had Tdap before.
keyPoints: Women are recommended to receive one dose of Tdap during each pregnancy.
The dose should be given from 27 through 36 weeks of pregnancy, whether or not Tdap was received before.
Babies and young children are recommended to have a 5-dose DTaP series, and adolescents one Tdap booster.
Adults who have never had Tdap are recommended to get one booster, then a Td booster every 10 years.

items.title: Prophylactic vaccination against human papillomaviruses to prevent cervical cancer and its precursors
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 26 trials (about 73,000 girls and women) to see whether HPV vaccines protect against cervical precancer and whether they are safe. In girls and young women aged 15 to 26, the vaccines clearly lowered the risk of precancerous changes, especially those caused by HPV types 16 and 18. Serious side effects were no more common than with placebo, and the trials did not show a higher risk of miscarriage. The trials were too short to measure actual cervical cancer, and long-term follow-up is still needed.
keyPoints: High-certainty evidence that HPV vaccines protect against cervical precancer in girls and women aged 15 to 26, with the biggest effect for HPV16/18-related lesions.
Protection was greater in those not already infected with high-risk HPV when vaccinated.
In women vaccinated at 24 to 45, there was no clear difference in precancer between vaccinated and unvaccinated women overall.

Serious adverse events were similar between vaccine and control groups (high certainty), and miscarriage risk was similar (high certainty); effects on congenital abnormalities and stillbirth remain uncertain.

items.title: Treatment for recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis (thrush)
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at treatments for recurrent thrush (four or more symptomatic episodes in a year) in 23 small trials involving 2212 women. Antifungal treatment, taken by mouth or applied to the vagina, may reduce how often thrush comes back compared with placebo or no treatment. The evidence is low quality, and it is very uncertain whether tablets work better than topical treatments. The findings do not apply to pregnant women, women with diabetes or women with weakened immune systems, as these groups were mostly left out of the studies.
keyPoints: Oral or topical antifungals may reduce symptomatic recurrences of thrush at 6 and 12 months compared with placebo or no treatment (low-certainty evidence).
No clear difference was found between oral and topical treatment, or between different doses and treatment lengths (very low-certainty evidence).
Side effects were uncommon in both treatment and placebo groups, though they were poorly reported.
The results do not apply to pregnant or immunocompromised women or women with diabetes, and more research is needed on the best medicine, dose and frequency.

items.title: Guideline: Vulvovaginal candidosis (AWMF 015/072, level S2k)
items.summary: This German clinical guideline sets out how vaginal thrush (vulvovaginal candidosis) should be diagnosed and treated. About 70-75% of women get thrush at least once, and symptoms alone cannot reliably tell thrush apart from other causes of vaginitis, so the diagnosis should be confirmed before treatment. Common antifungal creams, vaginal tablets and oral tablets are generally well tolerated and work similarly well. Women without symptoms, and their partners, should not be treated.
keyPoints: Diagnosis should rest on symptoms plus seeing the yeast under a microscope, and be confirmed by a clinician before treatment starts.
Acute thrush can be treated with local antifungals (vaginal tablets, ovules or creams) or oral triazole tablets, and the different regimens give similarly good results.
Women with repeated Candida albicans thrush should have long-term, lower-dose maintenance treatment with oral triazoles.
In the last 6 weeks of pregnancy, antifungal treatment is advised to lower the chance of passing thrush to the baby, and local treatment is preferred in pregnancy.

items.title: Global burden of recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis: a systematic review
items.summary: This review pooled eight population-based studies from 11 countries (over 17,000 women) to estimate how common recurrent thrush is, meaning four or more episodes in a year. It found that about 138 million women worldwide are affected each year, and around 372 million over a lifetime. Rates were highest in women aged 25 to 34. The authors say affected women need better care and better treatment options.
keyPoints: Recurrent thrush (four or more episodes a year) affects about 138 million women worldwide each year.
About 372 million women are estimated to be affected at some point in their lives.
The 25 to 34 age group has the highest rate, at about 9%.
The number of affected women is expected to rise to almost 158 million a year by 2030.

items.title: Oral vitamin B12 versus intramuscular vitamin B12 for vitamin B12 deficiency
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at whether vitamin B12 tablets work as well as B12 injections into the muscle for people with low B12. It found only three small trials with 153 people in total. The evidence was low quality, but B12 levels rose similarly with both routes, and the tablets cost less. The trials did not report on symptoms or quality of life.
keyPoints: Low-quality evidence suggests oral and injected B12 raise blood B12 levels in a similar way.
Oral B12 cost less than injections in one trial, though this evidence was also low quality.
Very low-quality evidence suggests oral B12 appears as safe as injections.
No trial reported on symptoms of deficiency, quality of life, or how acceptable patients found the treatment.

items.title: 2024 Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia guideline for osteoporosis management and fracture prevention in postmenopausal women and men over 50 years of age
items.source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia
items.organisation: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia
items.summary: This is an updated Australian guideline on keeping bones strong and preventing broken bones in women after menopause and in men over 50. It encourages earlier spotting of poor bone health using personal risk factors and a fracture risk tool called FRAX. It says calcium and vitamin D supplements work better at reducing fracture risk in people who are actually low in these nutrients, rather than in healthy people living independently.
keyPoints: Earlier recognition of poor bone health is encouraged, using clinical risk factors and an absolute fracture risk tool such as FRAX.
Widespread population-based osteoporosis screening is not recommended in Australia because there is not enough evidence to support it.
Calcium and vitamin D supplements are more effective at reducing fracture risk in people with calcium and vitamin D deficiency, not in healthy people living in the community.
People at imminent or very high fracture risk are a group in whom early bone-building (osteoanabolic) treatment can be considered.

items.title: Population-based interventions for preventing falls and fall-related injuries in older people
items.summary: This Cochrane review looked at community-wide programmes meant to prevent falls and fall-related injuries in older adults, including offering free calcium and vitamin D3 supplements. Nine studies were included, but the evidence was very low quality, so the authors could not say whether these programmes work. One study found fewer fall-related hospital admissions among women offered calcium and vitamin D3, but the authors were unsure of this result.
keyPoints: Nine studies of community-wide falls prevention programmes were included, covering communities of between about 1,200 and 172,500 people.
In one trial, women offered free calcium and vitamin D3 had fewer fall-related hospital admissions, with no difference seen for men, but this finding was very low certainty.
The review found it uncertain whether community-wide multicomponent programmes (such as exercise, home changes and education) reduce falls or injuries.
The authors call for better-designed, larger trials, and no studies reported adverse events.

items.title: Clinical practice guidelines for vitamin D in the United Arab Emirates
items.source: Journal of Steroid Biochemistry and Molecular Biology
items.journal: Journal of Steroid Biochemistry and Molecular Biology
items.summary: This guideline looks at vitamin D deficiency in the United Arab Emirates and wider Gulf region, where it is very common. Hot weather, covering up, diet and low activity all make low vitamin D more likely. The authors reviewed published research and suggest daily vitamin D amounts for different groups, including babies, children, adults, older people, and women who are pregnant or breastfeeding.
keyPoints: For pregnant and breastfeeding women, 2000 IU of vitamin D per day is recommended, starting from the first trimester.
Breastfed babies are advised 400 IU/day up to 6 months, then 400-600 IU/day from 6 to 12 months, depending on diet and sun exposure.
Adults over 18 are advised 1000-2000 IU/day, and people over 65 are advised 2000 IU/day, all year round.
The aim of supplementing is to reach and keep a blood vitamin D level (25(OH)D) of 30-50 ng/mL.

items.title: Effects of vitamin D in pregnancy on maternal and offspring health-related outcomes: An umbrella review of systematic review and meta-analyses
items.summary: This review pulled together 16 earlier systematic reviews and meta-analyses, covering about 250,000 women, on vitamin D in pregnancy. Low vitamin D was linked with higher risks of preterm birth, smaller babies, recurrent miscarriage, bacterial vaginosis and gestational diabetes. Taking vitamin D supplements in pregnancy was linked with higher birth weight and lower risks of pre-eclampsia, miscarriage and some childhood conditions. The authors suggest vitamin D levels be monitored, especially in women at high risk of deficiency.
keyPoints: Vitamin D deficiency in pregnancy was associated with preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age or low birth weight babies, recurrent miscarriage, bacterial vaginosis and gestational diabetes.
Vitamin D supplements in pregnancy were linked with higher birth weight and lower risks of pre-eclampsia, miscarriage, fetal or newborn death, and ADHD and autism spectrum disorder in childhood.
In women with gestational diabetes, supplements were linked with lower risks of macrosomia (a very large baby), fetal distress, polyhydramnios and neonatal hospitalization.
The authors suggest vitamin D status be monitored in pregnancy, and that a dose above 400 IU/day may help prevent certain adverse outcomes.

items.title: Vitamin D supplementation for term breastfed infants to prevent vitamin D deficiency and improve bone health
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 19 trials (2,837 mother-baby pairs) to see whether vitamin D given to breastfed babies, or to breastfeeding mothers, helps prevent low vitamin D and supports bone health. Giving babies 400 IU a day raised their vitamin D levels and lowered the chance of vitamin D insufficiency. Giving vitamin D to breastfeeding mothers also raised babies' levels, but only in groups already at high risk of deficiency. The evidence was low to very low certainty, and there was not enough evidence to say whether either approach improves bone health or prevents rickets.
keyPoints: Vitamin D at 400 IU a day for breastfed babies, for up to six months, raised their vitamin D levels and reduced vitamin D insufficiency.
Vitamin D given to breastfeeding mothers raised their babies' vitamin D levels and lowered insufficiency and deficiency, but all these studies were in high-risk populations.
Direct supplements for babies raised infant vitamin D levels more than supplements for mothers did, though the evidence was very uncertain.
There was not enough evidence on bone strength, rickets or side effects such as high blood calcium; certainty was low to very low for all outcomes.

items.title: The efficacy and safety of GLP-1 agonists in PCOS women living with obesity in promoting weight loss and hormonal regulation: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.source: Journal of Diabetes and Its Complications
items.journal: Journal of Diabetes and Its Complications
items.summary: This review pooled results from four randomized trials (176 women) of GLP-1 medicines, such as semaglutide and liraglutide, in women with PCOS who live with obesity. Compared with placebo, the medicines were linked to lower BMI, smaller waist size, lower triglycerides and lower testosterone. They made no clear difference to total cholesterol or insulin resistance (HOMA-IR). Where side effects were reported, 49 of 112 women had mild ones such as nausea and abdominal pain. The number of studies and women was small.
keyPoints: GLP-1 medicines lowered BMI by about 2.4 points and waist size by about 5 cm compared with placebo.
Triglycerides and total testosterone levels were also lower with the medicines.
There was no significant difference in total cholesterol or insulin resistance (HOMA-IR).
Of 112 women with side effect data, 49 had mild effects like nausea and abdominal pain.

items.title: Conservative interventions for treating urinary incontinence in women: an Overview of Cochrane systematic reviews
items.summary: This overview pulled together 29 Cochrane reviews (112 trials, about 9,000 women) on non-surgical treatments for urinary leaks in women. Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) was better than no treatment for all types of leaking, for cure or improvement and for quality of life. Weight loss also led to more cure and improvement than no treatment in women with any type of urinary incontinence. The authors note that most of the evidence inside the reviews is of low certainty.
keyPoints: There is high certainty that pelvic floor muscle training works better than no treatment for all types of urinary incontinence, for both cure or improvement and quality of life.
Training that is more intense, more frequent or individually supervised probably works better (moderate certainty).
Weight loss gave more cure and improvement than no treatment for women with any type of urinary incontinence.
Electrical stimulation helped women with urgency leaks, and cones helped women with stress leaks (cones were better than no treatment, but not better than PFMT).

items.title: Lipid-based nutrient supplements for maternal, birth, and infant developmental outcomes
items.summary: This review looked at lipid-based nutrient supplements (nutrient-rich ready-to-use pastes) taken in pregnancy, using four trials with about 8,000 women in lower-income countries. Compared with standard iron and folic acid tablets, the supplements made little or no difference to weekly weight gain in pregnancy. Babies in the supplement groups were slightly heavier and longer at birth, but women had more anaemia than with iron-folic acid or multiple micronutrient tablets. The authors say the effects are small and the results should be read with caution.
keyPoints: Weekly weight gain in pregnancy was no different with the supplements than with iron-folic acid tablets or multiple micronutrient tablets.

Compared with iron-folic acid, the supplements were linked to slightly higher birth weight (about 53 g) and birth length (about 0.24 cm), and fewer small-for-gestational-age babies and stunted newborns.
Supplements were similar to multiple micronutrient tablets for all maternal, birth and infant outcomes studied.
Iron-folic acid and multiple micronutrients were better than the supplements at reducing maternal anaemia.

items.title: No. 367-2019 Canadian Guideline for Physical Activity throughout Pregnancy
items.source: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.journal: Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Canada
items.summary: This Canadian guideline looked at research on exercise during pregnancy. It found that staying physically active in pregnancy brings moderate benefits, including less excessive weight gain, and no harms were identified. Most pregnant women without medical reasons to avoid exercise can take part, and the guideline says to do what you can on days when tiredness or discomfort get in the way. The quality of evidence varied across the recommendations, from very low to higher.
keyPoints: Physical activity in pregnancy is linked to less excessive gestational weight gain and lower total weight gain.
It is also linked to lower risk of gestational diabetes, preeclampsia, gestational hypertension, Caesarean section and depression, and to fewer large-for-gestational-age babies.
Exercise was not linked to miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth, low birth weight or birth defects.
Women not yet active are advised to build up gradually, and those with certain medical conditions should talk to their obstetric care provider first.

items.title: Diet or exercise, or both, for preventing excessive weight gain in pregnancy
items.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 65 trials (49 with usable data, about 11,400 women) testing diet, exercise, or both to prevent too much weight gain in pregnancy. These approaches lowered the chance of gaining more weight than recommended by about 20%, and the reviewers rated this as high-quality evidence. There were possible extra benefits for some outcomes, especially for women at higher risk, but several results were uncertain or based on limited evidence.
keyPoints: Diet, exercise, or both reduced the risk of excessive weight gain in pregnancy by about 20% (high-quality evidence).
Low glycaemic load diets, exercise alone, and diet plus exercise all gave similar reductions.
Women in the programmes were slightly more likely to gain less weight than recommended (moderate-quality evidence).

There was no clear difference in pre-eclampsia, caesarean birth, preterm birth, or large babies overall, though combined diet and exercise helped higher-risk women with large babies and baby breathing problems.
